23 – 26 October 2023
Tbilisi, Georgia
Provisional agenda item 12 2 October 2023
Consideration of funding proposals –
Addendum VI
Funding proposal package for FP215
Summary
This addendum contains the following seven parts:
a) A funding proposal titled "Community Resilience Partnership Program";
b) No-objection letter issued by the national designated authority(ies) or focal
point(s);
c) Environmental and social report(s) disclosure;
d) Secretariat’s assessment;
e) Independent Technical Advisory Panel’s assessment;
f) Response from the accredited entity to the independent Technical Advisory Panel's
assessment; and
g) Gender documentation.

Note to Accredited Entities on the use of the funding proposal template
• Accredited Entities should provide summary information in the proposal with cross-
reference to annexes such as feasibility studies, gender action plan, term sheet, etc.
• Accredited Entities should ensure that annexes provided are consistent with the details
provided in the funding proposal. Updates to the funding proposal and/or annexes must be
reflected in all relevant documents.
• The total number of pages for the funding proposal (excluding annexes) should not
exceed 60. Proposals exceeding the prescribed length will not be assessed within the usual
service standard time.
• The recommended font is Arial, size 11.
• Under the GCF Information Disclosure Policy, project and programme funding proposals
will be disclosed on the GCF website, simultaneous with the submission to the Board,
subject to the redaction of any information that may not be disclosed pursuant to the IDP.
Accredited Entities are asked to fill out information on disclosure in section G.4.
Please submit the completed proposal to:
fundingproposal@gcfund.org
Please use the following name convention for the file name:
FP-ADB-Regional-2022/08/05

A.21. Executive summary
1. Climate Change Context
Increasing climate shocks and stresses in Asia and the Pacific region require local adaptation
solutions that deliver at scale. Evidence indicates that the impacts of heat waves, sea-level rise and
storm surges, changes in rainfall patterns, and increases in the intensity and frequency of extreme
weather events are already affecting the livelihoods, food security and nutrition, water security and health
of millions of people in the region, including the populations of Cambodia, Indonesia, Lao People’s
Democratic Republic (Lao PDR), Pakistan, Papua New Guinea (PNG), Timor Leste, and Vanuatu.3
Looking ahead, climate change is projected to increase climate risk with changes in the frequency,
intensity, extent, duration, and timing of extreme weather events, including unprecedented extremes,
and alteration of trends and shifts in the long-term average climate (see Box 1 in section B1).
Assessments shows that climate risk is likely to intensify and occur both sooner and at a larger scale
than previously assessed. Estimates for the Asia and the Pacific region show that growth will be
significantly impacted by climate change. Without climate action, the gross domestic product (GDP) in
the region could decrease by as much as 3.3 per cent by 2050 and 10 per cent by 2100, relative to the
base case.1 There is thus a clear and immediate need for adaptation solutions in the region that can be
implemented at scale. Moreover, the adverse impacts of climate change are manifested largely at the
local level due to the local socioeconomic, geographical, ecological, institutional and governance
characteristics. Hence, the need for local adaptation solutions that are tailored to the specific physical
and socioeconomic characteristics of local contexts.
Poor and vulnerable populations face the brunt of climate impacts and require targeted
adaptation solutions. Estimates suggest that climate change could push more than 100 million people
in developing countries below the poverty line by 2030, with Asia and the Pacific being one of the main
hotspots.2 This would undermine the progress in poverty reduction in the region and pose a threat to
achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The poor and vulnerable are affected
disproportionately (in relative terms) because of high levels of exposure and vulnerability (due to their
sources of livelihoods, incomes, and location) and low adaptive capacity (the adaptation and poverty
nexus).3 These populations have limited access to climate information, are often left out from formal
decision-making processes, and have limited knowledge and financial capacity to undertake adaptation
solutions. Thus, their local needs and priorities for adaptation often remain unmet. Women and men are
impacted differently, with women typically having lower levels of adaptive capacity than men due to
pre-existing gender inequalities dictated by cultural norms, and different roles and responsibilities at the
household and community levels.4 For these reasons adaptation solutions that are explicitly targeted
at poor and vulnerable people are required, with specific provisions for their empowerment, especially
of women.5 The pandemic due to coronavirus disease (COVID-19) has reinforced these inequalities, as
it is having a disproportionate impact on the poor and especially poor women, who are already burdened
with the ill-effects of climate shocks and stresses. Estimates suggest that severe long-term effects of this
pandemic could push an additional 78 million people into extreme poverty (under USD1.90 per day) in
developing Asia.6
Climate finance plays a critical role in facilitating transformational adaptation among the poor
and the vulnerable. Climate finance plays a key role in supporting adaptation solutions that improve the
well-being of the poorest. However, at present less than USD1 in every USD10 of climate finance
committed from dedicated climate funds explicitly seeks to support local climate action.7 Global financial
institutions can play a key role in addressing this imbalance by (i) making climate finance relevant and
unlocking the potential for to the poorest and most vulnerable to replicate adaptation measures;
(ii) facilitating systemic change by strengthening the meaningful participation of the poor and
vulnerable, especially women, in adaptation-related decision-making activities; (iii) acting at scale across
all levels – household, community, local and national governments; and (iv) ensuring sustainability by
3 Annex 2.1 of this proposal provides a detailed presentation of the country level climate risk assessments carried out as
part of the design and development of the program.

GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 4

helping local institutions mainstream adaptation and resilience in development processes. It is only by
such approach that climate finance can facilitate transformational change at the local level.
2. Proposed Intervention
A regional climate adaptation program targeted at the poor. The Community Resilience
Partnership Program (CRPP) is a regional partnership program of the Asian Development Bank (ADB)
which aims to help countries and communities in Asia and the Pacific region scale up investments in
climate adaptation, especially investments at the community level, that explicitly target the nexus
between climate change, poverty, and gender. The CRPP aims to contribute to transformational
change by: (i) mobilizing large-scale public investments that support community level adaptation of poor
and vulnerable people; (ii) developing national and local policies, plans, and programs that promote
financing for community-led adaptation; and (iii) increasing the meaningful participation of poor women
and men in resilience related decision-making. In doing so, the CRPP will address the points of
procedural and distributive justice so that the people most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change
can engage in a fair process and receive a fair share of the benefits of adaptation efforts.
The CRPP will support countries to meet their commitments to the Paris Agreement, the Sendai
Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, and the Sustainable Development Goals. The program responds
to the COP26 goal of scaling up adaptation to protect communities and natural habitats, and mobilizing
finance for climate adaptation measures that meet the needs of the poor and vulnerable communities
and to the decision of COP 27 which calls for scaling up of approaches in support of transformational
adaptation. The CRPP is also identified as flagship program under the locally led action track of the
Global Commission on Adaptation, which aims to spur financing for adaptation measures at the local
level, and to help create structures that support appropriate subsidiarity and give local actors greater
influence for adaptation-related decision-making. The CRPP is directly aligned with the core
recommendations of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Working Group 2 Report “Climate
Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability”, which highlights that largest adaptation gap exists
in low-income population group and that for adaptation efforts to be effective, they must be concentrated
on promoting climate justice and supporting the most economically and socially marginalized populations
and calls for integrated, multi-sectoral solutions that address social inequalities and cut across systems.8
Further, with its integrated multi-sector, regional programmatic approach and focus on communities and
locally implemented adaptation, the CRPP will directly contribute to a number of GCFs results as
outlined in the 2024-2027 strategic plan, including those related to Climate Information and Early
Warning Systems (CIEWS), Food, Ecosystems, Infrastructure, and elements of locally led adaptation
principles.
A programmatic approach for delivering pro-poor adaptation solutions at scale. The CRPP is
operationalized through the Community Resilience Financing Partnership Facility (CRFPF) which
was established by ADB in August 2021 and comprises two separate but interlinked components; the
CRPP Trust Fund (TF) focusing on upstream support to strengthen the enabling environment required
for implementing local adaptation measures at scale; and the CRPP Investment Fund (IF) focusing on
the efficient roll-out of local adaptation measures through a downstream investment program. CRFPF is
not a separate legal entity, but a facility administered within and by ADB. (See Figure 1)
The TF provides technical assistance and grant resources financed by development partners and
administered by ADB, to selected developing member countries (DMC) of the ADB to implement the
following three outputs: (1) Knowledge and action research on climate risk informed pro-poor
community-level solutions strengthened; (2) Institutional and community capacity to develop and deliver
climate adaptation investments at community-level strengthened; and (3) Inclusive and pro-poor
adaptation investment projects identified and prepared. The TF includes a dedicated Gender Window
with funds earmarked specifically for providing technical assistance and grants for identifying,
developing, and implementing investments that explicitly strengthen the resilience of women, particularly
poor women, and/or adaptation investments led by women that have a specific focus on supporting
women to build their resilience. The TF will have a budget of USD75 million with roughly 15% earmarked
for the Gender Window. To date, Government of United Kingdom, the Nordic Development Fund, and

such approach that climate finance can facilitate transformational change at the local level.
2. Proposed Intervention
A regional climate adaptation program targeted at the poor. The Community Resilience
Partnership Program (CRPP) is a regional partnership program of the Asian Development Bank (ADB)
which aims to help countries and communities in Asia and the Pacific region scale up investments in
climate adaptation, especially investments at the community level, that explicitly target the nexus
between climate change, poverty, and gender. The CRPP aims to contribute to transformational
change by: (i) mobilizing large-scale public investments that support community level adaptation of poor
and vulnerable people; (ii) developing national and local policies, plans, and programs that promote
financing for community-led adaptation; and (iii) increasing the meaningful participation of poor women
and men in resilience related decision-making. In doing so, the CRPP will address the points of
procedural and distributive justice so that the people most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change
can engage in a fair process and receive a fair share of the benefits of adaptation efforts.
The CRPP will support countries to meet their commitments to the Paris Agreement, the Sendai
Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, and the Sustainable Development Goals. The program responds
to the COP26 goal of scaling up adaptation to protect communities and natural habitats, and mobilizing
finance for climate adaptation measures that meet the needs of the poor and vulnerable communities
and to the decision of COP 27 which calls for scaling up of approaches in support of transformational
adaptation. The CRPP is also identified as flagship program under the locally led action track of the
Global Commission on Adaptation, which aims to spur financing for adaptation measures at the local
level, and to help create structures that support appropriate subsidiarity and give local actors greater
influence for adaptation-related decision-making. The CRPP is directly aligned with the core
recommendations of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Working Group 2 Report “Climate
Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability”, which highlights that largest adaptation gap exists
in low-income population group and that for adaptation efforts to be effective, they must be concentrated
on promoting climate justice and supporting the most economically and socially marginalized populations
and calls for integrated, multi-sectoral solutions that address social inequalities and cut across systems.8
Further, with its integrated multi-sector, regional programmatic approach and focus on communities and
locally implemented adaptation, the CRPP will directly contribute to a number of GCFs results as
outlined in the 2024-2027 strategic plan, including those related to Climate Information and Early
Warning Systems (CIEWS), Food, Ecosystems, Infrastructure, and elements of locally led adaptation
principles.
A programmatic approach for delivering pro-poor adaptation solutions at scale. The CRPP is
operationalized through the Community Resilience Financing Partnership Facility (CRFPF) which
was established by ADB in August 2021 and comprises two separate but interlinked components; the
CRPP Trust Fund (TF) focusing on upstream support to strengthen the enabling environment required
for implementing local adaptation measures at scale; and the CRPP Investment Fund (IF) focusing on
the efficient roll-out of local adaptation measures through a downstream investment program. CRFPF is
not a separate legal entity, but a facility administered within and by ADB. (See Figure 1)
The TF provides technical assistance and grant resources financed by development partners and
administered by ADB, to selected developing member countries (DMC) of the ADB to implement the
following three outputs: (1) Knowledge and action research on climate risk informed pro-poor
community-level solutions strengthened; (2) Institutional and community capacity to develop and deliver
climate adaptation investments at community-level strengthened; and (3) Inclusive and pro-poor
adaptation investment projects identified and prepared. The TF includes a dedicated Gender Window
with funds earmarked specifically for providing technical assistance and grants for identifying,
developing, and implementing investments that explicitly strengthen the resilience of women, particularly
poor women, and/or adaptation investments led by women that have a specific focus on supporting
women to build their resilience. The TF will have a budget of USD75 million with roughly 15% earmarked
for the Gender Window. To date, Government of United Kingdom, the Nordic Development Fund, and

The IF will be a program to provide grant and loan financing to seven selected DMCs, namely, Cambodia,
Indonesia, Lao PDR, Pakistan, Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste, and Vanuatu, to implement local
adaptation measures as part of ADB financed projects that are targeted at the poor and vulnerable
population. The IF will deliver three climate change related outputs that are the focus of this proposal
(4) information and systems for delivering applied climate-risk informed local investments at scale
improved; (5) climate resilient pro-poor livelihoods investments implemented; and (6) pro-poor climate
adaptation infrastructure investments implemented. All projects financed by the IF will be implemented
by the respective governments following ADB’s procedures. The GCF is requested to provide
USD100 million as grants and USD20 million as loan for the seven countries identified above in support
of the IF of this program, while the ADB will provide USD 555 million of grant and loan financing. The
program will utilize GCF resources to co-finance 10-15 projects implemented under the IF only, for
outputs 4, 5 and 6 as shown in Table 1 below.
Figure 1: CRPP Program Architecture
Source: ADB
The GCF funds for the CRPP IF will be ring-fenced within the ADB GCF Trust Fund which was created
pursuant to the Accreditation Master Agreement. Usage of GCF funds for individual projects will be based
on criteria outlined in this proposal which will be included in a dedicated CRPP IF Implementation
Guidelines to be developed during inception. The 7 countries identified above as recipients of the IF
grant and loan financing have been selected based on a combination of factors including (i) high levels
of climate risk and pockets of poverty; (ii) national commitments to scale up climate adaptation
investments targeted at the poorest populations; (iii) advanced levels of decentralization that promotes
local actions, including local climate actions and ensures sustainability of such actions; (iv) climate
adaptation and resilience priorities in ADB’s country partnership strategy for the country and indicative
pipeline of investments.
Value added of a regional program. The ADB recognises that transformational change often benefits
from the kinds of strategic, coordinated response that can be pursued through programs. By adopting a
programmatic approach, the CRPP will be able to demonstrate stronger coordination and strategic
alignment between its projects in different countries, unified by the overarching vision and common
objectives of strengthening community resilience, and thereby allow delivering sustained climate results
and impacts in the GCF results areas efficiently, effectively and at scale. The programmatic approach

will bring cost efficiency, higher implementation effectiveness and facilitate shared learning and

3. Climate Impacts/Benefits
Climate resilient sustainable development. The anticipated impact of the CRPP is that climate
resilient sustainable development in Asia and the Pacific is advanced. This represents a paradigm shift
from current development pathways that are failing to adequately respond to current and future climate
risks. Improved resilience of poor and vulnerable communities is considered a key pre-requisite for
bringing about a paradigm shift towards climate resilient sustainable development. As such, the outcome
of the program is expected to be that climate resilience of approximately 3.2 million poor and vulnerable
people, in seven countries in the Asia and the Pacific region is strengthened. This outcome marks the
pathway towards achieving the programs impact and will be the result of investment in adaptation options
that support systemic change and transitions in socio-ecological systems that are necessary
processes for large-scale transformations and a core enabler of climate resilient development. Table 1
below provides a summary of the outputs that have been identified as necessary for achieving this
outcome and the types of activities that would be financed by GCF under the CRPP IF and their
anticipated contribution to building climate resilience.
Unique programmatic concept for scaling up local adaptation measures in the region. The CRPP
is unique in its ability to develop localized climate adaptation solutions tailored to the needs of the poor
and vulnerable populations; and to leverage a range of large ADB supported investments (projects) in
social development, gender equality, livelihoods and governance to deliver on adaptation outcomes. The
CRPP will directly contribute to the implementation of ADB’s ambitious climate targets as set out in its
Strategy 2030 and its ambition of providing climate finance of USD100 billion between 2019-2030, of
which USD34 billion will support adaptation.4 As a multi-country program that comprises a varied but
strongly interconnected set of outputs supporting upstream actions to strengthen the enabling
environment for adaptation and actions for rolling out of adaptation measures through downstream
investments (projects), the CRPP will enable a coordinated approach to the deployment of adaptation
financing across different geographies and contexts. This programmatic approach allows for the
accumulation and transfer of knowledge and skills between countries and within countries, facilitating
scalability, replication and sustainability of adaptation solutions that are demonstrably effective over
the course of the program implementation period. It also allows for the reduction of costs for key functions
such as monitoring, evaluation and learning and gender mainstreaming.
4 ADB has set targets of providing $80 billion in climate finance from its own resources over the period of 2019 to 2030 and of ensuring that
75% of the number of its committed operations will support climate change mitigation and adaptation by 2030. ADB 2018. Strategy 2030.
Achieving a Prosperous, Inclusive, Resilient, and Sustainable Asia and the Pacific. Manila.

B.1. Climate context
1.Climate Change Context
Climate risk is a key threat to sustainable development. Countries in Asia and the Pacific region are
highly exposed to the damaging impacts of climate change. Prolonged heat waves, sea-level rise, changes
in rainfall patterns, and increases in the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events are having a
major impact on economies, natural and physical assets, and are compounding development challenges.
Between 2000-2019, the region experienced 3,068 disaster events accounting for 42% of global events. The
region experienced 41% of all flooding events and with a total of 1.5 billion people affected, accounting for
93% of people affected by floods worldwide; followed by tropical cyclones accounting for 79% of people
affected and 90% of deaths globally.9 For example, in Cambodia, annual flooding along the Mekong River
and Tonle Sap basins results in yearly losses of between USD100-170 and in 2015, climate related disasters
resulted in losses of USD1.5 billion (equivalent to 10% of GDP).10,11 In 2015, Cyclone Pam, a category 5
tropical cyclone, struck Vanuatu killing 11 people, damaging over 15,000 buildings and causing economic
losses around 64% of GDP.12 The economic costs associated with disasters across the region are
increasing. Estimates suggests that on an annual average basis, the costs of disasters to the region have
increased from USD1.8bn during the 1970s, to USD73.8bn between 2004 and 2013, a forty-fold increase,
representing 49% of global average annual losses.13
Climate risk is likely to intensify and occur both sooner and at a larger scale than previously
assessed with vast adverse impacts on development. Looking ahead, ongoing climate change is
projected to alter the frequency, intensity, extent, duration, and timing of extreme weather events, and is
likely to result in unprecedented extremes.14 The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)
Working Group 2 Report “Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability” states with high
confidence that global warming, reaching 1.5°C in the near-term, would cause unavoidable increases in
multiple climate hazards and present multiple risks to ecosystems and humans (Box 1 at the end of this
section highlights how the CRPP climate rationale is closely aligned to key headline messages from the
IPCC’s Sixth Assessment Report (AR6)). In PNG, for example, intensive rainfall events are expected to
increase by 20-30% by 2090;15 and in Lao PDR due to increased rainfall in its sub-basins, the Mekong River
will have higher discharge leading to increased floods.16,17 Climate change is also projected to alter trends
and induce shifts in the long-term average climate that will have major impacts in the region. For example,
a study estimates that Pakistan experienced 126 heat waves between 1997–2015, around 7 per year, and
these numbers are expected to increase in the future, with estimates suggesting that the country will
experience 12 heat wave events annually by 2030, 20 such events by 2060 and 26 events by 2090.18
Similarly, it is likely that climate change increased the impact of the 2022 flood disaster in Pakistan. Monsoon
rainfall in Balochistan and Sindh is estimated to be 50%–75% more intense than it would be in the absence
of climate change.19 The impacts are projected to be disproportionately high for Asia compared to other
regions, with estimates suggesting that the economic impact of climate change on Asia will be double those
of the global average by 2060.20 The Pacific Islands are recognised as among the most vulnerable, with
studies estimating that climate change impact could be equivalent to 12-13% of the GDP for the region under
a high global emission scenario, and 5% of GDP even with average temperature rises of under 2°C.21 Recent
evidence suggests these may be under-estimates, because of the increased threat of sea-level rise,22 which
will pose very large risk for atolls and small islands. Recent assessments highlight that even under the Paris
consensus scenario in which global warming is limited to 1.5°C to 2°C above preindustrial levels, much of
the land area, ecosystems, and socioeconomic sectors of Asia and the Pacific will be significantly affected
by climate change impacts,23 thus, emphasizing the need for adaptation. While the level of risk significantly
varies, the countries selected under this program are all at high risks. According to Notre-Dame GAIN Index
2020, the rank of the selected countries range between 97 and 152 out of 192 countries (Cambodia 140,

these numbers are expected to increase in the future, with estimates suggesting that the country will

GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 10
B
Indonesia 97, Lao PDR 142, Pakistan 152, PNG 149, Timor Leste 111 and Vanuatu 142).5 The higher the
country score, the higher the vulnerability to climate change and other global challenges in combination with
its readiness to improve resilience.
Adverse impacts of climate change will be largely manifested at the local level. This is because, the
underlying drivers of exposure and vulnerability, including socio-economic, ecological, institutions and
governance are inherently context-specific and reflected at local scale.24 Thus, adaptation solutions will be
needed at the local level, which captures a granular knowledge on hazards (historic and observed changes
in weather patterns) and their interaction with factors contributing to exposure (such as land use changes)
and vulnerability (such as existing social norms which decides women’s social and productive role in the
community) of and how such interaction leads to adverse impacts on people, assets and livelihoods.. It will
also require understanding traditional practices and resources deployed by local communities to deal with
climate shocks and stresses, and how such practices can be strengthened and scaled up.
Poor and vulnerable populations face the brunt of climate impacts. Estimates suggest that climate
change could push more than 100 million people globally in developing countries below the poverty line by
2030, with Asia and the Pacific being the main hotspot (along with sub-Saharan Africa).25 For example,
studies show that while Indonesia’s poverty level has declined significantly in the last decade, about 27%
of the country’s population have incomes that are marginally higher than the poverty line and could slide
back into poverty if food prices surge or if farm incomes suddenly decline due to prolonged drought from El
Niño.26 Many households in Lao PDR have a high probability of falling into extreme poverty even when
exposed to relatively low frequency flood and drought events and in Cambodia, an event occurring once in
every five years has approximately a 50% chance of pushing a household into extreme poverty.27 The poor
and vulnerable are affected disproportionately (in relative terms) because they have high climate sensitivity
(due to their activities, incomes and often their location in high-risk areas), they are often close to climate
thresholds already, and they have low adaptive capacity.28 They typically rely on fewer and more vulnerable
assets and basic services, depend on climate sensitive sectors for livelihoods, have limited access to climate
information, have limited technical and financial capacity to implement adaptation measures, and are often
left out from formal decision-making processes, which increases their vulnerability to climate impacts.
Subsistence-oriented communities around Asia and the Pacific are already observing clear-cut impacts of
anthropogenic climate change.29 Women in Asia and the Pacific represent the majority of small-scale and
subsistence farmers and are often responsible for the use and management of natural resources. In many
cases, the effects of climate impact require the poor to adopt negative coping strategies including reducing
quantity and nutritional quality of food consumption, incurring high level of indebtedness, unsustainable use
of scarce natural resources, and making trade-offs in investments regarding education, health, and
livelihoods that may impact their long-term well-being and further affect their poverty level. Further, climate
impacts could disrupt ecosystem services and lead to severe effects on livelihoods which in turn would affect
human health, migration dynamics and the potential of conflicts.30
Women and men are impacted differently by climate change, with women typically lacking equal
preventative and coping capacity due to pre-existing gender inequalities. Multidimensional poverty
significantly limits women’s ability to confront climate change. In Asia, women account for 80% of all people
living on less than USD2 per day (UN Women 2018)31, and their economic activities are often highly
concentrated in sectors that are dependent on natural resources such as agriculture. For example,
agriculture accounts for 65% of women’s total employment in Pakistan, 64% in Lao PDR, and 60% in Papua
New Guinea32. Women also tend to be overly burdened with household work and caring for children, the
sick, and the elderly; women do not always have the same rights as men to land; women often have less
access to financial services, technology, information, and early warning systems; and women, particularly
rural women, are often held back from fully participating in their community and in formal decision-making
processes33,34,35. All of these factors contribute to increased vulnerability and lower adaptive capacity, and
are closely related to socially created gender functions, systemic discriminations, and the power imbalances
between women and men. While it is crucial to recognize and address women’s vulnerabilities to climate
5 The Notre-Dame GAIN Index summarizes a countries vulnerability to climate change. Higher the country score, higher the vulnerability to
climate change and other global challenges in combination with its readiness to improve resilience.

change and understand the structural causes for them, it is fundamental to refrain from categorizing women
as innately weak, passive receivers of protection and support. In the past, this approach has prevented
women from being recognized as active agents in resilience-building programs. The adoption of programs
designed on the assumption that women are powerless further exposes them to climate change shocks and
disasters, as well as hinders the realization of women’s rights to full and equal participation and decision-
making36. Women’s unique knowledge, skills, and perspectives, mean that they can contribute positively to
the identification of appropriate adaptation measures and ensure that they are implemented effectively and
efficiently. Women can also play a leadership role in accessing public and private resources for adaptation,
which in turn can give them recognition within the community and promote their position in the family and
wider society, creating a positive feedback loop for women’s empowerment. These different experiences
between men and women in terms of their vulnerability and role of resilience building within communities are
not adequately reflected in exiting adaptation policy and practice in CRPP countries, and this require specific
attention.
The COVID-19 pandemic has further highlighted the need for building resilience of the poor and
vulnerable population. The pandemic is having a disproportionate impact on the poor and the vulnerable,
including women, already burdened with the ill-effects of climate shocks and stresses. The poor, who often
migrate internally to deal with seasonal lean periods are being forced to make difficult choices to deal with
the crisis, which will have implications on their well-being. During this crisis, women and girls can also face
higher risks of losing jobs or income, dropping out of school, increased unpaid care work, and domestic
violence.37 Estimates suggest that in PNG, the COVID-19 pandemic could result in an increase of the poverty
rate from 27.2% to 31.7%; and in Vanuatu, from 13.9 % to 18.3% in 2020.38

Headline messages from the IPCC AR6-WG2 contribution includes:
− There is high confidence that global warming, reaching 1.5°C in the near-term, would cause
unavoidable increases in multiple climate hazards and present multiple risks to ecosystems and
humans. For 127 identified key risks, assessed mid and long- term impacts are up to multiple
times higher than currently observed.
− In Asia, climate change will exacerbate fundamental challenges around water and food insecurity,
poverty and inequality, and increased frequency and severity of extreme events. Even at 1.5°C
and more so at 2°C, climate change will significantly constrain the functioning and wellbeing of
human and ecological systems in some places and for some people.
− There is high confidence that vulnerability is higher in locations with poverty, governance
challenges and limited access to basic services and resources, and high levels of climate-sensitive
livelihoods (e.g., smallholder farmers).
− There is high confidence that vulnerability at different spatial levels is exacerbated by inequity
and marginalization linked to gender, ethnicity, low income or combinations thereof.

2. Context
The paragraphs below provide brief description of climate risk context of CRPP IF countries, with more
details provided in Annex 2.1.
Cambodia: Cambodia is ranked 140th out of 181 countries in the ND-GAIN Index41, due a combination of
high vulnerability and low readiness. The country has a tropical monsoon climate, with two distinct seasons,
a rainy season from May to October and a dry season from November to April. Average temperatures are
relatively uniform across the country and annual average rainfall is high (especially in the highlands and
along the coast), most of which falls during the Monsoon. However, there is high annual variability due to
the influence of the Monsoon and the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO).

B
The country has a varied topography, with mountainous and highland regions, the central plains, and a
coastal zone, but it is dominated by the Mekong River, which flows directly from the north to Vietnam in the
south. The Tonle Sap Lake, an outlet of the Mekong, is located in the northwest region, and covers almost
10% of the country’s surface area during the monsoon peak. The central alluvial plains of the Mekong and
Tonle Sap represent approximately 80%of the country. These basins are characterized by a flood-pulse
hydrology with fluctuations in water levels between seasons, and are critical for agriculture and fisheries.
The combination of the monsoon, climate variability from the ENSO, and the geographical terrain makes
Cambodia extremely vulnerable to weather-related extremes (floods, storms, and periodically droughts).
These occur almost every year and lead to high losses, reported at USD1.4 billion over the last twenty years
(EM-DAT, 202142: DESINVENTAR, 202143) with annual damages of USD100 to 250 million (UNDRR
201944). Seasonal flooding is essential to agricultural and fisheries production, however, river and flash
floods lead to major losses. Cambodia ranks as one of the world’s most flood exposed countries in the
world45 in terms of the proportion of the population affected by floods (at 20-25%). There are also periodic
droughts. During the 2015-16 El Nino drought event, 2.5 million people were affected, and three-quarters of
the wet season paddy rice production experienced a loss of more than 25% in yield (World Bank, 201746).
Tropical storms are rare, though in 2009 Typhoon Ketsana had a large impact (USD132 million in Cambodia,
UNDRR, 2019). These weather-related impacts particularly affect rural people because of the reliance on
rain-fed agriculture, and the disproportionate impact on the poor. Analysis by ADB (2017) finds that many
households in Cambodia have a high probability of falling into extreme poverty even when exposed to
relatively low intensity flood and drought events47.
Recent observations show that the climate of Cambodia is changing (UNDP, 201248: Cambodia 2nd NC,
201549; World Bank, 201950:). There is a clear warming trend, with 0.2°C per decade reported since the
1960s, and slightly above this in the dry season, and an increase in the number of ‘hot days’. The patterns
of annual rainfall trends are more uncertain, with some areas experiencing increases and others decreases,
although there are indications of increasing variability and increasing extreme rainfall. The projected
temperature increases for Cambodia indicates a further rise of 1°C to 2°C by mid-century (central multi-
model ensemble values, for RCP2.6 and RCP8.5, relative to baseline 1986-2005 period, World Bank, 202051:
World Bank/ADB, 202152) and similar increases are found in downscaled modelling analysis (Thoeun,
201553). It is difficult to model rainfall changes due to the influence of Monsoon dynamics, but most climate
models (and also the downscaled analysis) project increases in annual rainfall by the mid-century (2050s).
There is more confidence from the climate models that heavy precipitation events will increase, which would
increase the flood risks across the country. Modelling analysis for the Mekong indicates higher discharge
leading to increased floods54,55,56 with greater areas of land and more people at risk of flooding (USAID,
201457). There has also been modeling of the potential climate change impacts on Tonle Sap lake and
floodplain (Oeurng et al., 201958), which indicates large possible impacts on the fisheries sectors. For the
agriculture sector, Chun et al (201659) report that Cambodia could suffer the largest reductions in rice yield
in all Southeast Asia, and Jim et al (2018) also project large yield reductions for the country. These could be
amplified by the possible increased annual likelihood of drought60 and also by increases in heat and humidity
which will reduce labour productivity (Dunne et al., 201361). There are also projected increases in health
impacts, driven by a projected increase in vector borne disease (WHO, 201562). Finally, there will be impacts
from sea-level rise and storm surge along the 435 kilometres long coastal belt. Economic modelling studies
estimate that climate change will reduce Cambodia’s total GDP by 1.5 to 2.5% by 2030 and 3.5% to 10% by
2050 (RGC, 201563: UNDP, 201864).
Indonesia: Indonesia is ranked in the top-third of countries in terms of natural hazard risk (59 out of 191) by
the 2020 INFORM Risk Index. In particular, Indonesia has high exposure to flooding, tropical cyclones and
tsunami. Between 2005 and 2015, Indonesia recorded more than 1,800 disaster events.65 Studies have
estimated the costs of climate change in Indonesia could be more than 6% of GDP annually by 2100, more
than double the global average loss.66 Despite high exposure to natural hazards, Indonesia ranks moderately
in terms of its vulnerability and coping capacity, where it is ranked in the top half (102 and 88 respectively).
However, vulnerability and coping capacity among the poorest groups is likely to be quite different, and
inequality in the country remains high, with the bottom 40% of the population accounting for 17.7% of
consumption67. Prior to COVID-19, an estimated 61.8 million people, or 21.5% of the population, were
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

=== PAGE 17 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 13
B
considered poor or have a high risk of falling into poverty, making them vulnerable to shocks.68 This figure
is likely to be significantly higher post COVID-19 impacts. Roughly 7% of urban population live below the
poverty line and almost equal percentage of population live just above the poverty line. The rural and urban
poor will bear the brunt of the climate change burden as poorer households in Indonesia are much less likely
to take adaptive measures and plan for longer-term horizons than wealthier households, making them more
exposed to environmental shocks and disasters.69 The impact on livelihoods and food security is a particular
concern. For example, Indonesia is positioned as one of the most vulnerable countries to potentially extreme
heatwaves according to climate model projections.70,71 Heavy manual labour jobs are commonly among the
lowest paid whilst also being most at risk of productivity losses due to heat stress.72 The poor in Indonesia
are also particularly vulnerable to food price rises, which could become more common and pronounced due
to climates impact on food production and widespread harvest failure resulting from unusual and extreme
climate conditions. For the 20-25% of the country’s population that have incomes marginally higher than the
poverty line, if food prices surge or if farm incomes suddenly decline due to the impact of climate extremes
the could slide back into poverty.73 A 100% increase in food prices could increase the number of Indonesians
in extreme poverty by just over 25%.74
Poor and vulnerable households in rural and urban areas are particularly exposed to flood risk as they
frequently reside on low lying lands prone to flooding and suffer from the lack of access to good quality
infrastructure and services. As of 2010, assuming protection for up to a 1-in-25 year event, the population
annually affected by flooding in Indonesia is estimated at 1.5 million people and expected annual urban
damage is estimated at USD1.4 billion.75 There are not enough facilities and infrastructure available to abate
these existing flooding conditions76 and the risks are expected to increase with climate change, with large
numbers of coastal cities facing sea level rise and high-density built environment. Climate change could
amplify coastal flood risk 19-37% by 2030 (measured by Expected Annual Damage).77 Indonesia is
particularly exposed to sea-level rise, with the country ranked the fifth highest in terms of population
inhabiting the lower elevation coastal zone78. It is estimated that by 2030 around 5.5-8 million people could
reside in a 100-year floodplain (an area exposed to 1-in-100-year coastal floods resulting from storm surges),
growing to 9.5 – 14 million by 2060. These estimates assume a modest sea-level rise of 10cm by 2030 and
21cm by 2060.79 Estimates suggest that the number of Indonesians exposed to river flood risk will increase
by 75% in four decades between 2015 and 2055.80 Climate change is expected to increase the annual urban
damage from flooding by USD6.1 billion under the RCP8.5 emissions pathway (AQUEDUCT Scenario B).81
Even under lower emissions pathways consistent with the Paris Climate Agreement, almost all Asian
countries face an increase in the frequency of extreme river flows. What would historically have been a 1-in-
100 year flow, could become a 1-in-50 year or 1-in-25 year event in most of South, Southeast, and East
Asia.82
In rural areas, the dependence on agriculture for livelihoods is of particular concern for climate change
impacts. Nationally, roughly 40 percent of livelihoods are dependent on agriculture, however in some areas,
such as East Nusa Tenggara, rural households’ have a historically much higher dependence on agriculture
(more than 80% as of 2010), and here food security related concerns such as malnutrition is very high.83 Of
the 25 million farm households nationally, 17 million are rice farmers with an average land possession of 0.6
ha.84 Rice is a major staple in Indonesia and its production is vulnerable to changes in rainfall seasonality
and water scarcity. The climate of Indonesia is mainly influenced by the El Nino Southern Oscillation
(ENSO), where drier conditions are experienced during El Niño events and wetter conditions during La Nina
event.85 Droughts are expected to increase in frequency and intensity given the association of accentuated
drought with El Niño events, which are expected to increase in frequency and intensity through warmer
global temperatures.86,87 At present, 14% of Indonesia 453 districts are recorded as having no months of
surplus water. By 2025, this is projected as approximately 20% and 31% by 2050.88 Crop water demand
estimates suggest projected changes will impact the rice growing period between November and March and
that there will likely be insufficient water for the second growing period, March to June, when chillies and
tobacco are grown.89 Delayed rainfall can increase the risk of annual rice deficits, with such events projected
to increase from climate change. Naylor et al. (2007) project an increase in the probability of 30-day delay
in the wet season from 9-18% today to 30-40% by 2050 (for the main rice-producing areas of Java and
Bali).90 In South Kalimantan the future water requirement in rice production will increase by around 56% in
dry season (July) and 25% during wet season in September and October.91 Further, USAID assumes the

burden to these rural households as total agricultural loss among the provinces of East, Central, and West
Java provinces can account for 19 percent, 15 percent, and 9.5 percent, respectively.92 Rice is also
particularly sensitive to temperature changes, with some estimates suggesting that an increase of 1oC could
reduce national production by 10–25%93 which is well within the range of projected increase over the next
century 94.
Lao People’s Democratic Republic (Lao PDR): Lao PDR is a landlocked country in Southeast Asia. A
large part of the country is mountainous, but there is a large central area, as well as low-lying alluvial plains
along the Mekong River. It is ranked 142th out of 181 countries in the ND-GAIN Index95, and as the 36th most
vulnerable country globally. Rural areas in Lao PDR account for nearly 90% of the poor population, and rural
poverty is almost three times higher than in urban areas. The poverty head count rate in the central provinces
is some of the highest in the country and is showing the slowest rate of reduction.96
Lao PDR has a tropical monsoon climate. The climate is hot and tropical, with the rainy season between
May and October, a cool dry season from November to February, and a short hot, dry season in March and
April. The central region experiences high temperatures and high average annual rainfall (which is
concentrated in monsoon months), however, there is high variability due to the influence of Monsoon
dynamics and the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO). The combination of the monsoon climate, high
variability, and the geographical terrain makes Lao extremely vulnerable to weather related extremes,
notably from floods, storms, landslide and droughts (UNDP, 201097). The whole country experiences regular
flooding and there are also frequent storms: three of the five costliest events on record having taken place
since 2009 (EM-DAT, 202198: DESINVENTAR, 202199). Typhoon Ketsana in 2009 and Haima in 2011
caused damages of USD 94 million and USD 66 million respectively, and in 2018 a confluence of storm and
flood disasters affected over 600,000 people and led to losses of USD 371 million (UNDRR 2019100). There
are also periodic droughts: in, 2015 a severe drought, driven by a strong El Niño event, damaged tens of
thousands of hectares of rice, and fruit crops (Sutton et al., 2019)101 including in the central region. Historical
damage data indicates that annual expected losses range between 3.3% and 4.1 percent of GDP (World
Bank, 2017102).
Disasters disproportionate impact on the poor, and the rural poor are particularly vulnerable to ENSO-related
shocks (Sutton et al., 2019103). Rural areas experience widespread food insecurity due to the reliance on
rain-fed agriculture, and these households have a high probability of falling into extreme poverty even when
exposed to relatively low frequency flood and drought events (ADB, 2017).104
Recent observations show that the climate of Lao PDR is changing. There is a clear warming trend, with 0.1
to 3°C per decade reported (GFDRR, 2011105, World Bank, 2019106) across the entire country. The patterns
of annual rainfall trends are more uncertain (Lao PDR, 2013107, World Bank, 2019, Westra et al., 2014108),
although there are trends of increasing variability and increasing extreme rainfall.
Future climate change will exacerbate existing risks. The projected temperature increases for Lao PDR
indicates a further rise of broadly 1°C to 2°C by mid-century (central multi-model ensemble values, for
RCP2.6 and RCP8.5 respectively, relative to a baseline 1986-2005 period (World Bank, 2020109: World
Bank/ADB, 2021110111). It is difficult to model rainfall changes due to the influence of Monsoon dynamics, but
most climate models project increases in annual rainfall by the mid-century (2050s) and there is more
confidence that heavy precipitation events will increase. This will increase the flood risks across the country.
Modelling for the country’s rivers – from northern watershed, through the central region, and in the Mekong
- indicate higher discharge leading to increased floods112,113114 with greater areas of land and more people
at risk of flooding, and higher value at risk (USAID, 2014115). These effects will be exacerbated by climate
change, notably increases in heat and humidity (including heatwaves) which will reduce labour productivity
(Dunne et al., 2013116). There are also projected direct and indirect impacts of climate change on agriculture
itself, with reductions in yields in Lao PDR (Behnke et al., 2018)117, noting these could be amplified by the
possible increased annual likelihood of drought118.
Pakistan: Ranked 18 out of 191 countries by the 2020 Inform Risk Index119, Pakistan faces some of the
highest climate related disaster risk levels in the world. It has high exposure to flooding, including, riverine,
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 15
B
flash, and coastal, as well as exposure to tropical cyclones, droughts and heatwaves. Disaster risk in
Pakistan is also driven by its social vulnerability. Pakistan’s vulnerability ranking (37th) is driven by its high
rates of multidimensional poverty. Geographically, the largest area of vulnerability is the Indus River Delta,
which is a hotspot for storm surge, soil erosion and cyclones120. This area has very high vulnerability121, as
it is particularly low-lying and flat, with around 4,750 km2 below 2m above sea-level122. Around 5 million
people in Pakistan live in this low-lying coastal area, but because of population growth, it is projected that
the population could increase six-fold to reach 30 million people by 2060. The coastal provinces of Sindh
and Balochistan, in which Pakistan's 990km coastline is located, have the highest rural poverty rates among
Pakistan’s provinces and the highest urban-rural poverty gaps.123 Coastal erosion and storm surge waves
are already threatening towns and farms situated along the coast and saline intrusion continues to be a
major challenge in the coastal zone, degrading land quality and agricultural yields124,125. Cyclones do arise
the Arabian sea, and when they hit landfall in Pakistan in this area, they can cause major impacts. For
example, a strong cyclone hit Pakistan in 1999, killing some 6200 people, and there have been major storms
recorded in 2004, 2007 and 2010, all of which affected the project area. In 2007, storm surges caused by
Cyclone Yemyin had significant impacts on lives and property126.
Recent observations show that the climate of Pakistan and Sindh region are changing already and many of
the issues described above are likely to intensify due to climate change, affecting many marginal and
deprived communities. There is a clear warming trend, which has accelerated since the 1960s (with reported
0.5 to 1°C of warming), and higher numbers of heatwaves and hot days.127,128,129,130,131 Data from the World
Bank downscaled analysis132 shows that the projected temperature increases for Pakistan will be above the
global average. By mid-century (2050s) a further rise of 1.5°C to 2.5°C (central estimate), relative to a
baseline 1986-2005 period is projected. There are also projected increases in hot and very hot days. Multiple
sources report that rainfall in the coastal area has declined by 10 – 15% since the 1960s. However, heavy
rainfall events have increased, with the heaviest rain intensities recorded over the last decade.133,134 Changes
in the seasonality, regularity, and extremes of precipitation highlights the risk of increased frequency and
intensity of flood and drought events135. Coastal areas of Pakistan have experienced changes in mean sea
level in the past, with observations at Karachi indicating an increase in the mean sea level of about 1 mm/yr
during the 20th century.136,137 Under low emission scenarios, it is likely that the coastal areas will experience
significant sea level rise over the long-term. However, an upper range, with 0.6 to 1.1 metres has been
shown as likely by 2100 under a high-emission scenario.138 Recent analysis has also found that climate
change has had a major role in increasing cyclone activity in the Arabian sea.139 The IPCC SROCC140
projects that the average intensity of tropical cyclones, the proportion of Category 4 and 5 tropical cyclones
and the associated average precipitation rates are projected to increase for a 2°C global temperature rise
above any baseline period (medium confidence). This, combined with rising mean sea levels will contribute
to higher extreme sea levels associated with tropical cyclones (very high confidence). Coastal hazards will
also be exacerbated by an increase in the average intensity, magnitude of storm surge and precipitation
rates of tropical cyclones.
These changes in climate are likely to have a significant impact on water resource availability, heat stress,
land availability and soil quality, affecting agricultural yields and rural agrarian livelihoods, in a country where
Agriculture employs 42.3% of the Pakistan’s workforce and contributes 21% to gross domestic product
(GDP). Of the 24.3% of population below the national poverty line, over 80% are in rural areas, and comprise
a large proportion of small-scale farmers (20%), landless farmers (10%) and agricultural laborers (12%)141.
The projections of sea level rise are a particular concern for the communities living in the coastal zone. Work
by the UK Met Office (2014) estimated that without adaptation, around one million people will face coastal
flooding annually by the period 2070–2100. As sea level rises, there is an increased risk of river banks being
overtopped and of flooding of adjacent land further up the estuaries. Without intervention, saltwater will
penetrate further upstream and inland. A key issue for livelihoods is thus the potential increase in salt water
intrusion affecting water supplies, coupled with broader issues of water availability from the changes due to
climate change and demand increases. The Second National Communication from GoP (2018) reports that
the Sindh area will suffer the most from water logging and salinity because of poor drainage systems.
Papua New Guinea: The high levels of disaster risk faced in Papua New Guinea (PNG) are reflected in its
ranking in the 2019 INFORM Risk index (26th out of 191 countries). PNG’s ranking is driven by moderate
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

B
levels of exposure to flood, drought and cyclone, but particularly by its lack of coping capacity. On this
indicator PNG is ranked as having the 11th lowest coping capacity in the world. PNG was also ranked 158th
out of 181 countries in the 2016 ND-GAIN climate change vulnerability ranking. This heightened vulnerability
is largely due to widespread poverty and poor infrastructure, among other factors. PNG has consistently
ranked among the lowest 30 countries in the Human Development Index. The country ranked 153rd out of
189 countries surveyed in the 2018 UNDP Human Development Report142 and, although precise figures are
difficult to come by, poverty rates of between 30-40% have been reported and an adult literacy rate of around
50%143. The monopolization of natural resources by a wealthy minority, is believed to be a significant
contributor to income and wealth inequality which are also very high in PNG, and recent global research
suggests this may also contribute to reduced resilience to disasters.144 One assessment suggests the
financial burden of the impact of disasters is around 3% of GDP annually.145 That same study estimates the
number of people affected by natural hazards at 7 million between 1990-2012.
The UNDP (2018) estimate that 70% of households in PNG remain dependent on subsistence agriculture146.
These communities are highly vulnerable to climate-related hazards and their impacts on livelihoods and
food security. For example, a major drought associated with ENSO in 1997 highlighted the nation’s food
insecurity, with over a million people (around 20% of the population) facing food shortages. Saline intrusion
resulting from sea-level rise has already been documented damaging the production of small-holder
farmers.147 PNG’s population is particularly dependent on sweet potato production, with its Second National
Communication to the UNFCCC suggesting 63% of calories in rural areas derive from this source. It is
significant then that a review of multiple studies conducted by ADB suggested that sweet potato yields in
PNG may decline by as much as 10% by 2050 as a result of changing climate conditions. Indeed, all the
crops assessed, including cassava, maize, rice, sugarcane and taro, showed negative yield trends of a
similar magnitude.148 The rise in night-time minimum temperatures is believed to be a particularly important
driver of these losses, with staple crops such as rice reported to have vulnerability in this regard.149 Maximum
and minimum temperatures are projected to rise notably faster than average temperatures, pointing towards
a less stable and more frequently heat stressed climate in the future. Historical data for PNG suggest that
temperature rise has been fastest in the minimum temperatures, with daily maximum temperatures rising
broadly in line with the average.150 In addition, under higher emissions pathways (particularly RCP8.5) PNG
may transition to a chronically heat-stressed environment, with the CCKP model ensemble projecting a
potential 100 day increase in the number of days surpassing 35oC by 2080-2099. 151 Even increases in the
range of 9-26 days above 35oC (ensemble median estimate) under the three lower emissions pathways
represent a potential hazard to livelihoods in the country.
In addition to losses due to changes in the suitability of the climate conditions, production losses are already
being experienced in coastal areas due to saltwater contamination of soils and groundwater, and across the
country due to flood and drought. At present PNG faces an annual median probability of severe
meteorological drought of around 4%, as defined by a standardized precipitation evaporation index (SPEI)
of less than -2. Past drought incidents in PNG have led to significant disaster events, with a notable drought
in 1997 resulting in widespread famine.152
Coastal, river (fluvial), and surface (pluvial) flooding also represent a major risk. The UNDP suggest that
18% of the country’s landmass is either permanently or regularly inundated153. Lafale et al. (2018) suggest
medium confidence should be placed in the projected future trend of increased annual precipitation. In
contrast, the projections which suggest the frequency and intensity of extreme rainfall events will increase
are associated with high confidence.154 The intensity of sub-daily extreme rainfall events appears to be
increasing with temperature, a finding supported by evidence from different regions of Asia and the Pacific.155
As of 2010, assuming protection for up to a 1-in-10 year event, the population annually affected by river
flooding in PNG is estimated at 33,000 people and the damage to GDP is estimated at USD73 million.156 By
2030 under the RCP8.5 emissions pathway (AQUEDUCT Scenario B) climate change is expected to
increase the annually affected population from river flooding by 20,000 people, and the GDP impact by
USD90 million. What would historically have been a 1-in-100 year flow, could become a 1-in-50 year or 1-
in-25 year event.157 Willner et al. (2018) estimate that the population affected by an extreme flood could
increase by 35,000-56,000 people by 2035-2044 (assuming present day population distributions) as a result

of climate change. Population growth and poorly planned development have the potential to increase this

PNG’s Second National Communication suggests a further 8,000 people are affected by coastal flooding
every year, causing over USD10 million in damages. Every decade around 15 tropical cyclones pass through
PNG’s exclusive economic zone, around a quarter of which are category 3 or stronger (severe events). A 1-
in-100 year cyclone landfall was estimated to cost around 8.4% of GDP as of 2011.159 However even
cyclones passing a long way from PNG’s land mass can have a significant local impact, with flooding and
inundation of low lying islands documented as a result of elevated water levels.160 Climate change is
expected to interact with cyclone hazard in complex ways which are currently poorly understood, however,
modelling of climate change impacts on cyclone intensity and frequency conducted across the globe also
points to a general trend of reduced cyclone frequency but increased intensity and frequency of the most
extreme events.161. Known associated risks include the action of sea-level rise to enhance the damage
caused by cyclone-induced storm surges, and the possibility of increased windspeed and precipitation
intensity. Sea-level rise can vary spatially, and work by the Australian Bureau of Meteorology and CSIRO
has suggested that end-of-century sea-level rise could vary by as much as 10cm across the South Pacific
region, meaning countries such as PNG should be prepared for above average sea-level rises162.
Timor-Leste: Floods, droughts, landslides and cyclones are the major natural hazards in Timor-Leste.
According to the 2020 World Risk Report, in terms of exposure and vulnerability to natural hazards, Timor-
Leste ranks 20th globally (24th in exposure, 51st in vulnerability (of which 43rd, 42nd and 82nd in susceptibility,
lack adaptive capacity and lack coping capacity)163. In terms of climate disruptions and adaptation, Timor-
Leste is assessed as having high vulnerability and low readiness based on its scores on the ND-GAIN Index.
The overall country score of 43.8 ranks Timor-Leste as position number 111 – the 47th most vulnerable, and
89th least ready country on the index. Flooding is the most frequent disaster, with riverine and flash flooding
both occurring during periods of extreme rainfall; significant flood events were recorded in 2001, 2003, 2006,
2013, 2019 and 2020164. Droughts also occur regularly in Timor-Leste, and pose a particular threat to
agricultural production in the provinces of Oecusse, Dili and Atauro. The country experienced a major
drought from 2015-2017 which caused sharp reductions in agricultural yields, with a decrease of 40% in
Maize production, and 57% in Rice production165. It impacted approximately half the area of maize and rice
planted in the country, with 50% of households, reporting loss of livestock, and 50% suffering from food
insecurity as a result166. Such events have significant implications for poverty, food security and well-being
in a country where estimates suggest that 30% of the population were living on less than the internationally
recognised poverty line of USD1.90/day, 45% were classified as living in multi-dimensional poverty167, and
approximately 80% of the population are reliant on the agriculture sector.168 Most agriculture is subsistence,
and many rural areas suffer from food insecurity, due to a combination of low productivity, high population
growth and unpredictable rainfall coupled with extreme climate events169.
Staple crops in Timor-Leste are sensitive to rising temperatures and the impacts associated with extreme
rainfall, changes in the seasonality of rainfall, seawater inundation and salinization of coastal aquifers.170
The majority of agriculture in the country is rain-fed, and as such is vulnerable to changes in the timing and
amount of rainfall, and increasing variability. The supply of water (particularly water scarcity during the dry
season) will likely be a significant constraint on agricultural output171. Agricultural systems, including
livelihood conditions and food insecurity issues, will be affected both by increases in extreme events, as well
as changes in temperature and rainfall resulting from climate change172. According to climate models173, the
months of Jun-Sep, largely corresponding to the current dry season, are likely to become even drier, and
there is a clear signal for increases in rainfall from February-May. There are indications that the onset of the
rainy season may be delayed, with increased rainfall occurring during a shorter rainy season174. The intensity
of rainfall is expected to increase in Timor-Leste, with larger increases in extreme rainfall towards the end of
the century. Under RCP4.5 there is a clear signal of increased heavy rainfall, with an average +14.5%
increase in the number of days exceeding the 99th percentile by mid-century, and a 38.6% increase in days
for the 2066-2095 period.
The El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) exerts a strong influence over rainfall variability in Timor-Leste. El
Niño conditions bring drier conditions and shorter, delayed wet seasons, often causing droughts, whilst La

Niña conditions cause higher rainfall even in the dry season and are linked to higher tropical cyclone activity.
For the period 1950-1999 Dili recorded its two record low rainfall totals during the El Niño events of 1982-83
and 1997-98, and central provinces can see rainfall totals reduce by up to 50% of the annual average175. A
significant source of agricultural losses during El Niño years is false starts to the rainy season, where the
initial onset of rains is followed by an abnormal dry period before the season reliably starts. These false
starts can cause crop failure as there is not enough rainfall to support crop growth following planting, for
example in Manatuto, farmers reported frequent false starts during previous El Niño events, and having to
plant 3-4 times due to the losses suffered. Modelling of maize indicates reductions in yield in the range of 5-
20% in the absence of adaptation, noting that much of this loss could be offset by supporting agricultural
water supply through activities such as irrigation and water harvesting176. These losses may be conservative,
as they do not attempt to capture any increase in losses from extreme events. The evolution of ENSO under
climate change will play an important role in determining drought and inter-annual variability in rainfall in the
country. Although, changes in the ENSO cycle are still not well captured by climate models, the latest
research indicates that El Niño events may become both more frequent and more severe over the course of
the century177,178.
Vanuatu: Disasters resulting from natural hazards are a very significant contributor to issues of social
deprivation and impede economic development in Vanuatu, costing on average an estimated 6% of GDP
every year.179 The nation’s exposure to natural hazards, extensive low-lying coastal zone, development
context, and precarious natural resource base mean it is amongst the most vulnerable nations to climate
change in the world, ranked 142nd out of 191 countries in the ND-GAIN Index. Vanuatu has very high
exposure and vulnerability to the impact of flood, tropical cyclones, and storm surge which can strike in
combination or isolation. Cyclones bring coastal and flash flooding even when only passing in the vicinity of
the island. According to its Second National Communication to the UNFCCC around 20-30 cyclones pass
over Vanuatu every decade, around 3-5 of which will cause severe damage. In 2015 Cyclone Pam, a
category 5 tropical cyclone, struck Vanuatu killing 11 people, destroying or damaging over 17,000 buildings
and displacing 65,000 people. The economic damages associated with the incident were estimated to be
equivalent to around 64% of GDP.180
The economy of Vanuatu, like surrounding island states, is based predominantly on the service sector (67%
of GDP value added), followed by agriculture (22%) and industry (11%). However, there is significant local
dependence on subsistence agriculture181 and issues of poverty and undernourishment are prevalent.
Fishing – both artisanal (in which a large proportion of the population participates) and commercial - and
offshore financial services are other mainstays of the economy.182 Vanuatu has a food trade deficit and
dependence on imports for food security equivalent to over USD50 per capita in 2011 giving it high
vulnerability to price shocks and disaster events.183 This heavy reliance on both natural resources for
agriculture and on tourism for livelihoods means that impact of extreme climate events in Vanuatu can be
catastrophic for, food security, poverty reduction and general well-being of the population.184 Cyclones can
cause devastating damage to agricultural products185 and known climate risks include the action of sea-level
rise to enhance the damage caused by cyclone-induced storm surges, and the possibility of increased wind
speed and precipitation intensity. Modelling of climate change impacts on cyclone intensity and frequency
conducted across the globe points to a general trend of reduced cyclone frequency but increased intensity
and frequency of the most extreme events.186, 187 Sea-level rise is not just a threat due to long-term
encroachment on coastal areas, but also due to the projected increase in the frequency of extreme sea-level
events.188 The return period of exceptionally high sea-levels, driven by climate circulations, is expected to
reduce, and low-lying pacific island nations are particularly at risk. 189 Vanuatu’s Second National
Communication reports sea-level rise at a rate of around 6 mm/year between 1990 and 2010 – slightly faster
than the global average over the same period.
Slower onset hazards also represent significant challenges. Most Pacific Island states are almost entirely
dependent upon rainfall to support agricultural production, and thus are highly vulnerable to rainfall
variability.190 Meteorological drought is expected to increase in frequency, with one study conducted for ADB
suggesting a potential doubling in the frequency of severe and extreme droughts by 2080 under
RCP8.5. 191 This represents a major risk as there is very high dependence on rainwater for
subsistence.192 The future projections of sea level rise are associated with increased risks of flooding, loss

Proposed interventions to scale up adaptation solutions targeted at the poor. It is in this context of
climate risk that the CRPP IF has been designed to support governments of these seven countries to scale
up adaptation solutions at local level, through the implementation of projects that are closely aligned with
national climate priorities. These projects (detailed examples provided in annex 2.3) will promote
adaptation solutions at local level that explicitly address the climate and poverty nexus and can be replicated
and scaled up through national policies and programs and thereby bring transformational change. It is
expected that CRPP supported solutions will allow overcoming a number of adaptation-related barriers
(described in the section B2), especially in the context of local level adaptation measures that can be
delivered at scale. Importantly, there is a current window of opportunity to implement such solutions hand-
in-hand with poverty reduction measures as countries invest in reaching the SDGs, and work to fulfil their
commitments to the Paris Agreement and Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, and COVID-19
recovery. This can ensure climate finance will reach the people most in need; and local institutions and
communities, especially women, will build adequate capacity to manage climate risk without jeopardizing
their hard-earned development gains. As described in Box 2 below, this approach proposed by the CRPP
directly responds to the IPCC’s call for integrated adaptation and poverty reduction solutions for increasing
adaptation effectiveness and enabling climate resilient development. In the absence of the CRPP, this
opportunity will be lost, and the countries will lock-in development to growing climate risks. This opportunity
is particularly important in the post-COVID world, where burdened governments may not prioritize integration
of inclusive and resilience considerations in the recovery process.
Box 2: The CRPP’s approach directly responds to the IPCC’s call for integrated adaptation and
poverty reduction solutions for increasing adaptation effectiveness and enabling climate
resilient development
The CRPP’s proposed approach towards implementing adaptation solutions through large-scale
investment projects targeted at the poor directly responds to the IPCC’s call for integrated, multi-sectoral
solutions that address social inequities, differentiate responses based on climate risk and cut across
systems. There is high confidence that such approaches increase the feasibility and effectiveness of
adaptation in multiple sectors. There is also high confidence that climate resilient development is enabled
when governments, civil society and the private sector make inclusive development choices that prioritise
risk reduction, equity and justice, and when decision-making processes, finance and actions are integrated
across governance levels, sectors and timeframes.197 Something that is fundamental to the CRPP’s
proposed approach.
