3. Related Interventions
The paragraphs below describe selected ongoing climate change adaptation projects in the target
countries, financed by the Adaptation Fund, GCF and the Global Environment Facility (GEF), that
complement activities being proposed under the CRPP and/or have the potential to be replicated by
projects financed by the CRPP. Any investments under the CRPP directed towards the replication and
scaling-up of previous or on-going interventions will be subject to a detailed analysis of evaluation results
and feasibility studies that take into account the context specific nature of adaptation interventions.
Cambodia. The trend of adaptation investments in Cambodia from large-scale funds reflects the
immediate need for increasing the resilience of the livelihoods of the rural poor and the importance of
adaptation of the agricultural sector for protecting livelihoods and improving food security and income
levels despite the impact of climate change. The GCF funded Climate-Friendly Agribusiness Value
Chains Sector Project and Public-Social-Private Partnerships for Ecologically-Sound Agriculture and
Resilient Livelihood in Northern Tonle Sap Basin Project along with the GEFs investments in Promoting
Climate-Resilient Livelihoods in Rice-Based Communities in the Tonle Sap Region and the Adaptation
Fund’s recently completed project on Enhancing Climate Resilience of Rural Communities Living in
Protected Areas of Cambodia represent significant investment on increasing food supply and incomes
through enhancing the resilience and productivity of target crops, and increasing agricultural
competitiveness. Such interventions present an opportunity to use this momentum to invest further in
targeted climate resilient rural livelihoods activities in the poorest and highest climate risk populations in
the country and capitalize on the related knowledge and enabling environment being created under these
projects, while filling in the funding deficits. Investments that have an explicit and targeted focus on
women’s empowerment would be a particular asset in a country where the transition of employment away
from agriculture has been greater for men than for women, but this is not necessarily reflected adaptation
interventions where 198￼ Cambodia is currently undergoing a process of change in which government
structures and administrative procedures are being adapted to develop local self-governance, as financial
and human resources and decision-making capacities are gradually being transferred to the local level.
This on-going decentralization process is seen as a significant opportunity to expand-on previous and
on-going adaptation interventions by ensuring that the processes and mechanisms of local-level
government investment decision-making incorporate the tools, information and methods from previous
and on-going adaptation projects, and thus scale-up in a sustainable way the progress made so far.
Indonesia. The Adaptation Fund is financing three projects in Indonesia, two of which are highly targeted
towards the most vulnerable populations in rural Sulawesi (Adapting to Climate Change through
Sustainable Integrated Watershed Governance in Indigenous People of Ammatoa Kajang Customary
Area and Community Adaptation for Forest-Food Based Management in Saddang Watershed
Ecosystem) and the third, Safekeeping-Surviving-Sustaining towards Resilience: 3S Approach to Build
Coastal City Resilience to Climate Change Impacts and Natural Disasters in Pekalongan City, has an
urban focus. Investments in Sulawesi reflect the emerging realization that there is a clear and present
threat posed by climate change to poor rural populations in remote and isolated parts of the country that
depend heavily on subsistence agriculture for their food security. Moreover, these projects show that
there is a clear recognition that local and context specific solutions are called for in such an
environmentally and socio-culturally diverse nation. However, these relatively small-scale investments by
the Adaptation Fund in Indonesia represent only a small fraction of the local-level adaptation financing
needs targeted at poor communities, in the world’s fourth most populous country where nearly 5% of the
population have a power purchasing parity of USD1.9 a day or less. The poorest and most vulnerable
populations in Indonesia are being left behind in terms of adaptation financing, and thus there is a need
for investment in projects that have the capacity to reach a significant number of people living with high
climate risk using existing mechanisms such as social protection and decentralized planning to deliver
adaptation financing directly to the end users. More specifically, the Pekalongan City Resilience Project,
which seeks to address urban flood risk, presents an opportunity for replication via the transfer of
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

B
knowledge and capacity to other cities on the Island of Java, thus strengthening the ability to generate
transformational change through delivering complimentary investments.
Lao PDR. Current climate change adaptation financing in Lao PDR from large scale adaptation funds is
targeted towards activities which generally focus on urban and peri-urban settings, such as the GCF
funded Building resilience of urban populations with ecosystem-based solutions in Lao PDR, the GEF’s
Integrated Water Resource Management and Ecosystem-based Adaptation in the Xe Bang Hieng River
Basin and Luang Prabang City, and to a large extent the Adaptation Fund’s Enhancing the climate and
disaster resilience of the most vulnerable rural and emerging urban human settlements in Lao PDR.
Those interventions that have a specific rural livelihoods targeted approach, such as the GEF funded
Climate Smart Agriculture alternatives for upland production systems in Lao PDR are focused in the
northern highlands. Rural areas in Lao PDR account for nearly 90% of the poor population, and rural
poverty is almost three times higher than in urban areas. Furthermore, the poverty head count rate in the
central provinces is some of the highest in the country and is showing the slowest rate of reduction.199
With the current focus of adaptation investment either in urban settings or in the rural northern highlands
there is the potential of neglecting large swaths of important agricultural communities in the central
provinces that are experiencing devastating impacts from floods and droughts, which are likely to worsen
due to climate change. However, there is a clear opportunity to capitalize on the nascent national
frameworks and knowledge base regarding the fore mentioned intervention areas, and to transfer,
replicate and scale up similar initiatives to other geographies and sectors with high climate risk.
Specifically, there is need to bridge the gap related to the conservation and expansion of vegetation in
wetlands for flood protection and watershed management in rural areas, by expanding on existing
activities that have a more urban focus, and thus addressing the pressing adaptation needs of the rural
livelihoods and agriculture sector. This can be complemented by replicating climate smart agriculture
activities that are currently focused in the north of the country, by transferring the knowledge and lessons
learned to, the lesser funded, central provinces that are highly exposed and vulnerable to the impacts of
climate change.
Pakistan. There is an identifiable gap in large scale climate adaptation investments in Pakistan that
relates to the coastal zones, and specifically protecting lives and rural livelihoods from extreme climate
events. Much of the focus of investment from large-scale adaptation funds in Pakistan has been in the
inland districts of the Indus River Basin and the northern provinces, and related to flood and drought risk
management, with Glacial lake outburst floods in the northern mountainous areas of the country receiving
particular attention (GCF funded Scaling-up of Glacial Lake Outburst Flood risk reduction in Northern
Pakistan; Adaptation Fund’s now completed Reducing Risks and Vulnerabilities from Glacier Lake
Outburst Floods in Northern Pakistan; and their new project Enhance community, local and national-level
urban climate change resilience to water scarcity, caused by floods and droughts in Rawalpindi and
Nowshera, Pakistan.) By focusing investment on climate adaptive infrastructure and livelihood adaptation
in the coastal zones of the Indus River Delta, interventions in Pakistan will not only fill a funding gap in
terms of geographical distribution, but also directly complement existing investments by GCF on
Transforming the Indus Basin with Climate Resilient Agriculture and Water Management, that focus on
the provision of climate information services for livelihood decision-making (from federal to farm level).
Balancing the geographical and sectoral distribution of adaptation financing in such a way is crucial as
Pakistan's 990km coastline is located in the provinces of Sindh and Balochistan, which have the highest
rural poverty rates among Pakistan’s provinces and the highest urban-rural poverty gaps.200 The recently
approved GCF funding for the Recharge Pakistan: Building Pakistan’s resilience to climate change
through Ecosystem-based Adaptation and Green Infrastructure for integrated flood risk management will
provide examples of community-based nature-based solutions which can be potentially scaled up in other
parts of the country.
Papua New Guinea. Papua New Guinea is yet to receive adaptation funding from GCF, although the
recently published National Adaptation Plan process was supported by the GCF Readiness and
Preparatory Support Programme. The programmatic, large-scale approach proposed by the CRPP
presents an important opportunity to channel GCF’s adaptation resources into a country that is
considered high climate risk, and where over 85% of the population live in rural areas where access to
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

B
markets, services and income-generating opportunities is limited.201 There is a great deal of scope to
scale-up and transfer knowledge and capabilities from investments from other large-scale adaptation
funds, such as the Adaptation Fund’s two projects on Enhancing adaptive capacity of communities to
climate change-related floods in the North Coast and Islands Region of Papua New Guinea, and
Adaptation of Small-Scale Agriculture for Improved Food Security of Resilient Communities in Papua
New Guinea (ASSA)and GEF funded Enabling sustainable production landscapes in Eastern Highlands
and Western Highlands Provinces for Biodiversity, Human Livelihoods and Well-being, which respectively
focus on the installation of flood protection measures, supporting the uptake and commercialisation of
climate resilient crop varieties, and improved information and decision-support systems for livelihoods.
Channeling new adaptation resources to the country as part of large-scale poverty reduction projects will
provide the possibility for delivering resilient livelihood interventions at-scale and capitalize on the smaller,
more targeted investments going into the country to date. This would be an important and necessary step
forward for building the adaptive capacity of subsistence and small-scale farmers that make up over 70%
of the PNG population. Furthermore, it is self-evident that with 37.5% of the population living below the
national poverty line (USD1.90 PPP/day)202 gender inequality at extremely high levels, with the country
ranking 159 out of 160 countries on the Gender Inequality Index,203 and one of the most culturally and
geographically diverse nations on earth, Papua New Guinea, requires carefully considered and specific
investment in adaptation solutions that are explicitly pro-poor and gender empowering and that are driven
by a local approach that promotes context specificity.
Timor-Leste. Climate change adaptation financing by large scale funds to date in Timor-Leste has leaned
towards the installation of localized protective measures for rural infrastructure (GCF funded
Safeguarding rural communities and their physical and economic assets from climate induced disasters)
and larger-scale protective works (GEF Funded Strengthening Community Resilience to Climate Induced
Natural Disasters in the Dili to Ainaro Road Development Corridor). Increasing investment in agricultural
diversification, and climate resilient value chain development would balance the portfolio of investments
in the country and complement the more infrastructure focused interventions to date and address the
high risk posed by climate change to the countries important agriculture sector of which more than 80%
of the population rely as a source of income and for their food security. This need has been acknowledged
with the recently approved GEF funded Adapting to climate change and enabling sustainable land
management through productive rural communities in Timor-Leste Project. This is a sector that will
require significantly more adaptation investment going forward. The benefit of having as yet unallocated
resources as part of a pragmatic approach, also leaves open the opportunity to channel further
investments to expand on demonstrably successful infrastructure activities and replicate or scale them
up in areas of high climate risk where new resilient rural livelihood activities are being undertaken.
Vanuatu. Due to its status as a small island developing state, with high climate risk, Vanuatu is a prime
target for climate adaptation financing. Large-scale investments include projects such as Adaptation to
Climate Change in the Coastal Zone in Vanuatu, which is due to start phase II implementation with GEF
co-financing. These investments represent large contributions to financing of climate risk management
activities but place a strong emphasis on the installation of protective infrastructure along with
strengthening national and local government frameworks for climate risk reduction. To date, GCF has
complemented these investments by targeting financing at strengthening climate information services in
the country through the Climate Information Services for Resilient Development in Vanuatu project. The
current landscape of adaptation investment activities in the country presents a significant opportunity to
extend the application of the enhanced CIS mechanisms and products from on-going GCF funded
activities and compliment the more infrastructure and strategic framework focused investments of GEF,
by developing national level mechanisms that can support the delivery of targeted and timely adaptation
finance directly to the hands of the poorest and most vulnerable populations. Such a systemic approach
to adaptation will enable those people that rely on fragile livelihoods that are frequently and increasingly
disrupted by climate change related shocks and stresses, to take steps both before and after the impact
of extreme events to ensure minimal negative impacts to their sources of income and food security and
take advantage of new opportunities specific to their individual needs.

B.2 (a). Theory of change narrative and diagram
1. CRPP Vision and Objectives
The CRPP aims to build the resilience of poor and vulnerable people to the impacts of climate change in 7
countries in Asia and the Pacific region. This is considered a critical step towards achieving the desired
impact of the CRPP, which is that climate resilient sustainable development in Asia and the Pacific
region is advanced. The program theory states that in order to build the resilience of poor and vulnerable
people to the impacts of climate change, four outcomes must be achieved; (i) the enabling environment
for knowledge, finance and implementation of local adaptation measures is improved; (ii) pro-poor
adaptation finance is mobilized at scale; (iii) food security of poor and vulnerable communities is
increased; and (iv) exposure of poor and vulnerable people to climate shocks and stresses is
reduced. The CRPP’s anticipated impact is closely aligned with the GCF adaptation paradigm shift objective
of achieving climate-resilient sustainable development and the CRPP’s outcomes encompass all four of the
GCF’s adaptation result areas.
Goal Statement: IF the CRPP Trust Fund and the CRPP Investment Fund are established and provide
upstream and downstream efforts to strengthen local adaptation measures in target countries THEN
development in Asia and the Pacific region will be more climate resilient and sustainable BECAUSE the
enabling environment for knowledge, finance and implementation of pro-poor local adaptation measures at
scale in CRPP countries is strengthened AND pro-poor adaptation finance is mobilised at scale AND food
security of poor and vulnerable communities is increased AND exposure of poor and vulnerable people to
climate shocks and stresses is reduced.
2. Barriers to Strengthening the Climate Resilience of Poor and Vulnerable People in Asia and the
Pacific Region.
Research that has formed the basis of the program design, has highlighted that strengthening the climate
resilience of poor and vulnerable people in Asia and the Pacific region requires large-scale adaptation
interventions that are explicitly targeted at the poor, promote empowerment, especially of women and girls,
and that focus on local level solutions. In the absence of such interventions, future climate impacts
(described in section B1 and Annex 2.1) are likely to have catastrophic consequences for poverty reduction,
growth and sustainable development in Asia and the Pacific region. Assessments and consultations
undertaken with a range of stakeholders, including national governments, local governments, civil society
organizations, grassroots women’s organizations, and development partners, during the preparation of the
CRPP, have identified the following barriers to implementing such interventions. These barriers are common
to all seven CRPP countries.
1. Lack of suitable, locally relevant, and accessible climate information to inform resilience
investments targeted at the poor. Programs targeted at the poorest population, such as social
protection, urban informal settlement upgrade, and community-livelihoods, typically do not
adequately consider how climate hazards (current and future) will interact with underlying drivers of
exposure and vulnerability (such as poverty) and may impact the achievement of the objectives of
such programs. This is due to a combination of reasons, including information deficits that stem from
limited nation-wide availability of climate information in a format that can be used for decision-making,
a lack of government capacity, especially at local level to use climate information, along with its
uncertainties, for planning, budgeting and investments, and a lack of resources to regularly update
such information. For example, in Timor-Leste, barriers for adaptation as identified in national
climate plans includes insufficient hydro-meteorological services, limited capacity to forecast potential
threats, weak coordination within and across sectors. It also reflects an underutilisation of weather
and climate information to support decision-making, including the limited use of impact-based
forecasting tools that communicate the potential impact of hazard/s on a community or area to inform
planning; and forecast-based financing, which uses forecasts to trigger timely preparedness action
before a hazard hits the exposed population. As a result, the longer-term objectives of these
programs are often compromised due to climate shocks and stresses. For example, in Indonesia, it
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

of achieving climate-resilient sustainable development and the CRPP’s outcomes encompass all four of the
GCF’s adaptation result areas.
Goal Statement: IF the CRPP Trust Fund and the CRPP Investment Fund are established and provide
upstream and downstream efforts to strengthen local adaptation measures in target countries THEN
development in Asia and the Pacific region will be more climate resilient and sustainable BECAUSE the
enabling environment for knowledge, finance and implementation of pro-poor local adaptation measures at
scale in CRPP countries is strengthened AND pro-poor adaptation finance is mobilised at scale AND food
security of poor and vulnerable communities is increased AND exposure of poor and vulnerable people to
climate shocks and stresses is reduced.
2. Barriers to Strengthening the Climate Resilience of Poor and Vulnerable People in Asia and the
Pacific Region.
Research that has formed the basis of the program design, has highlighted that strengthening the climate
resilience of poor and vulnerable people in Asia and the Pacific region requires large-scale adaptation
interventions that are explicitly targeted at the poor, promote empowerment, especially of women and girls,
and that focus on local level solutions. In the absence of such interventions, future climate impacts
(described in section B1 and Annex 2.1) are likely to have catastrophic consequences for poverty reduction,
growth and sustainable development in Asia and the Pacific region. Assessments and consultations
undertaken with a range of stakeholders, including national governments, local governments, civil society
organizations, grassroots women’s organizations, and development partners, during the preparation of the
CRPP, have identified the following barriers to implementing such interventions. These barriers are common
to all seven CRPP countries.
1. Lack of suitable, locally relevant, and accessible climate information to inform resilience
investments targeted at the poor. Programs targeted at the poorest population, such as social
protection, urban informal settlement upgrade, and community-livelihoods, typically do not
adequately consider how climate hazards (current and future) will interact with underlying drivers of
exposure and vulnerability (such as poverty) and may impact the achievement of the objectives of
such programs. This is due to a combination of reasons, including information deficits that stem from
limited nation-wide availability of climate information in a format that can be used for decision-making,
a lack of government capacity, especially at local level to use climate information, along with its
uncertainties, for planning, budgeting and investments, and a lack of resources to regularly update
such information. For example, in Timor-Leste, barriers for adaptation as identified in national
climate plans includes insufficient hydro-meteorological services, limited capacity to forecast potential
threats, weak coordination within and across sectors. It also reflects an underutilisation of weather
and climate information to support decision-making, including the limited use of impact-based
forecasting tools that communicate the potential impact of hazard/s on a community or area to inform
planning; and forecast-based financing, which uses forecasts to trigger timely preparedness action
before a hazard hits the exposed population. As a result, the longer-term objectives of these
programs are often compromised due to climate shocks and stresses. For example, in Indonesia, it

=== PAGE 36 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 32
B
is recognized that the current systems for social protection are not yet fully prepared to deal with new
trends adequately and calls for adaptive systems that includes early warning systems.204 There is
also a major knowledge gap, particularly at local level, regarding climate resilient measures, among
planners and extension agents, including how best to support, facilitate and scale-up good practice.
For example, the Vanuatu Framework for Climate Services developed in 2016 recognize the need
to build sufficient knowledge and skills to prepare for and respond to climate threats and the need to
improve the capacities of both providers and receivers and development of platforms.205
2. Limited access to adaptation finance for implementing local solutions at scale. The
government budgets are typically insufficient to address the rising climate impacts, especially when
the measures required are not just incremental adaptation (e.g., to make infrastructure resilient), but
transformational adaptation (e.g., system-level green infrastructure which is prioritized by the local
stakeholders and implemented and monitored by local communities). Moreover, there is a typical
preference for the use of limited public resources for projects that address short-term development
priorities, yield assured near-term benefits, and generate positive streams of direct or indirect
incomes. Investments in climate adaptation are further stymied in some cases by their nature as a
public good, where investors do not take into account their positive (and negative) externalities, such
as the benefits to downstream communities and neighbouring countries. Thus, there is a need to
address the barriers that prevent government and communities taking effective action. Without
sustainable and predictable long-term finance, it will not be possible for governments to deliver the
scale of local climate adaptation needed to address impacts on the poor and most vulnerable. For
example, lack of financing, especially sustained and predictable financing for adaptation is identified
as a constrained by Timor-Leste due to limited government budget.206 The Framework for
Implementation of Climate Change Policy of Pakistan notes that financing for climate change
adaptation is a challenge and there has been lack of interest from donors to support adaptation
actions. 207 The Vanuatu Climate Change and Disaster Risk Reduction Policy (2016-2030)
recognizes that though it is one of the most vulnerable countries in the world to climate change and
disaster risks, it received little funding for climate change adaptation.208 The COVID-19 pandemic will
increase pressure on domestic finances, thereby making it even more difficult to finance
transformational adaptation measures at the local level.
3. Weak institutional and technical capacity to mainstream climate adaptation in policy and
planning and implementing adaptation solutions. Factors such as inappropriate institutional
architecture, lack of capacity for implementation, limited coordination, and limited involvement of local
stakeholders (including local private sector and civil society organizations) lead to policy failures that
make it difficult to deliver adaptation at scale. For example, in the case of Indonesia, coordination
has been identified as one of the main challenges at national, local / regional level in planning and
implementation of adaptation and the RAN-API has identified increased capacity building as one of
its four priority actions.209 While the political will for adaptation exists and a policy and legal framework
is often in place, there is typically limited institutional capacity to steer pro-poor development in a
climate resilient direction. This stems from a lack of expertise in climate risk informed development
among policy makers and planners. While the National Adaptation Planning process is building
capacity and provides a key starting point, there is a need to integrate climate risk considerations into
all aspects of pro-poor policy, planning and budgeting, including decisions on fiscal transfers, which
will in turn lead to scale-up of transformational adaptation measures that helps in alleviating poverty
in the face of increasing climate shocks and stresses. There is also limited knowledge on innovative
adaptation measures, especially at the local level.
4. Negative perceptions - risk aversion around community-level actions. Under-investment in
climate adaptation at the local level is reinforced by a typical preference for the use of limited public
resources for national level projects that align to the existing political economy (i.e. to support existing
ministry budgets and development plans) The direct benefits (avoided costs), as well as the
economic, social and environmental co-benefits that local adaptation generates, such as alleviating
poverty, ecosystem services, health and other welfare benefits, even though they are greater than
less well-targeted national interventions, are rarely identified and captured to encourage greater
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

=== PAGE 37 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 33
B
investment. There is also lower appetite to finance local level interventions as they are subject to
implementation challenges and require longer time and higher overhead. These barriers can be
addressed by introducing support to ensure high quality bankable investments and delivering at scale
to achieve impact. For example, utilizing tried and tested poverty reduction programs (e.g.,
community-driven development programs) can be efficient channel to scale up adaptation at the local
level. Information on the business case for adaptation (the direct and indirect benefits) can help to
encourage uptake.
3. Pathways of Change
The CRPP theory of change described in this section represents the theory that underpins the design of the
program and has formed the basis for the identification of the activities and outputs that will help to overcome
the barriers identified above and achieve the desired outcome and impact. The theory of change posits that
in order to achieve the desired outcome of strengthened climate resilience of poor and vulnerable people in
Asia and the Pacific Region, investments under the CRPP need to be made across three different but closely
interlinked areas of intervention, hitherto referred to as pathways. The identification of three key program
objectives has guided the development of the program theory and they are closely integrated into the three
pathways of change described below. Meeting these objectives is considered critical to strengthening
resilience and redirecting the lives and livelihoods of poor and vulnerable people toward a more climate-
resilient and sustainable future. The three objectives are:
• Mobilizing large-scale public investments that support community-level adaptation of poor and
vulnerable people.
• Developing national and local policies, plans, and programs that promote sustainable financing for
community-led adaptation.
• Increasing the meaningful participation of poor women and men in resilience-related decision-
making.
By ensuring that these objectives are met, the CRPP will contribute to transformational change through
bringing about changes in culture and decision-making, reaching beneficiaries on a large scale, and ensuring
sustainability of adaptation financing at the local level.
Pathway 1: Strengthening the enabling environment for financing and implementing pro-poor local
adaptation measures at scale in CRPP countries. The objective of pathway 1 is to overcome the current
barriers related to (i) negative perceptions and risk aversion around community-level actions; (ii) weak
institutional and technical capacity to mainstream climate adaptation in policy and planning and implementing
adaptation solutions; and (iii) lack of suitable, locally relevant, and accessible climate information to inform
resilience investments targeted at the poor. The pathway leads to the achievement of Outcome 1; the
enabling environment for knowledge, finance and implementation of local adaptation measures is improved.
The path towards achieving this outcome and overcoming the above stated barriers includes implementing
the following activities under two outputs.
Output 1: Knowledge and action research on climate risk informed pro-poor community-level solutions
strengthened.
• Bringing together international research organisations, national academic institutions, grassroots
community development organisations, national and local governments, financial institutions, and
ADB, for coordinated and structured knowledge generation and learning, through action research
and the creation of a wide range of evidence and knowledge products on climate risk informed pro-
poor local solutions. This will increase awareness and understanding among national and local
decision-makers on the benefits of local level adaptation interventions.
• Carrying out policy dialogues at sub-national, national and regional level, bringing key stakeholders
together to exchange experiences and ideas and disseminate knowledge products. This will provide
an opportunity for local level actors including local governments, communities and civil society
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

=== PAGE 38 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 34
B
organisations to share their experiences, raise awareness and influence national and local policy
related to adaptation decision-making.
Output 2: Institutional and community capacity to develop and deliver climate adaptation investments at
community-level strengthened.
• Developing participatory climate risk assessment (covering hazard, exposure and vulnerability and
how these interact and evolve with changing socioeconomic conditions) and decision support tools
and procedures and building the capacity of governments and communities to use them for climate
risk informed development planning and implementation. By strengthening decision-making
processes, women and men will have the opportunity to participate in a meaningful way in decision-
making on local adaptation measures. Capacity building and increased access to climate information
will strengthen knowledge and skills which empowers local actors to act on adaptation.
• Building capacity of local governments and communities to access international climate finance for
adaptation projects. This will support the channeling of international climate finance to the local level
so that adaptation measures prioritized by communities can be implemented.
It is expected that the proposed interventions under the outputs presented above will combine to support
changing the culture and decision-making related to adaptation investments at the local level, including
increased participation of communities in adaptation decision-making processes. Changes in decision-
making is anticipated to result in new and improved climate risk informed policies, budgets and programming,
and alter the wider national and local policy environment, regulatory frameworks and governance structure
that directly and indirectly influence public and private investment in local level pro-poor adaptation. This
represents systemic improvements and in turn links to outcome 2 as it will facilitate the mobilisation of large-
scale investment and sustainable financing of local level adaptation measures, and thus contribute to
transformational change.
Supporting assumptions are that (i) research and knowledge products address critical gaps in understanding
and awareness with regards to inclusive, pro-poor local level adaptation (ii) policy dialogues and evidence
sharing workshops are effective in building a culture of collaboration and learning between CRPP
stakeholders, and (iii) climate risk assessments and other participatory tools and procedures for climate risk
informed development planning and implementation are appropriately designed and become institutionalized
within the planning process at the local level. The key potential risk in this pathway is that changing culture
and building capacity is slower and more resource intensive than expected.
Pathway 2: Mobilising pro-poor adaptation finance at scale. The objective of this pathway is to overcome
the barrier of limited access of governments and communities to adaptation finance for implementing local
solutions at scale by mobilising large-scale domestic and international resources for pro-poor adaptation at
the local level in CRPP countries. A lack of suitable, locally relevant and accessible climate information to
inform pro-poor investments is also considered a significant barrier to mobilizing adaptation finance at scale.
Investments in improving CIS and integrating them into pro-poor climate financing decision-making
frameworks is therefore a key activity for overcoming this barrier under this pathway. The pathway leads to
the achievement of Outcome 2: Pro-poor adaptation finance mobilized at scale. The path towards achieving
this outcome and overcoming the above stated barriers includes implementing the following activities under
two outputs.
Output 3: Investments supporting inclusive pro-poor, community level adaptation prepared.
This output focuses on mobilizing international climate finance, and will;
• Provide technical assistance to support DMCs to develop new, large-scale, investment projects that
implement adaptation measures at the local level. This will include providing TA resources for climate
risk assessments as part of investment project preparation and feasibility studies.
• Provide a platform for coordinating the mobilisation of government and financing partners’, including
ADB’s, resources for investing in adaptation solutions that benefit poor and vulnerable women and
men.

Output 4: Information and systems for delivering applied climate-risk informed investments at scale
improved.
This output focuses on mobilizing domestic financing, and will:
• Improve national policies, plans and distribution mechanisms related to social protection programs
and fiscal decentralization to ensure that they are responsive to climate change concerns. By
strengthening such in-country systems for the distribution of public funds the CRPP will support the
channeling of public funds for adaptation measures that can be targeted locally and meet local
adaptation needs, especially the needs of poor women and men.
• Support the enhancement of national climate information services (CIS) to meet the information
needs of decision-makers. National systems for the distribution of public funds for local adaptation
such as adaptive social protection and climate risk informed decentralized governance processes will
need to be informed by climate risk information, and thus require improved climate information
services infrastructure. This intervention directly supports overcoming the current barrier of lack of
suitable, locally relevant, and accessible climate information to inform resilience investments targeted
at the poor.
It is expected that the interventions described above will result in increased investment from international
financial institutions in local level pro-poor climate change adaptation in CRPP countries, and increased
investment from governments in local level pro-poor climate change adaptation. This will support
transformative change by (i) creating sustainable and predictable financing through improved mechanisms
for the delivery of public funds (ii) reach scale by benefitting a large number of poor and vulnerable people,
and (iii) create systemic change through improving the participation of women and men in adaptation related
decision-making (climate risk informed decentralisation). Outcome 1 and 2 are closely linked and interrelated
as we would expect to see that with an improving enabling environment for financing and implementing pro-
poor local adaptation measures at scale in CRPP countries, the increasing political will and institutional
capacity results in stepping up the mobilisation of both domestic and international finance at scale.
Supporting assumptions are that (i) a sufficient number of appropriate large-scale investment projects for
implementing adaptation measures at the local level are identified and, (ii) improving CIS systems and
frameworks will result in their increased use in pro-poor climate financing decision-making frameworks such
as social protection systems and decentralisation processes. The key potential risk in this pathway is that
COVID-19 impact further restricts already tight governments budgets and spending capabilities that results
in reduced availability of domestic and international financing for adaptation.
Pathway 3: Implementing large-scale pro-poor adaptation solutions to build long-term capacity to
deal with climate shocks and stresses. The objective of this pathway is to implement local adaptation
measures that specifically aim to build the capacity of poor men, women and children in areas of high climate
risk to adapt to multiple, long-term and future climate risks and to learn and adjust in the aftermath of extreme
events. This pathway will help to overcome the barrier of limited access to adaptation finance for
implementing local solutions at scale. The pathway leads to the achievement of two of the program’s
outcomes; Outcome 3: Food security of poor and vulnerable communities is increased; and Outcome 4:
Exposure of poor and vulnerable people to climate shocks and stresses is reduced. The path towards
achieving this outcome and overcoming the above stated barriers includes implementing the following
activities under two outputs.
Output 5: Climate resilient pro-poor livelihoods investments implemented.
• Implement large-scale investment projects that support community-based adaptation actions that are
targeted at the poor and vulnerable population that improve agroecological systems and agriculture
supply chains and information technology and risk management services, making their livelihoods
more climate resilient.
Output 6: Climate adaptation pro-poor infrastructure implemented.
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

=== PAGE 40 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 36
B
• Implement large-scale investments projects that support community-based adaptation actions that
are targeted at the poor and vulnerable population to reduce the likelihood of the occurrence and/or
the magnitude of climate-related hazards via the installation of natural or man-made barriers or
ecosystem-based infrastructure, that block or absorb rapid-onset hazards such as floods and
creeping hazards such as sea level rise.
It is expected that by implementing climate resilient pro-poor livelihoods investments, poor and vulnerable
people will have access to the financing required to apply and adopt new resilient livelihood techniques and
skills that will improve their access to safe and nutritious food despite the impacts of climate change. This
will result in improved food security. It is also expected that by implementing climate adaptation pro-poor
infrastructure investments, governments and communities themselves will have access to financing for the
installation/construction of measures that reduce the extent and severity of the impact of climate hazards,
thus reducing the exposure of poor and vulnerable people to climate shocks and stresses. By using new or
existing large-scale government programs as vehicles for the delivery of these adaptation solutions to the
local level, the CRPP can contribute to transformational change because it (i) builds on existing national
programs that meet the needs of poor and vulnerable population and are thus pertinent and have a high buy-
in from DMCs and can be easily replicated; (ii) they are large scale in nature, but individual activities are
tailored to local circumstances; and (iii) they can facilitate deep systemic change by addressing underlying
drivers of vulnerability, and promoting equity and justice; and (iv) ensure sustainability by strengthening local
public and private institutions and creating policy incentives, and financing structures as part of a holistic
implementation approach.
The two outcomes under this pathway are closely linked as the focus on nature-based solutions for reducing
exposure to climate hazards can also contribute to improved food security outcomes through the protection
and provisioning services that they provide. Outcomes 1 and 2 can also be viewed as precursors to the
achievement outcomes 3 and 4 and they provide the political will, institutional capacity and financing for the
investments that are ultimately expected to be implemented under pathway 3. However, by capitalising on
existing opportunities, pathway 3 can start independently of the progress made on outcomes 1 and 2.
Supporting assumptions are that (i) the new techniques and skills introduced for improved climate resilient
livelihood meet the context specific needs of the participating population (ii) there is a sufficient skilled and
non-skilled labor force available to meet installation needs of green adaptive infrastructure, and new
infrastructures are built to adequate standards, and (iii) new/improved infrastructures are well maintained.
The two primary potential risks associated with the pathway are (i) low capacity and willingness of end users
to apply and adopt new techniques and skills, and (ii) low capacity and willingness of end users to maintain
and operate new infrastructure.
Box 3: The CRPP and Systems Transitions for Climate Resilient Development
Climate Resilient Development (CRD) has emerged as one of the guiding principles for climate policy and
is identified by the IPCC in its 6th Assessment Report as a core requirement to pursue sustainable
development. CRD requires the adoption of adaptation measures to meet basic needs for each human
being, eliminate poverty and enable equitable, just and sustainable development.210
System transitions have been highlighted as necessary processes for large-scale transformations and a
core enabler of CRD, requiring social, institutional and technological change within societal sub-
systems.211 The CRPP has been designed to contribute to progress in core system transitions that
catalyze broader societal transformations that steer development in a climate resilient direction.
By including adaptation options (detailed in section B3) that are targeted at the poor and vulnerable
population, and have been identified by the IPCC as offering the potential for change within the key
systems, as part of investments in new or existing large-scale government poverty reduction programs,
the CRPP can support faster transitions that contribute to more fundamental system transformations.

Co-benefits: The CRPP will have environmental, economic, social and gender co-benefits and will deliver
against a number of the SDGs, including 1 no poverty, 3 good health and wellbeing, 11 sustainable cities
and communities and 13 climate action. Some of the interventions supported by the CRPP are also likely to
have mitigation co-benefits (as highlighted in section b.3) However, two specific co-benefits are considered
to be central to the philosophy of the program.
1. Women’s participation in decision-making and leadership: Promoting gender equality is a core
thrust of the CRPP as is creating and/or improving national and local policies and planning
frameworks, so that there are policy incentives and procedures in place for the inclusion of local
people in adaptation decision-making. By emphasizing women’s participation in the strengthening of
such governance structures, women will have the opportunity to participate in a meaningful way in
decision-making on local adaptation measures. The explicit targeting of women through women
focused investments and resource flows will help to break generations of gender inequalities in
economic and human capital endowments and voice and agency that shape their climate adaptive
capacity.
2. Reduced inequalities. This social co-benefit is highlighted because of the explicit focus on low
income and disadvantaged groups, and the focus on poverty reduction and addressing existing
inequalities associated with climate change. The interventions will have positive distributional benefits
by targeting these groups, increasing the flows of finance and responsibility to them.

B.3. Project/programme description
Components, Outputs and Activities.
As outlined in section B.2, the CRPP comprises two separate but interlinked components; the CRPP Trust
Fund (TF), which focuses on upstream support to strengthen the enabling environment required for financing
and implementing local adaptation measures at scale; and the CRPP Investment Fund (IF) which focuses
on the efficient roll-out of local adaptation measures through downstream investment program. CRFPF is
not a separate legal entity, but a facility administered within and by ADB.
CRPP TF. The TF, established in August 2021, is financed by development partners and administered by
ADB. The trust fund provides technical assistance and grant resources for improving knowledge and
understanding, and strengthening institutions, processes, financial architecture, and capacity needed for
building local resilience. This would ultimately lead to a suite of investments which can be implemented by
governments with support from financial institutions. Some of these investments will be financed by the
CRPP IF. The TF will support implementation of outputs 1, 2 and 3 of the wider CRPP program (described
below). The technical assistance projects financed by CRPP TF will primarily be implemented by ADB and
the two key CRPP TF partners, including the International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED)
and the Huairou Commission (HC). Under the CRPP TF, ADB will engage IIED to implement some of the
activities related to action research and knowledge management under output 1, and HC to implement some
of the activities related to capacity building under output 2. Detailed implementation guidelines have been
developed as part of the process of operationalising the CRPP TF. Recognizing that longer-term, flexible,
and predictable funding is needed for supporting transformational adaptation at the local level, the TF will be
implemented over a period of 10 years, between 2021–2030. Implementation will be carried out in a phased
manner with phase 1 (2021-2025) with a total amount of USD75 million. To date, the Government of United
Kingdom, the Nordic Development Fund, and the French Development Agency has confirmed financial
support for the TF, among to a total of ~ USD68 million. Discussions are ongoing with other bilateral donors
and foundations to support the TF. All developing member countries of ADB are eligible to receive support
from the CRPP TF. However, due to limited availability of funding, the CRPP TF will support selected
countries. This will include all seven countries that are part of the CRPP IF plus selected additional countries.
Thus, the USD 75million from the CRPP TF will support countries included in the CRPP IF plus additional
countries. The CRPP TF will not be financed by GCF.
Gender window under CRPP TF: In order to promote investments in women-focused resilience building,
the CRPP TF has a dedicated “gender window”, amounting to approximately 15% of the TF. This window
will provide technical assistance grants to (i) undertake policy dialogue and analytical studies which make
the case for dedicated women-focused investments in adaptation at local level; (ii) undertake project
feasibility studies for such investments; and (iii) build capacity of women machineries in country and civil
society organizations, especially grassroots women’s organizations to identify, prioritize and implement local
adaptation solutions. The window will also provide grant resources to grassroots women’s organizations to
implement small-scale innovative adaptation solutions and pilot projects as part of the lesson learning and
evidence generating process. Outside of the Gender Window, gender considerations will be mainstreamed
in all activities supported by the CRPP, including projects being financed by CRPP IF.
CRPP IF. The IF will be financed by GCF and administered by ADB. It will be a program to provide critical
grant and loan resources to implement local adaptation measures as part of ADB financed investments
(projects) in seven countries that are targeted at the poorest population. Without GCF financing, these
projects will not implement local adaptation measures aiming for transformational changes. Recognizing the
importance of providing longer-term financing, the IF will have a time period of 2023–2030. Projects seeking
financing from IF will need to be likely approved by ADB Board between 2024 and 2027 and complete
implementation by 2030. The IF will have a total of USD120 million (USD100 grant and USD20 loan) from
GCF for seven countries and will leverage at least USD555 million from ADB’s resources and USD75 million
from bilateral donors and foundations through CRPP TF to support at least 10-15 projects. Under CRPP IF,
each of the seven countries will haveat least one project and will receive between USD10 million and USD40

program (described below). The allocation and use of resources under the IF will be aligned with CRPP

Components, Outputs and Activities.
As outlined in section B.2, the CRPP comprises two separate but interlinked components; the CRPP Trust
Fund (TF), which focuses on upstream support to strengthen the enabling environment required for financing
and implementing local adaptation measures at scale; and the CRPP Investment Fund (IF) which focuses
on the efficient roll-out of local adaptation measures through downstream investment program. CRFPF is
not a separate legal entity, but a facility administered within and by ADB.
CRPP TF. The TF, established in August 2021, is financed by development partners and administered by
ADB. The trust fund provides technical assistance and grant resources for improving knowledge and
understanding, and strengthening institutions, processes, financial architecture, and capacity needed for
building local resilience. This would ultimately lead to a suite of investments which can be implemented by
governments with support from financial institutions. Some of these investments will be financed by the
CRPP IF. The TF will support implementation of outputs 1, 2 and 3 of the wider CRPP program (described
below). The technical assistance projects financed by CRPP TF will primarily be implemented by ADB and
the two key CRPP TF partners, including the International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED)
and the Huairou Commission (HC). Under the CRPP TF, ADB will engage IIED to implement some of the
activities related to action research and knowledge management under output 1, and HC to implement some
of the activities related to capacity building under output 2. Detailed implementation guidelines have been
developed as part of the process of operationalising the CRPP TF. Recognizing that longer-term, flexible,
and predictable funding is needed for supporting transformational adaptation at the local level, the TF will be
implemented over a period of 10 years, between 2021–2030. Implementation will be carried out in a phased
manner with phase 1 (2021-2025) with a total amount of USD75 million. To date, the Government of United
Kingdom, the Nordic Development Fund, and the French Development Agency has confirmed financial
support for the TF, among to a total of ~ USD68 million. Discussions are ongoing with other bilateral donors
and foundations to support the TF. All developing member countries of ADB are eligible to receive support
from the CRPP TF. However, due to limited availability of funding, the CRPP TF will support selected
countries. This will include all seven countries that are part of the CRPP IF plus selected additional countries.
Thus, the USD 75million from the CRPP TF will support countries included in the CRPP IF plus additional
countries. The CRPP TF will not be financed by GCF.
Gender window under CRPP TF: In order to promote investments in women-focused resilience building,
the CRPP TF has a dedicated “gender window”, amounting to approximately 15% of the TF. This window
will provide technical assistance grants to (i) undertake policy dialogue and analytical studies which make
the case for dedicated women-focused investments in adaptation at local level; (ii) undertake project
feasibility studies for such investments; and (iii) build capacity of women machineries in country and civil
society organizations, especially grassroots women’s organizations to identify, prioritize and implement local
adaptation solutions. The window will also provide grant resources to grassroots women’s organizations to
implement small-scale innovative adaptation solutions and pilot projects as part of the lesson learning and
evidence generating process. Outside of the Gender Window, gender considerations will be mainstreamed
in all activities supported by the CRPP, including projects being financed by CRPP IF.
CRPP IF. The IF will be financed by GCF and administered by ADB. It will be a program to provide critical
grant and loan resources to implement local adaptation measures as part of ADB financed investments
(projects) in seven countries that are targeted at the poorest population. Without GCF financing, these
projects will not implement local adaptation measures aiming for transformational changes. Recognizing the
importance of providing longer-term financing, the IF will have a time period of 2023–2030. Projects seeking
financing from IF will need to be likely approved by ADB Board between 2024 and 2027 and complete
implementation by 2030. The IF will have a total of USD120 million (USD100 grant and USD20 loan) from
GCF for seven countries and will leverage at least USD555 million from ADB’s resources and USD75 million
from bilateral donors and foundations through CRPP TF to support at least 10-15 projects. Under CRPP IF,
each of the seven countries will haveat least one project and will receive between USD10 million and USD40
million. . The IF will provide grant and loan resources to implement outputs 4, 5 and 6 of the wider CRPP
program (described below). The allocation and use of resources under the IF will be aligned with CRPP |  |

theory of change, results framework, project principles and eligibility criteria (described later in this section

Interaction between the CRPP TF and CRPP IF. Some of the ways in which the CRPP TF and CRPP IF
will interact are as follows: (i) all upstream support related to action research, capacity building and
knowledge management provided through the CRPP TF will benefit the countries included in the CRPP IF;
(ii) in some cases CRPP TF may support the development of the climate rationale and project preparation
of a project, implementation of which will be financed by the CRPP IF; (iii) in some cases the CRPP TF may
support implementation of a pilot, which if found to be successful, will be scaled up through the CRPP IF;
(iv) in some cases a project may receive support from both CRPP TF and CRPP IF for implementation; (v)
projects that are financed by the CRPP IF but may not have received direct project preparation-related
support from the CRPP TF, but nevertheless lessons from such projects will be shared with the wider set of
countries that are part of the CRPP TF to advance knowledge on local adaptation; and (vi) monitoring,
evaluation and learning of the CRPP TF and CRPP IF will be undertaken together using a common results
framework. Thus, by combining upstream actions and downstream program, the two components of the
CRPP – TF and IF, will contribute to achieving the outcome defined in the previous section.
The design of the CRPP has been significantly influenced by the lessons from similar programs, especially
in Africa, funded by the Pilot Programme for Climate Resilience under the Climate Investment Fund and as
described in Box 4 below.
Box 4: Lessons from Implementation of the Pilot Programme for Climate Resilience in African
Countries
High level coordination across multiple sectors: The PPCR implementation has found that
coordination across multiple sectors supported at the highest levels of government was the most effective
approach for shaping a program of resilient investments and is promising for implementation effectiveness
and anticipated scaling up. The CRPP program design has factored this lesson by prioritizing the outputs
under CRPP TF which has a large focus on strengthening institutional coordination. Moreover, ADB has
direct relationship with ministries of finance and planning in the countries which play a key role in
strengthening coordination across sectors.
Linking and leveraging investments: The PPCR experience highlights that the expectation from
countries for linked and leveraged funds at scale through formal MDB collaboration was pivotal for country
buy-in. Both linked investments and leveraged investments were instrumental in advancing and catalyzing
countries’ resilience pathways. This lesson has been factored in the CRPP program design which aims to
provide grant resources from GCF in combination with concessional loans and grants from ADB, thereby
supporting countries to access funds for adaptation at scale.
A responsive country-based approach to resilience planning: The programmatic approach of PPCR
allows for consistency in goal and outcome within a flexible and responsive framework that considers
country capacities, political structures, and overall development regimes. This lesson has led to the design
of the CRPP as a program (and not simply a multi-country project) with multiple strongly interlinked, but
also independently robust, outputs which will provide flexibility to the countries to develop projects while
ensuring an overarching vision and common objective of strengthening community resilience. So too, not
all outputs will be implemented in all countries, thereby ensuring the GCF resources are used to fill critical
gaps, while being guided by a wider common program framework.
Facilitating private sector engagement: Upfront technical assistance and targeted advisory services
have been critical for overcoming barriers to engaging the private sector on climate resilience. This
includes piloting new modalities of climate adaptation, validating their commercial viability, and creating

an enabling environment for successful investments. This lesson has been factored in the design of the

Outputs under the CRPP TF: The CRPP TF supports activities under outputs 1, 2 and 3. Activities under
these outputs will not be financed by GCF, but as they underpin and enable the achievement of the overall
programme objectives, they are described below.
Output 1: Knowledge and action research on climate risk informed pro-poor community-level
solutions strengthened. Knowledge and support technical assistance will be provided to strengthen
knowledge, awareness and capacity of national and local institutions and communities for pursuing climate
risk informed pro-poor development, especially for improving inclusive decision-making in the context of
adaptation and resilience at the local level. Grant resources will also be provided to implement small-scale
innovative adaptation solutions and pilot projects as part of the lesson learning and evidence generating
process. This output will address issues related to risk perception in support of overcoming barriers related
to risk aversion for community adaptation solutions.
Activities. Activities will include supporting governments and communities to (i) conduct research and
analysis for identifying a suite of transformational adaptation investments that meet local needs and are
aligned with national climate priorities; (ii) organize workshops, seminars or other evidence sharing events
on pro-poor adaptation solutions to share experiences of using innovative financing options for adaptation,
including private sector financing; (iii) organise a series of policy dialogues to bring together a diverse range
of key stakeholders (both nationally and internationally) to identify solutions to overcome key barriers in
scaling up transformational adaptation that benefits poor and vulnerable populations and explore
opportunities to enhance the effectiveness and equitableness of adaptation finance delivery
mechanisms; and (iv) document and share lessons, including lessons emerging from COVID-19 response,
which are critical for building future resilience, and for sharing experiences of using innovative financing
options for adaptation, including private sector financing. Recognizing the importance of adopting adaptive
management principles, the output will include a monitoring and learning system to gather lessons on what
works and what needs to be improved.
Output 2: Institutional and community capacity to develop and deliver climate adaptation
investments at community-level strengthened. This output will strengthen institutions and build national
and local capacity to develop and deliver community-level adaptation investments at scale, that meet the
needs of the poor and vulnerable population. In doing so, this output will support overcoming the barriers
related to weak institutional and technical capacity for delivering adaptation at the local level.
Activities. Activities will support (i) the development and institutionalisation of procedures and mechanisms
for the devolution of responsibilities for adaptation planning and implementation, ensuring inclusiveness and
participation of poor and vulnerable people; (ii) the implementation of training and capacity building
workshops for government officials on applying climate risk information in the formation of plans, policies,
and programs; (iii) creating mechanisms and building the capacity of local governments and civil society
organisations for monitoring and evaluating adaptation investments; (iv) building capacity within national and
local institutions and civil society organisations, including the private sector, to access international climate
finance for adaptation projects, including linkage with Enhanced Direct Access pilot, where appropriate. This
capacity building will also build on existing GCF readiness and National Adaptation Plan related activities.
Output 3: Inclusive and pro-poor adaptation investment projects identified and prepared. This output
supports governments in developing large-scale bankable adaptation projects, that are aligned with national
adaptation priorities and address the nexus between climate and poverty, with special emphasis on women.
As such, this output supports the mobilisation of large-scale domestic and international financing for local
level adaptation and contributes to overcoming the barrier of limited access to finance for adaptation at the
local level. Selected projects prepared under this output will be implemented through the CRPP IF outputs
4, 5 and 6.

Activities. Activities under this output will; (i) support governments to prepare (feasibility studies) for
adaptation investments identified and prioritized under outputs 1 and 2; and (ii) explore the potential of
accessing concessional development and climate finance for implementation of such projects by engaging

there is no need for GCF Project Preparation Facility funding. However, the activities will be closely aligned
with the National Adaptation Plans (NAP) and GCF readiness funding and country work programs.
Gender Window: The CRPP Gender Window will support the identification, development, and
implementation of investments that have the explicit objective of strengthening the resilience of women to
climate change. As such, support will be provided through (i) technical assistance for creating an enabling
environment for financing women-focused adaptation measures, identifying investment opportunities and
preparing investment projects; and (ii) grant financing, on a selective basis, for implementing investments
identified and prepared under the technical assistance. Examples of how the Gender Window can be
leveraged to enhance gender equality outcomes of the Investment Fund in CRPP countries, include; (i)
generating the necessary political will, and commitment from governments and communities to invest in
women-focused adaptation measures that help tackle climate change; (ii) creating policy incentives and
procedures for the inclusion of women in adaptation decision-making at the local level and building their
capacity to use participatory tools and procedures for climate risk informed development planning and
implementation which can empower local women to act on adaptation; and (iii) place women at the centre
of the design of large-scale investments that explicitly strengthen the climate resilience of women,
particularly poor women, and/or adaptation investments that are led by women.
When approached together, output 1, 2 and 3 will strengthen the enabling environment in the countries for
scaling up adaptation solutions that directly benefits the poor and vulnerable populations, including women.
Outputs under CRPP IF: The CRPP IF will support activities under outputs 4, 5 and 6. These outputs will
be co-financed by ADB and GCF. In some cases, the outputs may also receive grant co-financing from
bilateral donors through the CRPP TF and/or other partner financing institutions. Selected projects emerging
from the TF will be delivered using the IF. The focus will be to deliver transformational adaptation solutions
through large-scale investments explicitly targeted at the poor and vulnerable population. The CRPP IF
proposes to combine USD555 million of ADB finance with USD120 million of financing from the GCF to
support implementation of local adaptation measures as part of ADB financed investments (projects) in
seven countries. These are also the type of investments that can support green, inclusive and resilient
COVID-19 recovery, thereby, ensuring CRPP’s alignment with COVID-19 recovery. Annex 2.2 describes
the importance of supporting these outputs in the context of increasing climate risk and barriers in scaling
up adaptation, and provides a detailed analysis of the linkages of activities with international standards and
frameworks.
Output 4: Information and systems for delivering applied climate-risk informed investments at scale
improved: Enhanced climate risk information services that can provide reliable, tailored information based
on the past, present and potential future climate will be critical for better understanding of potential risks over
various timescales, and to manage current and future climate risks across sectors. Climate information
services have also been identified by the IPCC as a key adaptation action for enabling systems transitions.
It is critically important that such information captures physical and socioeconomic information of the local
area, through engagement with local stakeholders, including women. While there has been improvement in
weather and climate forecasting and provision of downscaled climate change projections, existing climate
information services are not well focused on the user needs (sectors and at various levels) and also do not
reach “the last mile”. Often the poor and vulnerable communities whose livelihoods are climate sensitive do
not have access to usable and timely information, nor do the local governments for which such information
is fundamental to planning and financing adaptation solutions in their constituencies. Global analysis on

climate information services reveals that capacities to deliver climate-risk and reliable early warning
information services varies across countries and the functional capacities on monitoring and evaluation of
results and benefits of the use of climate services remain weak.212 Slow progress in improvements and weak
capacities to adapt such practices can be a major barrier to deal with dynamic climate risks. The State of
Climate Services, 2019 report notes that “while investments have substantially increased over the past
decade, more and better investments are still needed to ensure the provision of high-quality climate
information and services for climate-resilient action.”213
In addition, the World Meteorological Organization has identified that there is a need to invest specifically in
enhancing countries’ capacities when it comes to impact-based forecasting. Alerts need to go beyond
producing accurate forecasts and timely warnings, to better understand and anticipate the likely human and
economic impacts due to severe weather and explain what a forecast means for each given location,
specifically the types of impacts associated with the forecast to more effectively trigger early action based
on the warnings.214 Such understanding of impact is critical for informing policy and for ensuring the benefits
reach the end users such as farmers.215 This output will support countries in developing, maintaining and
using climate risk information services for pro-poor decision-making purposes for resilience, thereby
overcoming barriers related to lack of suitable, locally relevant and accessible climate information and
understanding of impacts. It will also help the large-scale mobilisation of domestic resources for pro-poor
adaptation through integrating climate risk information into decision-making frameworks for social protection
and decentralised investment planning, thus contributing to overcoming the barrier of limited access to
adaptation finance for implementing local solutions at scale. It will support the following types of activities
that are closely linked to adaptation options for advancing systems transitions, particularly Land, Oceans,
Ecosystems and Societal systems, as identified by the IPCC WG2.216 These activities will be selected based
on assessment of ongoing initiatives in respective countries in order to ensure complementarity and avoid
duplication. The activities are also closely aligned with the four pillars of the UN's newly launched Early
Warnings for All (EW4A) Initiative, which stipulates that every person in the world should be protected by
an early warning system by 2027 and aims to deliver MHEWS in over 100 countries and will contribute to
outcomes such as; improved access and quality of risk data; and strengthened capacity for developing
procedures for holistic anticipatory action based on early warnings.
Activity Area 4.1. Climate information services for key sectors to meet local adaptation needs. Under
this activity area, it will support activities such as (i) development and strengthening of national frameworks
for climate services guided by the five pillars of the Global Framework for Climate Services which includes
user interface platforms, climate services information systems, observations and monitoring, research,
modelling and prediction, and capacity building; (ii) improvements in multi-hazard early warning systems to
support impact based forecasting, especially in the context of agriculture and water resources sector – this
will be structured around the key elements identified by the WMO on Multi-hazard Impact-based Forecasting
and Warning Services, including partnerships, development of information and services, functional
requirements, capacity development and validation; and (iii) adapting and scaling up of gender-responsive
climate information services and demonstrate its application to manage farm level climate risk.
Activity Area 4.2: Climate risk informed social protection systems. Under this activity area, it will
support activities such as (i) development/strengthening of national policy frameworks and regulations on
adaptive and shock responsive social protection following the four building blocks identified by the World
Bank, namely, programs, data and information, finance, and institutional arrangement and partnerships; (ii)
through provision of hardware and software that allows acquisition, analysis, storage and visualization of
hazard, exposure and vulnerability data which can be integrated in national social protection data systems,
and trainings in undertaking climate risk-informed targeting (including community-based targeting) of social
protection program beneficiaries; (iii) through the provision of early warning equipment and trainings on
modelling, forecasting and early warning capacity, which can support forecast based financing through social
protection programs, based on lessons learned from similar initiatives being undertaken by humanitarian
agencies such as the Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies; (iv) through the provision of ICT infrastructure
that can be deployed in social protection programs to facilitate transfer of assistance in the aftermath of
extreme events in high risk areas; and (v) in providing trainings for social protection field workers to build
their capacity on disaster preparedness measures. COVID-19 pandemic has further highlighted the

importance of adaptive and shock responsive social protection and thus many countries are in the process
of strengthening social protection systems as part of their inclusive COVID-19 recovery, which directly
