provided through social protection programs.
Activity Area 4.3 Climate risk information systems for decentralization policies. This will support
national governments in strengthening decentralization policies and frameworks from climate risk
perspective based on experiences of the United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF) in introducing
performance-based climate resilience grant mechanism under its Local Climate Adaptive Living Facility
(LoCAL); specifically, (i) national and local governments in the preparation of climate risk and vulnerability
assessments and dissemination of such information in order to inform government programs on
decentralization and build capacity of local governments through trainings, workshops and consultations in
using the results of climate risk and vulnerability assessments to develop local adaptation plans, identify
adaptation investments as part of local development plans, mobilize finances for adaptation, formulate
incentives to scale up adaptation, and increase awareness among local stakeholders on adaptation; (ii) local
governments in integrating climate adaptation into local development planning and budgeting processes
including undertaking capacity building, improvement of methodologies, and strengthening public
participation processes, especially to engage local women in decision-making related to resilience building;
and (iii) implementation of adaptation measures that have been prioritized in local development plans
through the provision of small scale grants (such as grants tied to results or performance) to grassroots
women’s organizations using existing budgeting and fiscal transfer mechanisms and building capacity for
procurement and monitoring of resilience interventions. With the shared goals of increasing awareness of
and capacities to respond to climate change at the local level, mainstreaming climate change adaptation into
local government planning and budgeting systems and investments and increasing the amount of finance
available for local adaptation to climate change adaptation, the CRPP provides a significant opportunity to
replicate and scale-up some of the key activities implemented under LoCAL.
Output 5. Climate resilient pro-poor livelihoods investments implemented. Many low-income countries
in Asia and the Pacific region have predominantly agrarian societies. In Papua New Guinea for example
87% of the total population live in rural areas, and Cambodia (76%), Vanuatu (74%), Timor-Leste (69%),
Lao PDR (64%) and Pakistan (63%) all have majority rural populations. Agriculture accounts for a significant
proportion of GDP in many of these countries (Vanuatu 27%, Pakistan 23% and Cambodia 23%) and many
rural households in poor communities depend on subsistence agriculture for their livelihoods and food
security217. In Lao PDR for example, 50% of rural households are subsistence farmers with incomes below
USD300 per year and only about 30% are food secure. In Papua New Guinea and Vanuatu, employment in
agriculture is more than 50% of total employment. These people’s livelihoods are heavily dependent on
natural resources, such as rainfall that are directly influenced by changes in weather and climate, and poor
communities often inhabit marginal land on hillsides, in deserts and floodplains, and on coastal zones that
are highly exposed to floods, droughts and storm surges, which can erode their natural asset base. Subtle
changes in rainfall and temperature, as well as increasing extreme events can have significant multiple
impacts on their income and food security. This output will therefore support poor and vulnerable
communities to build their capacity to adapt to climate change by adopting adaptation measures that help to
create climate resilient sustainable livelihoods. New adaptation interventions will be needed at the farm level
to transform agroecological systems (e.g., the adoption of climate resilient crop varieties and improved soil
and water management), provide farmers in poor communities with access to climate information, early
warning and risk management services that meets their specific needs and support adoption of new
production practices (e.g., index-based weather insurance), and supply chains from local to national level
that are robust and ensure a stable supply of agricultural products and safe and nutritious food despite the
impacts of climate change (e.g., improving transport and logistics infrastructure etc.).
Activities under this output will be guided by the Sustainable Livelihoods Framework (SLF), first proposed
by the then UK Department for International Development, which identifies five types of assets or capitals
upon which livelihoods are built upon, namely; human (set of skills, knowledge, ability to work, and good
health), socio-political (quantity and quality of social resources as networks and access to wider institutions
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

=== PAGE 49 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 45
B
in society), natural (fresh water, soil quality, forests, healthy ecosystems), physical (infrastructure, services,
and productive assets), and financial (cash and other liquid resources, such as savings, credit, remittances,
pensions). The SLF has been effectively applied for exploring the many complex factors influencing
household food security and climate resilience and thus provides a useful conceptual basis for the
identification of the activities under this output.218 With its focus on capacities, vulnerabilities and livelihood
strategies, the SLF helps develop resilience-building strategies that can be effective in increasing the
capacity to cope with and adapt to climate-related impacts. This livelihood resilience perspective is
particularly useful in the context of the CRPP as it provides a basis for assessing people’s capacity for, and
differences in, perceiving risk and taking anticipatory actions, either individually or collectively, and places
people at the center of the analysis, located within, rather than dominated by, ecosystems, technologies,
political contexts, markets and resource networks.
This output will finance the following types of activities. The activities will be selected based on assessment
of ongoing initiatives in respective countries in order to ensure complementarity and to avoid unnecessary
duplication. The activities are closely aligned to the GCF paradigm shifting investment pathways outlined in
the Agriculture and Food Security Sectoral Guide, as well as the adaptation options identified by the IPCC
as offering the potential for progressing transitions in Land, Ocean and Ecosystems and Societal systems.
Some activities, such as promoting the uptake of climate smart agricultural practices are also anticipated to
have mitigation co-benefits.219
Activity Area 5.1: Climate resilient agroecological systems. The main focus will be preserving and
increasing natural capital, such as water and soil for productive purposes, and building human capital, as
identified in the SLF, through supporting knowledge and skills generation in relation to climate resilient
production practices. This output is closely aligned with the GCF Agriculture and Food Security Paradigm
Shifting Investment Pathway 1: Promoting resilient agroecology. This activity area will support activities such
as (i) provision of agriculture extension services, especially to women farmers, for new climate resilient crop
varieties and production systems to enhance crop productivity based on the local farming systems, agro-
ecological zones and climate risks; ii) supporting the adoption of agro-forestry (which also may have
additional mitigation benefits such as sequestration of carbon in biomass and soil) through developing the
skills required to establish and manage an agroforestry system (selection of trees and crops, marketing of
products, creating an enabling environment); (iii) promotion of effective and efficient use of water by adapting
and scaling up water retention, communal water harvesting and storage; iv) supporting integrated land and
water management and improvement of soil management techniques and drainage systems such as
terracing which refers to the division of hills and mountains into narrow, graduated steps to facilitate crop
cultivation, and minimum/no tillage that helps conserve soil moisture, reducing evaporative loss, thus
requiring less water than conventionally tilled field; (v) provision of small revolving grants that can support
upfront capital for women farmers to adopt climate-resilient practices and vi) supporting national
institutions to offer climate resilient employment through improved technical and vocational education and
training (TVET), including trainings targeted at women employed in agriculture.
Activity Area 5.2: Information technology and risk management services for climate resilient
livelihoods. The focus will be to build human and financial capital, as identified in the SLF, through improving
access to digital information services and low-cost risk transfer mechanisms. Building on the climate
information generated through the expanded and upgraded climate information services under output 4, this
activity area will support activities such as (i) investing in information technology systems to facilitate rapid
information flows to small-holder farmers (ii) developing low cost risk transfer mechanisms for small-holder
farmers, such as weather indexed based micro-insurance schemes tailored to individual country contexts,
to support the adoption of climate resilient production practices, (iii) Design and deliver capacity building
programs on financial literacy for insurance consumers (iv) design and deliver trainings and awareness
raising for social protection program beneficiaries, especially women, on climate-resilient livelihoods (linked
to output 4.2). This activity area is closely aligned with the GCF Agriculture and Food Security Paradigm
Shifting Investment Pathway 2: Facilitating climate informed advisory and risk management services.
Resources from the CRPP IF will not be used to cover cost of insurance premium for disaster risk financing.

Activity Area 5.3 Climate resilient agriculture supply chains. The focus will be to build human capital
and physical capital, as identified in the SLF, to deal with climate impacts to the agricultural supply chain.
This activity area is closely aligned with the GCF Agriculture and Food Security Paradigm Shifting Investment
Pathway 3: Reconfiguring food systems. This will support activities such as i) improving the transport and
logistics infrastructure, especially through the use of ICT solutions, to successfully bring products to market
despite the impact of extreme weather events due to climate change; (ii) introduction of protective measures
to the siting and storage of seeds, tools, vehicles and energy infrastructure as well as installation of new or
improved post-harvest storage and processing facilities to protect against the impact of climate change on
productive inputs and marketable produce; (iii) providing technological solutions and capacity building for
improved food processing strategies that can help increase the value and durability of perishable foods such
as fruits and vegetables. The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the importance of resilient agriculture
supply chains and are therefore being prioritized by countries as part of COVID-19 recovery and will
contribute to outcomes related to increasing food security of poor and vulnerable population.
Output 6. Climate adaptation pro-poor infrastructure implemented. There are urgent needs to scale up
investments in adaptation infrastructure, i.e., infrastructure that has a primary purpose of building resilience
to climate change (not climate proofing of development infrastructure) and would minimize the exposure and
physical vulnerabilities of the poor and vulnerable communities to the impacts of climate change and protect
their productive assets. Moreover, when designed in close collaboration with local stakeholders, such
infrastructure can provide additional benefits. For example, by favouring green over grey coastal
infrastructure to reduce impacts of storm surges, it is possible to deliver additional social and environmental
benefits, that help build community resilience, as well as providing economic benefits. This output will support
following types of activities. The activities will be selected based on assessment of ongoing initiatives in
respective countries in order to ensure complementarity and to avoid duplication. They are also closely
aligned to the adaption options identified by the IPCC as supporting Land, Ocean and Ecosystem transitions
and urban and infrastructure system transitions. Some activities will also have important mitigation co-
benefits, such as rehabilitation of mangrove forests which could potentially mitigate upwards of
−27.6 ± 1.7 Mg CO -e per hectare per year.220
2
Activity Area 6.1 Ecosystem-based infrastructure. This will support activities such as (i) national and
local governments in collaboration with national scientific organizations in identifying locally appropriate
green infrastructure to reduce exposure and vulnerability of climate impacts on lives and livelihoods of poor
and vulnerable communities; (ii) in undertaking trainings for local governments, communities and
community-based organizations in planting, rehabilitation and maintaining green infrastructure; (iii) local
governments/communities (especially women’s groups) by providing small grants for planting and
rehabilitation of green infrastructure; and (iv) in developing policy, legal frameworks and financial models for
scaling up investments in green infrastructure in partnerships with private sector. The implementation of the
activities will be guided by the IUCN Global Standards for Nature-based Solutions, which serve as a
mechanism for developing a consistent approach to designing and implementing nature-based solutions,
including ecosystem-based adaptation measures, and will thereby guide the CRPP to deploy such
investments in a systematic way, and ensure quality in the design and execution.
Activity Area 6.2 Flood and landslide protection infrastructure. This will support activities such (i)
undertaking local planning processes to identify and prioritize small scale protective infrastructure and
recognize is linkages with wider infrastructure systems; (ii) in undertaking civil works for small scale flood
protection and/or landslide protection measures, especially measures that use a combination of grey and
green measures and are prioritized by local communities; and (iii) in undertaking trainings for local
governments and communities, especially women, in maintenance of protective infrastructure.
Activity Area 6.3 Multipurpose emergency shelters. This will support activities such as (i) undertaking
local planning, with active participation of women, to identify the need of multipurpose emergency shelters
to save the lives and livestock of poor and vulnerable population in times of extreme weather events; (ii)
local governments in constructing emergency shelters (with gender inclusive and socially appropriate design
features) to reduce the exposure of poor and vulnerable population to extreme weather events; (iii) in
undertaking trainings for local governments and communities in planning and maintenance of multipurpose

emergency shelters; and (iii) in undertaking capacity building for local communities on disaster preparedness
including evacuation planning.
Outputs 4, 5 and 6 will deliver adaptation activities through the provision of combined grant finance with
major investment funding to deliver adaptation at scale at the local level. Since these outputs will be part of
wider ADB investments with governments, this will ensure scale, replicability and sustainability.
Ideas on Project Concepts
The following paragraphs provide a summary of ADB investments (projects) that while currently in their very
early stages of conceptualization, have the potential to align with the objectives of CRPP (subject to findings
of climate risk and adaptation assessments to be undertaken during project preparation). Some of these
project concepts are described in more detail in Annex 2.3, and demonstrate examples of large-scale
interventions that could serve as vehicles for the delivery of the specific local adaptation solutions described
above using the CRPP IF resources provided by GCF. Without financing from the IF, activities proposed
under these projects that explicitly promote adaptation to climate change at the local level will not be
implemented.
Cambodia: The proposed Climate Resilient Smallholder Development Project will build on the
successful implementation of past and ongoing ADB financed Tonle Sap Poverty Reduction and
Smallholder Development Project. The project promoted community-driven development through livelihood
improvement groups (LIGs) and provided them with group revolving funds managed by a committee of
members. At the end of the first production cycle, LIG members will repay the value of the inputs to the
group to establish a group revolving fund from which group members can subsequently borrow to finance
future activities. The LIG model has been shown to be a viable mechanism to enable the poor to build up
assets and subsequently to access funds from formal rural credit organizations. The LIG model enhanced
the income-earning opportunities of its members supported by credit, skills development, and market
access. The project promoted community-led smallholder development, while incorporating climate
resilience and climate risk reduction mainstreaming in agriculture development activities and project
designs. Moving forward the proposed project will build on the LIG model to strengthen community-led
adaptation actions. It will integrate four types of adaptation measures related to (i) rural infrastructure
resilience by rehabilitating rural infrastructures responding to the climate resilience condition; deploying
climate resilience varieties of crops and livestock and bio-engineering to strengthen infrastructure; (ii)
community resilience through building social networks focusing on adaptation and disaster risk
management (adaptive social protection); (iii) institutional resilience through strengthening capacity of local
institutions to integrate adaptation and disaster risks concern in development planning; and (iv) financial
resilience by mobilizing green finance and introducing insurance solutions in rural area to support
adaptation and disaster risk management efforts. The proposed project directly contributes to the activities
under output 4 and output 5 of the CRPP.
Lao PDR: The proposed Building Resilience and Reducing Rural Poverty Project will build the resilience
of rural poor in Lao PDR to climate change by expanding the coverage of the non-contributory social
assistance and integrating shock responsive features that will enable it to rapidly expand as necessary in
response to the impacts of climate and weather-related hazards, such as floods. The inclusion of shock-
responsive features will help deliver vital income support to households in the instance of a shock, such as
floods to smooth consumption and minimise negative coping strategies. The project will expand coverage of
the existing nutrition-sensitive conditional cash transfer (CCT) program implemented by the Ministry of
Agriculture and Forestry (MFA) and the World Bank into new geographic locations that have high levels of
climate and disaster risk, strengthen underdeveloped systems for the delivery of cash transfers, and build
the capacity of MFA and the Ministry of Planning and Investment (MPI) to implement priority social protection
programs. Specific actions will include, (i) integrating vulnerability to climate-risks and shocks into the social
registry and selection criteria for geographic locations and households that can receive the assistance based
on climate risk; (ii) link the social registry with early warning systems; and (iii) provide operational and
technical assistance for day-to-day implementation and project management functions such as
environmental and social safeguards management. Thus, support from the CRPP IF will support Laos
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

=== PAGE 52 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 48
B
government to make their existing social protection system more responsive to climate related shocks and
thereby use such system in the future to reach to vulnerable households in the aftermath of disasters. Further
to these activities, the program proposes to pilot an economic inclusion programme which will deliver a
package of interventions tailored to address climate vulnerabilities in selected households in conjunction
with the CCT. These may include; (i) skills training for climate resilient agriculture and non-agriculture income
generating opportunities; (ii) savings and credit support through linkages to financial services and digital
banking mechanisms; and (iii) life skills training on climate issues such as disaster preparedness and health
and livestock management in post-flood situations. This innovative climate-resilient economic inclusion pilot
will generate rigorous evidence on impact and cost-effectiveness to inform social protection and climate
adaptation policies in Lao PDR, and contribute to the global evidence base on how these programs need to
be tailored to build longer-term resilience to climate change. The project directly contributes to the activities
under output 4 and output 5 of the CRPP.
Lao PDR: The proposed Flood and Drought Mitigation and Management Project aims to increase the
resilience of rural livelihoods and reduce the economic losses from floods and droughts as a result of
increasing extreme weather events caused by climate change in Lao PDR. Flood and drought events already
occur and have been increasing in frequency over the last three decades, affecting the large proportion of
the population that relies on agricultural activities as the primary source of livelihood, and live on or below
the national poverty line. The project will address specific adaptation needs in the country and fill the current
gaps in adaptation financing by focusing on managing the risk and impacts of more frequent and intensified
floods and droughts on the lives of poor rural households in the three central provinces of Bolikhamxai,
Khammouan and Vientiane Capital. The project is expected to harness flood water for usage during dry
season and droughts and reduce damages from floods using strategies such as the planting of permanent
tree crops and/or natural regeneration of upland areas, balanced with lowland community outreach
initiatives, improve water reliability during droughts by adapting and scaling up water retention, communal
water harvesting and storage, provide modernized agrometeorological information systems and improve
nutrition awareness and facilities. The project contributes to Lao PDR’s climate change priorities by aligning
to the first target of the country’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) through investing in improved
vegetative cover of watersheds as a means of flood control and by promoting crop and nutrition
diversification. It will also support post COVID-19 economic recovery and rural resilience by (i) generating
rural employment through construction; (ii) increasing incomes through the reduction of flood damages and
losses and diversification into high value crops; and (iii) investing in better diets and sanitation. Floods,
drought, and epidemics stretch women’s resources, further exposing them to vulnerabilities. By targeting the
activities at the rural population where women in Lao traditionally take on a high proportion of the household
and farm responsibilities, the project will be able to directly support women’s gender specific needs.221 The
project directly contributes to the activities under output 5 and output 6 of the CRPP.
Pakistan: The proposed Sindh Coastal Resilience Project will enhance resilience of coastal area
livelihoods and infrastructure in the Sindh province of Pakistan through integrated water resources,
drainage, and flood risk management schemes; and restored natural protection buffers. It will reforest
mangrove species along with other fresh and saline tolerant tree species in strategic areas. In doing so, the
project will address the specific adaptation needs of the rural agrarian populations that live in the coastal
zone of the Indus Delta that are exposed to present and future climate extremes and slow onset climate
related hazards and fill an identifiable funding gap in this regard. The project will support women to play a
role in building coastal resilience as decisionmakers, stakeholders, and educators. Specifically, the project
will contribute to reducing coastal erosion rate, provide protection from storm surge, and reduce saline
intrusion. The pertinence of the project for climate adaptation in Pakistan is also reflected in the fact that
both the updated NDC (2021), and Sindh Climate Change Policy (2022) identify the Indus River delta and
coastal region as priority areas in need of (i) improved climate risk assessment, planning, and emergency
response; (ii) enhanced water resources and coastal zone management; (iii) climate-resilient protective
infrastructure; and (iv) restoration of ecosystems. The project directly contributes to the activities under
output 6 of the CRPP.
Papua New Guinea: The proposed Improved Technical and Vocational Education and Training for
Climate Resilient Employment Project aims to strengthen climate resilience through technical and

B
vocational education. In PNG, over 85% of the population are classified as rural and depend on small-scale
and subsistence farming. Further, many of these rural people live in remote and inaccessible locations. The
ongoing efforts of this population to transition out of marginalization and poverty are likely to be undermined
and reversed by climate change. In response, the project focuses on the vulnerable, small-scale farming
communities in eight target provinces. Each province is exposed to a specific set of climate hazards. The
government has prioritized strengthening the technical and vocational education (TVE) system to reduce the
poverty of the rural poor and achieve sustainable development. Building on this, the project focuses
specifically on training and vocational education for vulnerable people in the agriculture and construction
sectors. It includes specific measures to support women and informal workers. Through the TVE system,
the project will develop climate resilient agriculture, climate resilient construction processes and will help
some vulnerable people to transition out of agriculture into climate resilient livelihoods. The project will
mainstream climate change adaptation into the governance, the incentive systems, the management, the
curricula, the training modules and the training programs of the TVE system. In addition, it will pilot practices
and techniques in college-community partnerships – a learning process. The project directly contributes to
the activities under output 5 of the CRPP.
Timor-Leste: The proposed Agriculture Value Chains and Water Harvesting Project aims to enhance
the sustainability of rural livelihoods in Timor-Leste by increasing the resilience of poor subsistence farming
families to the negative impacts of climate change. Specifically, the project focuses on protecting and
improving the productivity of small-scale agriculture by using climate-smart approaches, including
investments in water and forest management and conservation. To ensure the sustainability of project
investments, the project also aims to enable smallholder producers, especially women, to expand their
participation in, contribution to, and benefit from agricultural value chains. The project will support activities
in the municipalities of Dili (non-urban), Manatuto, Manufahi, and Oecusse which together represent the
country’s six agro-ecological zones and associated farming systems and are areas that have been identified
as being at high risk from the impacts of climate change and include communities with high levels of poverty.
The project is in line with the priorities of the NDC, the National Adaptation Programme of Action to Climate
Change, and GCF country program. The project directly contributes to the activities under output 5 and 6
of the CRPP.
Vanuatu: The proposed Climate Change and COVID-19: Building Comprehensive Resilience in Poor
and Vulnerable Groups in Vanuatu Project will respond to climate challenges by creating, modifying and
enhancing climate responsive social protection systems and enhancing climate resilient livelihood support
mechanisms. Existing social protection initiatives provide targeted support payments to the vulnerable.
These are temporary, typically raised in response to disasters, and dependent on international partners.
Moreover, they do not consider climate change impacts, they are small scale and lack the institutional
capacity required to upscale. Given the projected increase in extreme weather events due to climate change,
Vanuatu requires social protection systems that are able to effectively protect the vulnerable against climate
shocks. Thus, the project will strengthen the capacity of social protection systems to function in advance of
and through climate extremes, to respond to the specific challenges of both slow and rapid onset climate
disasters, and to meet the needs of the most vulnerable. Building on existing, related initiatives in Vanuatu,
the project will also help vulnerable populations to adapt to climate change and become climate resilient by
establishing schemes that develop resilient livelihood skills and practices. The project includes a strong focus
on women. The project notably contributes to the activities under output 4 of the CRPP.
Project Eligibility criteria
Projects that seek GCF co-financing under the CRPP IF will be subject to a strict assessment and selection
process, that will be based around a framework of criteria that is closely aligned with GCF investment criteria,
while also reflecting the core values and priorities of the CRPP. These criteria are also aligned with the
selection critical for CRPP TF. In order to be considered for GCF co-financing, project proposals must also
demonstrate close alignment to the IRMF of the GCF and its indicators. The project eligibility criteria will be
applied in addition to due diligence conducted by all projects (such as safeguards) and conduct of economic
analysis as per ADB’s ongoing practice. The eligibility criteria would include the following. See Annex 2.4
for more details.

i. Impact potential: Following criteria will be used to determine the project’s impact potential
a. The project must clearly set out the specific climate risks (hazard, exposure and vulnerabilities),
under current and future conditions of climate change and socioeconomic development, that the
project aims to address, articulating a clear causal narrative between specific activities and their
objective of reducing climate risk. Projects that include arguments that are well evidenced and
quantified using reliable data sources and information will be prioritized. [Required]
b. Prioritization will be given to those projects that have targeting intervention (TI) for poor population
– (TI-household); (TI-Geographic); or (TI- SDG)222 [Strongly Desired]
c. The project must clearly describe the adaptation benefit that is expected to be generated by the
implementation of the project activities. Only projects that identify measurable adaptation benefits
will be prioritized.
d. Projects must align to GCF adaptation result areas and prioritization will be given to those projects
that have higher expected final targets for the related indicators.
e. Prioritization will be given for projects with a higher expected total number of beneficiaries relative
to total population (disaggregated by gender)
f. Prioritization will be given for projects with lower cost per beneficiary
ii. Paradigm shift potential: The potential of the sub-project to catalyze impact beyond a one-off
project investment will be determined through following criteria:
a. The project must clearly describe how the project outcome will be sustainable in the long run
i.e., through integration into national/local development processes, through securing additional
public and/or private financing; and capacity of national/local institutions to implement similar
activities without GCF funding. [e.g., climate risk informed national targeting systems for social
protection programs] [Required]
b. Prioritization will be given to projects which demonstrate the potential of being replicated
elsewhere in the same country or other countries in region. [e.g., successful agroforestry
initiatives replicated in different ecological zones of a country] [Strongly Desired]
c. The project promotes innovation, such as, through the development and/or adoption of new
technology or approaches which can help address adaptation barriers in the region. [e.g., use of
ecosystem-based solutions to improve water management in urban informal settlements]
[Desired]
d. The project promotes sharing of knowledge and learning within and with other CRPP countries
[Required]
iii. Sustainable development potential: All projects must demonstrate sustainable development
potential by identifying at least one positive co-benefit from the following and have associated
indicators. Prioritization will be given to projects that demonstrate more than one co-benefit.
[Required]
a. Economic co-benefits –explicitly aim at poverty reduction
b. Social co-benefits – human health and social development through improved food and nutrition
security and reduced loss of life resulting from the impact of extreme weather events
c. Environmental co-benefits –improved ecosystem services and biodiversity
iv. Gender: Gender is a standalone criterion that projects must meet independently of the
environmental, social and economic co-benefits. The project must either be categorized as Gender
Equity Theme (GEN) or Effective Gender Mainstreaming (EGM) as per Guidelines for Gender
Mainstreaming Categories of ADB Projects6 [Required] A project is assigned “gender equity theme”
(GEN) if the project outcome directly addresses gender equality and/or women's empowerment by
narrowing gender disparities, including under the five pillars: (i) women’s economic empowerment
increased, (ii) gender equality in human development enhanced, (iii) gender equality in decision-
making and leadership enhanced, (iv) women’s time poverty and drudgery reduced, and (v) women’s
6 The projects of the Asian Development Bank have four gender mainstreaming categories (i) category I: gender equity as a theme (GEN);

elements (NGE).

v. Needs of the Recipient: Following criteria will be used to determine how far the project meets the

a. The project aims to overcome barriers related to technical, institutional and/or financial barriers

generating outputs and non-market elements. [Required]
b. Resources from CRPP IF are blended with ADB grants and/or loans (to act as ADB co-financing)
in order to augment the volume of financing available for adaptation and better tailor
concessionality to achieve transformative investments which would otherwise not proceed. The
ratio GCF financing: ADB Grant/Loan should at least be 1: 4 [Required]
c. Projects should ensure that the concessional resources from GCF do not displace or substitute
investments that might have taken place anyway using regular ADB borrowing. [Required]

B.4. Implementation arrangements (max. 1500 words, approximately 3 pages plus diagrams)
1. Executing Entity of CRPP
As Executing Entity for the CRPP, ADB will be responsible for the overall Program, particularly the provision
of technical assistance support under CRPP TF (Component 1), and the provision of grants and loans for
projects under CRPP IF (Component 2).
Subject to GCF Board approval for this funding proposal, ADB and GCF will enter into a program-specific
legal agreement (the “Funded Activity Agreement” or “FAA”) in accordance with the AMA, which will set out
the specific details concerning GCF’s provision of and ADB’s administration of the GCF funds.
GCF funds for the CRPP will be ring-fenced within an ADB GCF Trust Fund which was created pursuant to
the AMA, and as such benefit from the same privileges and immunities as ADB’s resources. Usage of GCF
funds will be based on criteria outlined in this proposal which will be included in dedicated IF Implementation
Guidelines to be developed during inception. These guidelines will complement the program Term Sheet
and FAA, and include further guidance on implementation arrangements, project selection and prioritization,
monitoring and evaluation, and reporting.
For Projects implemented by an executing agency and/or implementing agency (each as defined by ADB),
where such agency will be using or channeling GCF Proceeds for the purposes of the Funded Activity and/or
such agency will execute, carry out or implement Funded Activities, the executing agency and/or
implementing agency will be the Executing Entity. In such cases, in addition to the implementation
arrangements described in this Funding Proposal, ADB will enter into a subsidiary agreement with the
relevant Executing Entity.
2. CRPP IF Legal Arrangements
Under CRPP IF, ADB will offer concessional loan and grants to sovereign borrowers to be funded by GCF.
For each CRPP IF project, ADB will sign separate loan and/or grant agreements with the sovereign
borrowers/beneficiaries for each source of financing (i.e. ADB’s own resources and GCF funds), and through
this, each project will be implemented in compliance with ADB policies and CRPP requirements. Depending
on the structure of the project, ADB will also enter into project-level agreements with relevant borrower’s
agencies for the implementation of projects. Such agencies may include financial intermediaries, such as
National Development Banks and potentially, GCF Direct Access Entities, where feasible. If additional co-
financing from other partner financial institutions are also included, these will be provided in parallel to the
ADB and GCF funded loans and grants. Loans funded by GCF funds are expected to be pari passu with the
ADB loans, except for the interest rate and tenor applicable to the GCF funds.
For each project, ADB enters into separate legal agreements with borrowers/recipients for each financing
source. A loan/grant from ADB’s own resources will be covered by one legal agreement, while the
loan/grant from GCF funds will be covered by another legal agreement, with cross-references between the
two as appropriate. (Figure 3)

ADB and GCF funded loans and grants. Loans funded by GCF funds are expected to be pari passu with the
ADB loans, except for the interest rate and tenor applicable to the GCF funds.
For each project, ADB enters into separate legal agreements with borrowers/recipients for each financing
source. A loan/grant from ADB’s own resources will be covered by one legal agreement, while the
loan/grant from GCF funds will be covered by another legal agreement, with cross-references between the
two as appropriate. (Figure 3)

3. CRPP IF Flow of Funds
Figure 4 shows the flow of funds related to CRPP TF and IF, in line with the program description and

The CRPP IF will be implemented from 2023 to 2030. Projects seeking financing from IF will need to be

which will be supported by the program will be identified in accordance with ADB’s country programming
process and selected using the eligibility criteria presented in this proposal. Disbursement requests from
ADB to GCF are expected to be made on an annual basis in accordance with the expected ADB approval
dates, and projected disbursement plans and timelines of the projects in the CRPP pipeline. Funds will be
disbursed by GCF into existing ADB trust fund that has been established for GCF financed projects, and
subsequently deployed to approved projects in accordance with ADB policies and procedures.
Payments of interest and principal for GCF funded projects loans will be repaid back to ADB, into the ADB
GCF Trust Fund. Principal, interest payments, and any unused funds or income will be subsequently
returned to GCF.

4. CRPP TF Legal arrangement and Flow of Funds
The CRPPTF was established in 2021 as a multi-donor trust fund under CRFPF to support TA projects, and
any other activities that may be agreed upon between financing partners and ADB. Contributions from
bilateral donors will be held and administered by ADB separately from ADB’s other resources. Contributions
to financial partnerships will be effected through an Instrument of Contribution or through the signing of a
trust fund contribution agreement.
5. Role of ADB
As a GCF AE, ADB and GCF have entered into several project-specific legal agreements which are under
implementation, delivering climate impacts throughout ADB’s developing member countries.
In its capacity as AE and Executing Entity, ADB will administer grants and loans from GCF under the
CRPP IF as follows:
• Provide grants and loans as per the CRPP IF terms and requirements, alongside loans using ADB
own funds and other ADB-administered parallel financing (as appropriate), applying the same duty
of care and due diligence for all sources.
• Carry out such management and administration of the GCF funds for grants and loans in
accordance with its policies, procedures and practices, and with at least the same degree of care
as it uses in the administration of its own funds or other donor funds, consistent with the AMA.
• Establish a governance structure of the CRFPF will comprise of (i) CRFPF Partnership Group; (ii)
CRFPF Steering Committee (iii) CRFPF Working Group; and (iv) CRFPF Secretariat.
• Oversee and manage the dedicated CRPP Project Structuring Team, staffed by full-time and
intermittent experts, including an additional experts specifically engaged for the CRPP, with the
following responsibilities:
o originate projects and develop a pipeline for CRPP funding,
o provide support to structure projects and identify financing partners;

6. Governance Structure of CRPP
The CRPP will be operationalised through the Community Resilience Financing Partnership Facility
(CRFPF), implemented and managed by ADB, the Accredited Entity. The Facility will aim to mobilize financial
and knowledge resources from various development partners to support scaling up of climate adaptation
investments at local level. A key objective of the Facility is to help strengthen partnerships in the climate
adaptation space, especially in the context of local actions for climate adaptation, among governments,
donors, civil society, and the private sector, and influence regional and global directions on community led
adaptation and thereby advance elements of locally led adaptation principles.
The governance structure of the CRFPF will comprise of (i) CRFPF Partnership Group; (ii) CRFPF Steering
Committee (iii) CRFPF Working Group; and (iv) CRFPF Secretariat. (Figure 5).
CRFPF Partnership Group: The CRFPF Partnership Group will be the primary advisory body to ensure the
expected outcomes of the CRPP are achieved. The CRFPF Partnership Group will have a Chair and a Co-
Chair. A representative from ADB will serve as the Chair. A member from one of the CRPP financing partners
will serve as the Co-Chair. Specific roles and responsibilities of the CRFPF Partnership Group will include:
(i) selecting the co-chair (on an annual basis); (ii) providing strategic direction to the CRPP in line with the
results framework; (iii) review and approve CRPP annual report; (iv) establishing linkage between CRPP
and other global and regional resilience programs; (v) providing guidance on mobilization of resources for
CRPP TF; (vi) approving the TOR for CRPP-related strategic studies and evaluations to guide the results
and assess the impact of the program; and (vi) providing inputs and attend the annual CRPP Partnership
Forum.
The Members of the Partnership Group will include (i) Asian Development Bank – represented by the CRFPF
Facility Manager; (ii) Countries and financial institutions that provide financial contribution to the TF and/or
IF; (iii) countries that receive CRPP support; (iv) Non-financing partners - International Institute for
Environment and Development and Huairou Commission; and (vii) Independent technical advisors (two
positions, on an annual basis). Such an inclusive governance structure will enable successful delivery of the
CRPP programmatic approach and be able to influence wider actions in support of community-resilience,
thereby enabling larger impact of the program beyond its immediate footprint.
CRFPF Steering Committee: The CRFPF Steering Committee will be responsible for (i) approving CRFPF
annual work plan based on endorsement received from financing partners; (ii) approving allocation of
resources for specific projects in alignment with the eligibility criteria defined in the CRFPF TF and IF
implementation guidelines; and (iii) approving the CRFPF annual report based on endorsement from
financing partners. The Steering Committee will be chaired by Director General, Climate Change and
Sustainable Development Department (CCSD) of ADB and the members of the Steering Committee will
include the Directors General of the user departments, i.e. ADB departments applying for resources from
CRPP TF and IF. The Chair of the CRPP Steering Committee will the designated authority for approving
allocation of CRFPF resources for specific projects. After approval by the CRPP Steering Committee for
fund allocation, the proposals will be processed in accordance with all relevant policies and procedures for
technical assistance and grant approval, including without limitation, consulting services and procurement,
social and environmental safeguards, financial management and reporting, and anticorruption and
governance.

CRFPF Working Group: The CRFPF Working Group will be responsible for reviewing project proposals

sub—projects and sharing the minutes with GCF; (v) monitoring, evaluation and learning; (vi) fostering
partnerships with relevant institutions and programs at global and regional level; and (vii) disseminate the
CRPP results and achievements. The role of gender expert will be to ensure gender requirements are being
met.

7. Allocation of Resources
The administration of different funds under the CRFPF is governed by respective Implementation Guidelines
that would be endorsed by the respective CRFPF financing partners and approved by the CRFPF Steering
Committee on or before the first fund allocation. The CRPP IF Implementation Guidelines will be endorsed
by GCF before approval by CRFPF Steering Committee. The Implementation Guidelines can be amended
from time to time, reflecting revisions in CRFPF operations. The Steering Committee will approve any change
or amendment after concurrence by the respective financing partner(s), and the Facility Manager will
communicate the changes and amendments to the financing partner(s) and relevant ADB user departments.
Procedure for Allocation of Resources from CRPP TF: The procedure for allocation of resources from
TF (not funded by GCF) will include the following steps:
▪ Project proposals for TF can be initiated by countries, development partners, and ADB. In Q1 of each
year, the CRPP Secretariat in close consultation with the CRPP Partnership Group will prepare the
annual work plan which would include the list of prioritized project proposal. The work plan for the TF
will be approved by the financing partners of the CRPP TF.
▪ ADB user department will prepare project proposal using the application form (to be developed as
part of Implementation Guidelines) and draft concept paper in standard ADB concept paper format
and will submit them to the CRPP Secretariat, depending on the nature of application. Applications
will be reviewed in batches.
▪ The applications will be reviewed by the CRPP Secretariat to ensure that they comply with the
eligibility criteria described in the Implementation Guidelines and priorities in the annual work plan. If
the application does not meet the criteria, the CRPP Fund Manager will discuss the issues with the
user department for revision or withdrawal. If the application complies, the application will be included
in the batch for circulation to the CRPP Working Group, as the case may be. The CRPP Fund
Manager will make a recommendation to the CRPP Working Group on each proposal based on three
criteria: (i) compliance with the implementation guidelines for the use of the funds, (ii) estimated
amount of climate finance, and (iii) the overall responsiveness to the eligibility criteria. The CRPP
Fund Manager will also advise the respective working groups on the availability of CRPP TF
resources to support the applications.
▪ The working groups will have seven working days for review, comment, and endorsement. The user
department will then have five working days to take the comments into consideration and revise (if
necessary) the application. Once completed, the CRPP Fund Manager will forward the applications
to the CRPP Steering Committee to approve the allocation of resources from the CRPP TF.
▪ After approval by the CRPP Steering Committee for fund allocation, the proposals will be processed
in accordance with all relevant policies and procedures for TA and grant approval, including without
limitation, consulting services and procurement, social and environmental safeguards, financial
management and reporting, and anticorruption and governance.
Procedure for Allocation of Resources from CRPP IF: The GCF funds for the CRPP IF will be ring-
fenced within ADB GCF Trust Fund which was created pursuant to the AMA. Usage of GCF funds for
individual projects will be based on criteria outlined in this proposal which will be included in a dedicated
CRPP IF Implementation Guidelines to be developed during inception. The procedure for allocation of
resources from CRPP IF (which will blend ADB and GCF finance) will include the following steps:
▪ Project proposals for CRPP IF can be initiated by ADB in discussion with relevant government. In Q1
of each year, the CRPP Secretariat in close consultation with the CRPP Partnership Group will
prepare the annual work plan which would include the list of prioritized project proposal.
▪ ADB user department will prepare project proposal using the application form (to be developed as
part of Implementation Guidelines) and draft project document in standard ADB format and will submit
them to the CRPP Secretariat, depending on the nature of application. Applications will be reviewed
in batches.
▪ The applications will be reviewed by the CRPP Secretariat to ensure that they comply with the
eligibility criteria (Annex 2.4). If the application does not meet the criteria, the CRPP Fund Manager
will discuss the issues with the user department for revision or withdrawal. If the application complies,
the application will be included in the batch for circulation to the CRPP Working Group, as the case

8. Track Record of ADB
ADB will administer the Community Resilience Financing Partnership Facility, which will include the CRPP
TF and the CRPP IF. ADB has vast experience in developing and financing climate adaptation projects and
in administering Trust Funds, as described in paragraphs below.
ADB commitments in scaling up in climate adaptation. ADB has an extensive experience in developing,
financing and implementing climate adaptation projects in Asia and the Pacific region. ADB has approved
its Strategy 2030, which recognizes “resilience” as a key objective for achieving sustainable and inclusive
development in Asia and the Pacific. ADB’s Strategy 2030 identifies seven operational priorities, including a
priority on “Tackling climate change, building climate and disaster resilience, and enhancing environmental
sustainability.” The Strategy sets out that in order to achieve its climate objectives, ADB will scale up its
climate financing targets to ensure that (i)’ 75% of the number of its committed operations (on a three-year
rolling average, including sovereign and non-sovereign operations) will be supporting climate change
mitigation and adaptation by 2030’; and (ii) ‘climate finance from ADB’s own resources will reach USD80
billion cumulatively from 2019 to 2030. Further, in 2021, ADB has announced its ambition of increasing total
climate finance from USD80 billion to USD100 billion by 2030, out of which around USD34 billion will support
climate adaptation. In 2021, ADB has also announced its commitment to align its new operations with the
goals of the Paris Agreement starting July 2023 for sovereign operations. Meeting these climate targets will
require expanding investments in climate adaptation and ensuring that the benefits of such investments
reaches the poorest and vulnerable population. It will also require strengthening country capacity to
undertake transformational planning and programming that encourages paradigm shift, closely aligned with
NDCs, National Adaptation Plans and National Disaster Risk Reduction Plans, which is directly aligned with
GCFs strategic priorities 2020-2023. The CRPP aims to help ADB achieve its ambitious climate objectives
and targets and develop and finance a new generation of adaptation projects.
ADB’s priorities on climate adaptation. ADB has been one of the leading MDBs on climate change. It has
been implementing a climate risk management framework since 2014. Application of the framework is
mandatory in all ADB investments and runs from the early concept phase of a project through to
implementation. The framework allows integrating climate risk considerations systematically in ADB financed
projects. However, recognizing the importance of increasing climate risk and its huge impact on vulnerable
countries and population, ADB aims to scale up investments in projects that have the primary purpose of
adaptation and addressing underlying drivers of vulnerability. It is expected that such projects can help steer
development in a resilient direction and catalyse transformational planning and programming, which is in
line with GCF’s strategic priorities 2020-2023. It is important that such projects advance resilience in four

B.5. Justification for GCF funding request
Why GCF financing?
The CRPP IF will use financing from GCF in order to support:
The poorest countries with high exposure to climate risk in implementing transformational
adaptation measures. The CRPP IF aims to support adaptation projects in (i) low-income developing
countries that confront severe structural impediments to sustainable development and climate change
adaptation, i.e. that are highly vulnerable to climate shocks and stresses and have low levels of adaptive
capacity (technical, financial and human) to undertake adaptation measures at scale; (ii) small islands
developing states that experience high climate related shocks today and face very high future climate change
risks, and have a narrow resource bases, thereby with high needs for adaptation; and (iii) in targeted poor
communities (rural and urban) in middle-income countries. While these countries have identified adaptation
as a climate priority, actions at scale remain limited due to lack of financing to support measures that aim for
transformational change. Targeting the poorest and most vulnerable countries is in line with the use of GCF
finance to meet the additional costs of climate action that would otherwise not be available for vulnerable
groups. The focus on the poorest countries and communities becomes even more important in the post
COVID-19 context, which has hit the poor the hardest.
The poorest and most vulnerable communities in enhancing their well-being despite increasing
climate impacts. The CRPP has an explicit focus on adaptation solutions at the local level. Thus, CRPP IF
will only support local adaptation measures that are targeted at the poorest and most vulnerable
communities. While government budgets and supporting international development, finance is helping these
groups, there are insufficient funds to address the rising costs of climate impacts, without which, the numbers
in poverty are projected to increase. Domestic budgets are not available to meet this shortfall. Part of this
shortfall will be addressed by concessional ADB funding with a combination of loan and grant depending on

as a climate priority, actions at scale remain limited due to lack of financing to support measures that aim for
transformational change. Targeting the poorest and most vulnerable countries is in line with the use of GCF
finance to meet the additional costs of climate action that would otherwise not be available for vulnerable
groups. The focus on the poorest countries and communities becomes even more important in the post
COVID-19 context, which has hit the poor the hardest.
The poorest and most vulnerable communities in enhancing their well-being despite increasing
climate impacts. The CRPP has an explicit focus on adaptation solutions at the local level. Thus, CRPP IF
will only support local adaptation measures that are targeted at the poorest and most vulnerable
communities. While government budgets and supporting international development, finance is helping these
groups, there are insufficient funds to address the rising costs of climate impacts, without which, the numbers
in poverty are projected to increase. Domestic budgets are not available to meet this shortfall. Part of this
shortfall will be addressed by concessional ADB funding with a combination of loan and grant depending on

=== PAGE 64 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 60
B
country status, but the rate of indebtedness of many governments means that not all interventions can be
supported through loans, even at concessional rates. However, without access to concessional financing,
these communities will not be able to undertake adaptation measures and thereby not escaping climate-
induced poverty. The situation has become even worst in the current pandemic. Targeting the poorest and
most vulnerable communities is in line with the use of GCF finance to meet the additional costs of climate
action that would otherwise not be available for vulnerable groups.
Projects promoting adaptation measures as public goods. Investments in adaptation are often stymied
by their public good nature. Such investments may be underfunded because investors do not take account
of their positive externalities, such as the benefits to downstream communities in flood risk management.
Moreover, as discussed earlier, a key barrier for scaling up adaptation is the fact that adaptation finance is
not reaching the local level, where it is needed the most. This requires improving national and local financial
systems through climate risk information, improved poverty and vulnerability databases for targeting, digital
technology to enable reliable transfer of resources, and local capacity to administer resources. Specifically
grant financing from GCF will be critical to help implement adaptation measures that act as public good,
especially in the post-COVID-19 context where the financial capacity of countries are already stretched, and
thereby enabling the flow of future adaptation finance to the front line.
Projects implementing transformational adaptation measures. The CRPP has a focus on promoting
transformational adaptation that address the nexus of climate change, gender and poverty i.e., measures
that aims at fundamentally changing systems and that challenges and seeks to dismantle the social, political
processes and structures that construct vulnerability, and allow it to accumulate and persist.
Transformational adaptation is particularly important when solutions are targeted at the poorest
communities, since the barriers faced by these communities are not just restricted to technical and financial,
but equally include social and political set-up, perceptions and biases. Thus, transformational measures will
allow adopting inclusive approaches, so that poor and vulnerable communities, especially women, have an
equal seat at the table and are in a position to interact with different stakeholders, leading to a process where
different interests are negotiated. Without financing, especially grant financing from GCF, it will not be
possible to promote such transformational measures. The proposed concessional finance from GCF through
CRPP will address the barriers to the uptake of transformational adaptation, and thus justifies GCF funding.
In turn, this will allow greater leveraging of ADB investment, thus increasing the total level of finance flowing
to the most vulnerable groups. While incremental adaptation is equally critical, it will be financed as part of
ADB’s regular financing.
Project outputs with non-revenue elements. Under-investment in adaptation is reinforced by a typical
preference for the use of limited public resources for projects that address short-term development priorities,
yield assured near-term benefits, and generate positive streams of direct or indirect income, particularly in
poorest countries. With loan financing, governments also prefer projects that support direct capital recovery.
However, the benefits of adaptation projects are realized in the form of reduces losses (which may not be
reaped for many years), rather than streams of positive income. Thus, grant resources from GCF will be
critical to help to reduce the cost of investment sufficiently to offset the incremental costs of climate-resilient
investment, especially where this is funding non-market elements (e.g., nature-based solutions, and thus
green over grey) or targeting extremely vulnerable groups where there is low potential for revenue
generation. Moreover, such measures often generate co-benefits, such as alleviating poverty, enhancing
development and other welfare benefits, which need to be better identified and captured to encourage
greater investments.
Overcoming risk perceptions of community level adaptation interventions. Implementing adaptation
measures that are local yet can be implemented at scale remains a challenge, partly due to the fact that
local measures have high transaction cost, are subject to local governance-related challenges and favour
for supporting national level projects that align to existing political economy. However, the benefits of
implementing adaptation measures at local level through local institutions and communities are many and
critical if long-term sustainability is to be ensured. The CRPP IF can demonstrate the benefits of
decentralized and inclusive solutions that are designed based on principles of subsidiarity. Thus,
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

=== PAGE 65 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 61
B
concessional financing will improve the bankability of community resilience projects with national
governments, allowing more innovative measures to be taken.
Thus, without GCF support, current opportunities for transformational adaptation for the poor and vulnerable
will not be realized. The GCF funds provided will serve the dual purpose of making the community resilience
investment more viable, while providing immediate adaptation benefits to local populations. By offering
critical resources from GCF in combination with the ADB’s finance, the CRPP IF will enable countries to
implement local adaptation measures, that they would otherwise not be able to do. GCF contribution of
USD120 million will leverage a further USD555 million of ADB finance and USD75 million of financing from
other bilateral donors (through the TF), representing more than fivefold leveraging ratio for every USD of
GCF finance invested. The GCF’s ability to offer grant finance will drive ADB’s co-financing into the most
transformational and paradigm-shifting investments as shown in Figure 6.
Level of concessionality: The CRPP aims to promote transformational adaptation measures that benefits
the poorest population. All projects seeking grant financing from CRPP IF will be designed to comply with
the use of GCF grant finance and with the principles set out in decision B.09/04. The grant elements will be
tailored to
▪ Cover the incremental cost or the risk premium required to make investments viable and/or
overcome risk perception, i.e., to meet the additional costs of ecosystem-based measures, cost of
building new livelihoods-related skills, or to create incentives for behavioural change.
▪ Showcase demonstration effect, i.e., where there is clear demonstration effect in relation to new
technology, approach or market, which if needed, is then further supported by TA through CRPP TF
to ensure scale-up.
▪ Cover technical assistance for climate resilient activities and integration.
▪ Cover the additional costs of climate action that would otherwise not be available, particularly for
transformational adaptation activities for poor and vulnerable groups.
Figure 6: Allocation of Funding Source by Adaptation Measures
In all cases, the projects will be designed to address barriers and create the enabling environment for
adaptation, to leverage on existing public and private finance, and to ensure there is no distortion or
displacement of existing public or private sector funds. The following paragraphs set out the concessionality
argument for each of three outputs proposed for financing under CRPP IF:

B
Output 4: The GCF grant finance for climate information for delivering climate-risk informed decisions is
targeted to address information failures that prevent climate resilient development and will be largely focused
on technical assistance provision (which is eligible for grant finance under B.05/07) to cover the additional
activities to strengthen climate services at local level, to integrate climate risk information into social
protection programs and decentralizations policies. It is also highlighted that these activities will cover
activities that explicitly target the most vulnerable groups.
Output 5: The GCF grant finance for climate resilient pro-poor livelihood investment will focus on addressing
risk perceptions for new climate-resilient livelihoods or markets, and to cover the incremental cost or the risk
premium required to make these new livelihoods or investments viable. Again, the activities will also be
targeted at the most vulnerable groups
Output 6: The GCF grant and loan finance for climate resilient pro-poor infrastructure investment is
targeted at the additional costs of green, resilience infrastructure, which are needed to deal with climate
risks and that would otherwise not be available, for poor and vulnerable groups. The primary focus is to
invest in ecosystem-based adaptation, as this provides a range of public good characteristics, and has
benefits in reducing non-market costs (providing environmental and social benefits).
B.6. Exit strategy
The CRPP is designed to promote sustainability through the adoption of the following approaches:
The CRPP will support outputs that are closely aligned with national climate priorities and to address climate
impacts that hinders the achievement of poverty reduction. With a key focus on mainstreaming, the CRPP
TF will catalyze impacts beyond a one-off project investment and deliver a paradigm shift by ensuring that
climate risk informed pro-poor development becomes the new normal. It will do so by strengthening policies
and regulatory frameworks that promote climate-sensitive development, and through capacity building on
use of climate risk information for decision-making, with policy makers, planners, and local government and
communities. This will ensure the sustainability of outcomes beyond completion of the project. The GCF
financing will be used through the CRPP IF to support rolling out of such climate-sensitive development,
especially in the context of localization and decentralization. By strengthening national and local
institutions, the CRPP IF will ensure that its interventions will contribute to building policy coherence around
climate resilience, and is taken up nationwide by relevant agencies. Countries’ ownership will be achieved
through stakeholder engagement and capacity building at various decision-making levels – government,
civil society organizations, communities, financial intermediaries, and the private sector. With such a wide-
ranging target, the CRPP will contribute to bringing about a paradigm shift.
Scaling up adaptation in the context of pro-poor development. The CRPP is based on the understanding
that poverty reduction strategies/programs financed by national and local budgets will not be achieved due
to the increasing impacts of climate change and thus need to be designed with a strong climate rationale.
Accordingly, the CRPP TF will work with countries to integrate the CRPP activities fully with such
opportunities, build capacity, and support in preparing such programs. Projects seeking finances from CRPP
IF will have to demonstrate that proposed adaptation outputs are embedded within large programs that are
being partly financed by government, and therefore will be continued beyond CRPP life span. For example,
it will support integration of climate risk information in national social protection policies and programs that
are embedded in national legislation and financed by government budgets.
Promoting adaptation through national curriculum systems. The CRPP recognizes that
transformational solutions will require building life skills among the poor and vulnerable communities on
addressing climate risk and exploring opportunities. The CRPP IF prioritizes development of new life skills
as part of technical and vocational training and curriculum that targets climate resilience in key sectors. The
integration of these elements into national curriculum being largely financed by government budget,
increases the level of sustainability by ensuring that these life skills are taught and will remain beyond CRPP
life span. For example, it will support integration of climate smart agriculture value chain practices in the
curriculum of government agriculture training colleges.

GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 63
B
Strengthening national and local institutions. A key focus of CRPP is to strengthen the capacity of
national and local institutions in order for them to develop and implement adaptation solutions and ensure
adaptation finance reaches the poor. While the CRPP TF aims to do so by building capacity of NDAs, all
projects seeking financing from CRPP IF will have a key focus on strengthening capacity of national and
local institutions. This will enhance climate resilience integration between institutions and to improve local
governance so that benefits of adaptation reaches all in a just and equitable manner and continues beyond
CRPP life span. For example, it will support building capacity of local governments to use climate risk
information in planning and budgeting processes in order to inform capital and recurrent expenditure.
Engagement of communities, especially women. Meaningful participation of communities, especially
women, is key for implementing sustainable transformational solutions at the local level. This is especially
true for CRPP which has a large focus on demonstrating social, economic and environmental co-benefits of
adaptation solutions, which is directly related to livelihoods and well-being of the poor communities. The
CRPP TF has a dedicated output on strengthening engagement of communities and building their capacity,
especially capacity of grassroot organizations through local policy and planning reforms. The CRPP IF will
support projects that demonstrate engagement of national and local stakeholders, including, government
and civil society organizations in developing the project and has an explicit role for communities in
implementation. Such engagement will increase the buy-in for the proposed adaptation solutions and thereby
contribute to its sustainability. For example, co-design of neighborhood scale ecosystem-based water
management measures with the women from urban informal settlement, will ensure the social and cultural
suitability of the measures and that local communities are involved in its maintenance beyond the project
period.
Creating opportunities for scaling up. A key focus of the CRPP TF is to support governments and
communities in accessing adaptation finance, including from the private sector. The financing support from
CRPP IF will have an impact beyond financing the targeted projects. By supporting local adaptation initiatives
in the region, it brings an explicit focus to the need for more such programming nationally, which could better
leverage and use government funds. The leveraging of GCF resources alongside ADB will create a critical
mass of fund volumes to achieve impact which will then open the way for mainstreamed sector and climate
support. For example, projects on ecosystem-based adaptation will explore the potential of strengthening
frameworks for private sector involvement to support long term sustainability and explore innovative options
for revenue generation such as leveraging ecotourism initiatives.

C.3 Capacity building and technology development/transfer
C.3.1 Does GCF funding finance capacity building activities? Yes ☒ No ☐
C.3.2. Does GCF funding finance technology
Yes ☐ No ☒
development/transfer?
Supporting capacity development is a key focus of all outputs under the CRPP IF. This includes building
capacity of national and local institutions on use of climate risk information for decision-making purposes;
and strengthening capacity of local communities in implementing adaptation solutions in the context of
livelihood diversification, climate smart land and water management, ecosystem-based infrastructure,
and operations and maintenance of climate adaptation infrastructure. Special emphasis is on building
capacity of poor and vulnerable women in adaptation planning and implementing adaptation measures.
All capacity building activities will adopt approaches that promote institutionalization and long-term
sustainability by partnering with local technical organization and civil society organizations, especially
grassroots women’s organizations. Such approaches will also help in replication and scaling up of
adaptation solutions in other sectors or parts of the country. GCF financing will be critical for undertaking
such capacity building activities.

EXPECTED PERFORMANCE AGAINST INVESTMENT CRITERIA
D.1. Impact potential
The impact of the CRPP will be contributing to a paradigm shift towards climate resilient sustainable
development in Asia and the Pacific region. The program will achieve this impact by strengthening the
resilience of poor and vulnerable people to the impacts of climate change in selected countries in the Asia
and Pacific region through implementing outputs related to (i) strengthening knowledge and action research
on climate risk informed pro-poor community-level solutions; (ii) strengthening institutional and community
capacity to develop and deliver climate adaptation investments at community-level; (iii) identification and
preparation of inclusive and pro-poor adaptation investment projects; (iv) improving information and systems
for delivering applied climate-risk informed investments at scale, (v) implementing pro-poor climate resilient
livelihood strategies and practices and (vi) implementing climate adaptation pro-poor infrastructure. In doing
so, the CRPP will directly address the specific risks and vulnerabilities to the poorest and most vulnerable
people and their livelihoods posed by increased weather extremes and slow-onset climate related hazards
that result from climate change. This will support transitions in key systems that are necessary for large-
scale transformations and a core enabler of climate resilient development outcomes and sustainable poverty
reduction, in line with the objectives of the Paris Agreement and the key recommendations from the WG2
contributions to the IPCC 6th Assessment Report.
The pathway towards the achievement of improved resilience includes the implementation of local climate
change adaptation measures delivered as part of at least 10-15 large-scale projects, co-financed by the
ADB. On completion of these projects, it is expected that a minimum of 3,219,400 of the poorest and most
vulnerable people will directly benefit and thus be more resilient to climate change as a result. Direct
beneficiaries are considered to be those people that are specifically targeted by the intervention and
participate in, or are recipients of, goods (e.g. agricultural extension), services (e.g. early warning/climate
information) or new knowledge or improved practices (e.g. water harvesting, agroforestry) related to the
three IF output areas, during the lifetime of the projects and are expected to a have a measurable adaptation
benefit from the intervention. The following table provides a breakdown of minimum expected direct
beneficiaries per CRPP country.

In addition to those directly benefiting from the activities under each project, there will be a number of people
that indirectly benefit. It is expected that a minimum of 4,465,000 people will indirectly benefit from the
program. Indirect beneficiaries are those people that are not specifically engaged by the project activities
and thus do not participate in, or receive the goods, services or knowledge of practices, but are located in
the coverage area and are perceived to have indirect access or exposure to them. This includes those that
live in areas where the installation of protective green infrastructure is considered to have reduced exposure.
For example, these may be people that live within the catchment area of an improved climate adapted
integrated water management system but have not been directly engaged in training or awareness raising,
or climate vulnerable people eligible for potential social protection payments based on upgraded targeting
criteria, but do not receive the payments during the project time-frame. The indirect beneficiaries will be
estimated for each project during the detailed design phase and reported on in the annual reporting to GCF.
