In populous countries such as Pakistan and Indonesia, targeted interventions such as the installation of
green infrastructure may have a relative beneficiary population of 1-2% of the total province or city
population. However, national level social protection and decentralization in those same counties may reach
5% total beneficiaries. Similarly, improved climate information services in Vanuatu have the scope to reach
80-100% of the population, and livelihoods improvements in Lao PDR and Cambodia could realistically reach
10-20% of the population in terms of total beneficiaries in the selected provinces of project implementation,
depending on the final intervention.
In all cases, women will make up at least 50% of the beneficiaries. However, this will be a minimum
requirement for all projects and it is anticipated that in many projects, women will make up more than 50%
of the total direct beneficiaries.
D.2. Paradigm shift potential
It is expected that the CRPP will catalyze following impact that will help achieve the paradigm shift of
Increased Climate Resilient Sustainable Development in Asia and the Pacific.
Scaling-up and replication. As described earlier, finance for local climate adaptation remains limited,
especially finances that targets the poorest communities. The CRPP TF aims to support countries in
identifying and developing local adaptation solutions that ensure no-one is left behind. The CRPP IF will only
support projects that demonstrate the potential of being replicated elsewhere in the same country or other
countries in the region. With GCF funding, these projects will be able to address relevant barriers to climate
adaptation, be they market failures, information failures, policy failures, or behavioural barriers. By
empowering government and communities with the knowledge and skills to take appropriate action to adapt,
improving systems for delivering climate-resilient investments, and proving their effectiveness through pilots,
the project will build the foundations for replication, support transitions in key systems and thereby drive a
paradigm shift towards climate resilient sustainable development. GCF funding will be used together with
the ADB investment to enable the project to deliver at scale. The CRPP through its TF and IF aims at
overcoming this barrier by mobilizing resources close around USD750 million for adaptation solutions
targeted at the poor and vulnerable communities. This means the GCF investment can spark a major scaling
up that is many times the original investment. Further, with a strong focus on partnership the CRPP aims at
leveraging and influencing further resources through national budgets, private sector, bi-lateral development
partners and civil society organizations, thereby multiplying the delivery of adaptation solutions.
Creation of enabling environment (and sustainability of outcomes). The CRPP will support outputs and
outcomes that are closely aligned with national climate priorities. The CRPP TF will therefore catalyze

impacts beyond a one-off project investment and deliver a paradigm shift by ensuring that climate risk
informed development becomes the new normal. It will do so by strengthening policies and regulatory
frameworks that promote climate-sensitive development, and through capacity building and use of climate
risk information for decision-making, with policy makers, planners, and local government and communities.
This will ensure the sustainability of outcomes beyond completion of the project. The GCF financing will be
used through the CRPP IF to support rolling out of such climate-sensitive development, especially in the
context of localization and decentralization. By strengthening national and local institutions, the CRPP IF will
ensure that its interventions will contribute to building policy coherence around climate resilience, and is
taken up nationwide by relevant agencies. Countries’ ownership will be achieved through stakeholder
engagement and capacity building at various decision-making levels – government, civil society
organizations, communities, financial intermediaries, and the private sector. With such a wide-ranging target,
the CRPP will contribute to bringing about a paradigm shift.
Contribution to the regulatory framework and policies. With a key focus on mainstreaming, the CRPP
will promote the integration of climate change considerations into policies and decision-making processes.
It has an explicit objective to shift to adaptive programming under output 4, increasing the use of climate
information in national social protection systems and building capacity of national agencies, local
government and civil society organizations. It also will improve climate risk information systems and integrate
them into decentralized decision-making processes. The CRPP IF programming will capitalize on on-going
decentralization processes to support governments build robust, science-based local climate assessment
frameworks that can inform planning processes, equipping decision-makers with the data, tools, guidance,
and information needed to inform local planning and investment. The focus on such actions is expected to
lead to paradigm shift towards climate resilient development as they are explicitly linked to actions identified
by the IPCC AR6 as highly likely to support systems transitions and contribute to transformational change224.
Innovative solutions and approaches. The CRPP builds on the lessons learned from the implementation
of large-scale resilience programs, which identify the need for innovative measures and approaches. These
lessons include: (i) resilience building is not just determined by what is supported but how it is supported,
including longer-term commitment; (ii) the need for adopting flexible programming approaches, including
longer-lead time for design of interventions; and (iii) the need for making resources available for facilitating
testing of ideas, learning, and evaluations. Accordingly, the CRPP is planned for a 10-year implementation
period. The CRPP TF will support three interrelated outputs (described as in section B2) including support
to development of investment ideas; and making resources available through a combination of technical
assistance and grant financing for pump priming of ideas and facilitating knowledge and learning. The CRPP
IF will support financing of adaptation projects. In particular, GCF financing will be used to finance activities
that can help overcome information, finance, institutional and gender-related barriers in an innovative way.
As a result, it is anticipated that the GCF financed CRPP IF, through the size and the type of investments,
will deliver transformational change.
Sharing of knowledge and learning. The CRPP TF has dedicated activities on knowledge and learning
which will contribute significantly to generation and sharing of knowledge on climate risk and resilience. It
will include a monitoring, evaluation and learning component, which will build collective learning processes,
and provide the information and mechanisms for sharing lessons. Learning is critical to operationalize
adaptive management principles at a program level. The CRPP TF will ensure that knowledge emerging
from GCF financed projects under the CRPP IF are shared with wider stakeholders. The multi-country nature
of the program means there will be very large potential for learning and replication, with the transfer of
experience between programmes.
Table 5 shows how the proposed GCF CRPP financed outputs (described in section B.3) will complement
past and ongoing similar initiatives in the CRPP IF countries that are financed by UNFCCC-related funds
and contribute to the paradigm shift. It should be noted that the review of current and past projects is just a
first step in the identification of specific interventions under the CRPP, the final projects that receive funding
for each country will result from comprehensive consultation with government counterparts, community
groups and other stakeholders to determine the specific opportunities for replicability and scaling-up of other
interventions based on lessons learned and national and local priorities.

presents a significant opportunity to link the modernising CIS
infrastructure with the well-established social protection
mechanisms to make them climate adaptive. Such a systemic
approach to adaptation will enable those people that rely on
fragile livelihoods that are frequently and increasingly disrupted
by climate related shocks and stresses, to take steps both
before and after the impact of extreme events to ensure minimal
negative impacts to their sources of income and food security
and take advantage of new opportunities specific to their
individual needs.

central provinces that are highly exposed and vulnerable to the

in large scale climate adaptation investments in Pakistan that
relates to the coastal zones. Much of the focus of investment
from large-scale adaptation funds in Pakistan has been in the
inland districts of the Indus River Basin and the northern
provinces. By focusing investment on livelihood adaptation in
the coastal zones of the Indus River Delta, interventions in
Pakistan will not only fill a funding gap in terms of geographical

by GCF that focus on the provision of CIS for livelihood

rural poverty rates among Pakistan’s provinces and the highest
urban-rural poverty gaps.226

between countries and build on the lessons learned from
previous projects. The specific added value of the CRPP in this
regard comes from its unique design that will combine GCF
grant financing with large co-financing from ADB, which would

Replication of effective interventions in geographical areas
with gaps. Within countries, the CRPP is an opportunity to
capitalize on the nascent national frameworks and knowledge
base regarding the fore-mentioned intervention areas, and to
transfer, replicate and scale up similar initiatives to other
geographies with high climate risk. For example, existing
activities and investments related to livelihoods in Lao PDR are
currently focused in the rural northern highlands and as such
there is the potential of neglecting large swaths of important
agricultural communities in the central provinces that are
experiencing devastating impacts from floods and droughts,
which are likely to worsen due to climate change, and where
the poverty head count rate is some of the highest in the country
and is showing the slowest rate of reduction.225 The CRPP can
capitalise on the knowledge, lessons learned and take
advantage of the related newly strengthened institutional
frameworks and fill the financing gap in the to the lesser funded,
central provinces that are highly exposed and vulnerable to the
impacts of climate change. Similarly, there is an identifiable gap
in large scale climate adaptation investments in Pakistan that
relates to the coastal zones. Much of the focus of investment
from large-scale adaptation funds in Pakistan has been in the
inland districts of the Indus River Basin and the northern
provinces. By focusing investment on livelihood adaptation in
the coastal zones of the Indus River Delta, interventions in
Pakistan will not only fill a funding gap in terms of geographical
distribution, but also directly complement existing investments
by GCF that focus on the provision of CIS for livelihood
decision-making (from federal to farm level). Balancing the
geographical distribution of adaptation financing in such a way
is crucial as Pakistan's 990km coastline is located in the
provinces of Sindh and Balochistan, which have the highest
rural poverty rates among Pakistan’s provinces and the highest
urban-rural poverty gaps.226

Promoting targeted gender-focused interventions. In
addition, the CRPP will, where appropriate, direct resources
towards activities in this area that have an explicit and
targeted focus on women’s empowerment, which would be
a particular asset in a country such as Cambodia where the
transition of employment away from agriculture has been
greater for men than for women, but this is not necessarily
reflected adaptation interventions where existing initiative may
not have such an explicit focus on women.

country that is considered high climate risk, and where over
85% of the population live in rural areas where access to
markets, services and income-generating opportunities is
limited. Channelling new adaptation resources to the country as
part of large-scale poverty reduction projects will provide the
possibility for delivering resilient livelihood interventions at-
scale. The programmatic approach will also facilitate the
replicated implementation of climate resilient livelihood projects
that has been demonstrated to be effective in supporting
transformative change in other CRPP countries, such as in
Indonesia and Timor-Leste thus reducing risk and maximizing
administrative efficiencies. This would be an important and
necessary step forward for building the adaptive capacity of
subsistence and small-scale farmers that make up over 70% of
the PNG population. Furthermore, it is self-evident that with
37.5% of the population living below the national poverty line
(USD1.90 PPP/day) gender inequality at extremely high levels,
with the country ranking 159 out of 160 countries on the Gender
Inequality Index, and one of the most culturally and
geographically diverse nations on earth, Papua New Guinea,
requires carefully considered and specific investment in
adaptation solutions that are explicitly pro-poor and gender
empowering and that are driven by a local approach that
promotes context specificity.

Indonesia is also yet to receive adaptation funding from GCF
and has only received relatively small grants from GEF for
building climate resilient livelihoods, this is in the world’s fourth
most populous country where nearly 5% of the population have
a power purchasing parity of USD1.9 a day or less. The poorest
and most vulnerable populations in Indonesia are being left
behind in terms of adaptation financing, and thus there is a
need for investment in projects that have the capacity to reach
a significant number of people living with high climate risk.

Support complementary interventions. Finally, the are some
countries where there has been a much greater emphasis on
climate adaptive infrastructure and further investment in
adapting rural livelihoods is required to compliment and
balance out the investment portfolio. In Timor-Leste
increasing investment in agricultural diversification, and climate
resilient value chain development would balance the portfolio of
investments and complement the more infrastructure focused
interventions to date and address the high risk posed by climate
change to the countries important agriculture sector of which
more than 80% of the population rely as a source of income and
for their food security. Investments in Vanuatu also represent
large contributions to financing of climate risk management
activities but place a strong emphasis on the installation of
protective infrastructure along with strengthening national and
local government frameworks for climate risk reduction, and so
there is a need for scaling-up investment in livelihood
adaptation activities.

D.3. Sustainable development
Through investments in local level adaptation, the CRPP directly targets the pillars of sustainable
development - environment, social and economic.
Environmental co-benefits. The CRPP TF will support countries to increase awareness and build capacity
to develop and implement large-scale adaptation projects, including projects that promote ecosystem-based
adaptation measures such as mangrove protection, management of urban waterways, and urban greening
projects. The CRPP IF will support implementation of such measured in the context of poverty reduction
programs in rural and urban areas, thereby promoting environmental co-benefits. Such measures become
critical in the context of community resilience, because often the livelihoods and well-being of poor and
marginalized populations are dependent on natural assets. Since such livelihoods are often impacted by
climate-related shocks and stresses, it would be critical to ensure natural-based solutions are adopted,
where appropriate (guided by decision on scale and subsidiarity) to strengthen resilience of poor population.
It is expected that CRPP TF and IF will promote nature based solutions through a wide range of investments,
such as (i) community infrastructure - adopting natural assets in place of/in mix with grey infrastructure to
build resilience of local communities; (ii) livelihoods – promoting nature-based solutions as part of climate
smart agricultural practices; (iii) well-being – promoting protection of natural assets as part of social
protection programs, such as public works programs; (iv) governance and decentralization – increasing role
of women’s group in protecting natural resources etc.
Social co-benefits. All interventions supported by CRPP TF and IF will have strong social benefits, because
of the explicit focus on low income and disadvantaged groups, and the focus on poverty reduction and
addressing existing inequalities associated with climate change. The interventions will have positive
distributional benefits by targeting these groups, increasing the flows of finance and responsibility to them,
and providing opportunities to participate collectively and create social networks, thus will lead to high gains
in social capital. The explicit targeting of women through a gender window will also lead to additional social
benefits. It is expected that CRPP TF and IF will promote a wide range of adaptation investments with social
co-benefits, including (i) adaptive and shock responsive social protection; (ii) community-driven development
in rural and urban areas; and (iii) climate resilient livelihoods support.
Economic co-benefits. There is a strong economic element to the investments to be promoted by CRPP
TF and supported by CRPP IF, which is captured through the triple dividend of investing in resilience.227 This
includes i) the economic activity stimulated by reduced impacts, forward-looking planning, long-term capital
investments and entrepreneurship as well as macro-economic benefits, and ii) development co-benefits from
resilience investments, including positive spills overs as well as non-market benefits. Moreover, with a focus
on inclusive governance, the CRPP will promote bottom-up processes, which are critical for inclusive
sustainable development.
Gender-responsive development impact. The CRPP seeks to address the gender-climate vulnerability-
poverty nexus, through supporting an integrated set of activities across both the Trust Fund and The
Investment Fund that combine to address structural drivers of women’s inequality, women’s disproportionate
vulnerability to climate change and multidimensional poverty. All projects supported by the CRPP Investment
Fund must either be categorized as Gender Equity Theme (GEN) or Effective Gender Mainstreaming (EGM),
meaning that specific targeted activities that address issues of women’s inequality must be identified in

project Gender Action Plans (GAPs), with associated budget allocation and monitoring and reporting plans.
For GEN projects, the project’s results framework must include outcome indicators that are specific to
promoting gender equality, thus gender becomes a fundamental part of the project’s design. The CRPP
Trust Fund has dedicated resources for undertaking upstream analytical and capacity building work that will
support the identification of the types of appropriate strategies and interventions that can be effective in
addressing issues of climate risk, gender inequality hand in hand with poverty reduction interventions. These
strategies are articulated at a higher level in the CRPP’s Gender Action Plan (GAP) presented in annex 8.2.
Promoting gender equality is a core thrust of the CRPP and which will be promoted through all projects
supported by the CRPP TF and CRPP IF. The focus on gender equality extends from existing evidence that
when grassroot women’s groups are involved in leading the identification and implementation of adaptation
measures the benefits are manifold. First, adaptation investments identified and prioritized by women are
not focused exclusively on women but aim to improve the lives of their families and communities. Second,
the strategies adopted by women highlight their leadership role in claiming resources and public recognition,
thereby bringing a shift in viewing women’s status from victims and passive beneficiaries to stakeholders
and drivers of resilient development.228 Such examples are also visible in the current pandemic response
where grassroots women’s groups have been instrumental in ensuring that government support reaches the
last mile. It is thus important that such women’s leadership roles are promoted in different investments
thereby boosting women’s adaptive capacity to deal with climate shocks and stresses. At the same time,
women-focused investments and resource flows are also necessary to break generations of gender
inequalities in economic and human capital endowments and voice and agency that shape their climate
adaptive capacity. An annex on Gender assessment and program-level action plan is included as an Annex
8.
Thus, the CRPP will deliver against several of the SDGs, including 1 no poverty, 3 good health and wellbeing,
5 gender equality, 10 reduced inequalities, 11 sustainable cities and communities and 13 climate action.
D.4. Needs of recipient
Addressing resilience needs of the poor and vulnerable population. The recipients of the program are
the poor and vulnerable, who by definition have high adaptation needs. These groups are likely to be the
most affected by climate change, and do not have the finance or capacity to anticipate, absorb, adapt to and
recovery from climate shocks and stresses, and need support to strengthen their assets, livelihoods and
well-being. Thus, the CRPP will directly meet the needs of these groups by supporting resilience
investments, as well as strengthening institutions and systems, to allow climate finance to reach the poor
and support local adaptation. Without external finance, it will not be possible to deliver the scale of climate
adaptation needed. In particular, GCF resources will help finance transformational change in areas that other
financial institutions tend to ignore. These resources also provide greater flexibility, through the provision of
grant finance alongside ADB financing, which is likely to be needed for community resilience investments.
This will allow tailored packages of community investment, allowing the combination of finance to deliver a
more transformative overall effect, because it allows the targeting of multiple barriers. Thus, there is a high
recipient need for GCF support. This will apply to the least developed countries, the small island developing
states, and the poorest in middle income countries.
Cambodia is an LDC in Southeast Asia with a population of 16.3 million in 2018, 76 percent of its population
lives in rural areas and the urban concentration is located in the most fertile river valleys and flood plains.
About 90% of the poor live in the countryside and around 4.5 million people remain near-poor, vulnerable to
falling back into poverty when exposed to economic and other external shocks.229 Cambodia’s population
relies heavily on agriculture, fisheries, and natural resources extraction providing 25% of GDP and employing
49% of the country’s labor force. Climate change shocks are projected to victimise 61% of the rural
Cambodian population; in particular, about 7 million smallholder farmers and 25,000 workers in construction
industry. Women are similarly more disadvantaged, especially in decision-making and income disparity.230
Still as an LDC, Cambodia’s fiscal management in solving local development problems is compounded by
climate shocks and the COVID-19 pandemic, such the constraints on the public budget management
requires outsourced assistance especially in dealing with uplifting conditions of the rural poor.

 | last mile. It is thus important that such women’s leadership roles are promoted in different investments | 
 | thereby boosting women’s adaptive capacity to deal with climate shocks and stresses. At the same time, | 
 | women-focused investments and resource flows are also necessary to break generations of gender | 
 | inequalities in economic and human capital endowments and voice and agency that shape their climate | 
 | adaptive capacity. An annex on Gender assessment and program-level action plan is included as an Annex | 
 | 8. | 
 |  | 
 | Thus, the CRPP will deliver against several of the SDGs, including 1 no poverty, 3 good health and wellbeing, | 
 | 5 gender equality, 10 reduced inequalities, 11 sustainable cities and communities and 13 climate action. | 
 |  | 
D.4. Needs of recipient |  | 
 | Addressing resilience needs of the poor and vulnerable population. The recipients of the program are | 
 | the poor and vulnerable, who by definition have high adaptation needs. These groups are likely to be the | 
 | most affected by climate change, and do not have the finance or capacity to anticipate, absorb, adapt to and | 
 | recovery from climate shocks and stresses, and need support to strengthen their assets, livelihoods and | 
 | well-being. Thus, the CRPP will directly meet the needs of these groups by supporting resilience | 
 | investments, as well as strengthening institutions and systems, to allow climate finance to reach the poor | 
 | and support local adaptation. Without external finance, it will not be possible to deliver the scale of climate | 
 | adaptation needed. In particular, GCF resources will help finance transformational change in areas that other | 
 | financial institutions tend to ignore. These resources also provide greater flexibility, through the provision of | 
 | grant finance alongside ADB financing, which is likely to be needed for community resilience investments. | 
 | This will allow tailored packages of community investment, allowing the combination of finance to deliver a | 
 | more transformative overall effect, because it allows the targeting of multiple barriers. Thus, there is a high | 
 | recipient need for GCF support. This will apply to the least developed countries, the small island developing | 
 | states, and the poorest in middle income countries. | 
 |  | 
 | Cambodia is an LDC in Southeast Asia with a population of 16.3 million in 2018, 76 percent of its population | 
 | lives in rural areas and the urban concentration is located in the most fertile river valleys and flood plains. | 
 | About 90% of the poor live in the countryside and around 4.5 million people remain near-poor, vulnerable to | 
 | falling back into poverty when exposed to economic and other external shocks.229 Cambodia’s population | 
 | relies heavily on agriculture, fisheries, and natural resources extraction providing 25% of GDP and employing | 
 | 49% of the country’s labor force. Climate change shocks are projected to victimise 61% of the rural | 
 | Cambodian population; in particular, about 7 million smallholder farmers and 25,000 workers in construction | 
 | industry. Women are similarly more disadvantaged, especially in decision-making and income disparity.230 | 
 | Still as an LDC, Cambodia’s fiscal management in solving local development problems is compounded by | 
 | climate shocks and the COVID-19 pandemic, such the constraints on the public budget management | 
 | requires outsourced assistance especially in dealing with uplifting conditions of the rural poor. |

Indonesia has the largest economy in Southeast Asia. With high economic growth, the poverty rates in the
country in recent decades have decreased from 24% in 1999 to 10% in 2020. Nonetheless, poverty remains
high in absolute numbers, because of the large population size, and thus numbers tens of millions of people.
Poverty rates are higher particularly in remote areas and among certain groups.231 While Indonesia has
urbanized rapidly, not everyone has equally benefitted from it, with nearly 7% of urban population living
under the poverty line and roughly equal percentage being near poor. Prior to COVID-19, an estimated 61.8
million people, or 21.5% of the population, were considered poor or to have a high risk of falling into poverty,
making them vulnerable to shocks.232 With COVID-19, it is estimated that those below the national poverty
line has increased and may reach 12.8% by the end of 2020.233 Inequality also remains high, with the bottom
40% of the population accounting for 17.7% of consumption, whereas the top 20% consumes 45.6%.234
Urban areas have higher inequality than rural areas.235 The absolute number of urban poor will continue to
increase as the country urbanizes and thus is an increasingly important target group in Indonesia’s poverty
reduction policies.236 To reduce poverty and stimulate economic inclusion, Indonesia has prioritized poverty
reduction programs, including social protection programs and urban informal settlements upgrade. These
programs do not consider long-term changes in climate and thus the impacts generated by these programs
will be undermined in the future due to increase in climate shocks and stresses. It is therefore critical that
such poverty reduction programs integrate climate resilience considerations to build adaptive capacity of
local institutions and communities.
Lao PDR is a landlocked country in Southeast Asia and is one of the LDCs. It is a highly vulnerable country
with low readiness. While the country’s economy has been growing, delicately balanced macroeconomic
outlook, weak human resources and infrastructure, and the recurrence of climate hazards continue to pose
challenges to the Lao PDR’s development.237 A large percentage of population remain close to the poverty
line: data from 2019 show that the poverty rate in rural areas was 23.8% compared to 7.0% in urban areas.238
Agriculture accounts for 16% of GDP and engages, to various degrees, over 65% of the population (of whom
more than half are women). The large section of the rural population engaged in agriculture are particularly
vulnerable to the impacts of natural hazards due to their large dependence on subsistence agriculture
production and inadequate social protection systems. With projected increase in temperature and intensified
precipitation, livelihoods and agricultural yields will be greatly impacted due to damage to rural infrastructure
by floods, increased crop evapotranspiration in the dry season with associated higher demand for water,
more frequent land inundation and consequently crop losses during floods, loss of livestock due to water
shortage or by destructive floods. Investments will be needed to support the rural poor in climate resilient
livelihood diversification, in improving land water management practices in response to change climate, and
in strengthening climate services for improved decision-making. As an LDC, Lao PDR lacks the financial
resources to address climate threats, especially for the most vulnerable, and the constraints on the public
budget mean Government cannot fill the adaptation funding gap. Moreover, the COVID-19 crisis is expected
to result in loss of jobs for almost half a million of people roughly 383,000 people are expected to pushed
deeper, or back into poverty. Such situation further exacerbates pre-existing vulnerabilities, for example,
the food insecurity in the northern rural provinces, being already a critical issue as seven months rice
availability deficit has been recorded even before the Covid-19 outbreak; and the 1.7 million school
children having their learning setback.239
Pakistan is characterized by diverse topography, ecosystems, and climate zones, and faces multiple climate
hazards: the country is one of the most vulnerable to climate shocks in the world today. As of 2015
approximately 24% of the population still lived below the national poverty line and 20% of the population
remained undernourished. However, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projects due to COVID-19 crisis
up to 40 percent of population will be living below the poverty line. Agriculture is still the largest employer,
occupying 42% of the workforce and contributes 21% to GDP, making potential climate impacts and
adaptation needs in the sector a high priority, especially given the high proportion of subsistence farmers.
However, it is expected that agricultural growth will lag if lockdowns continue and disrupt needed transportation,
logistical support, labor, and access to inputs for the next planting season.240 Pakistan is also a highly water
stressed country, ranked 14th globally in terms of water stress. The target area for the project is the coastal
areas, which are already affected by coastal and river floods, which are projected to increase significantly
with climate change. Poverty rates in these coastal areas are among the highest in the country. These

Papua New Guinea. Located in the South West Pacific, PNG comprises the eastern half of New Guinea
island, four additional islands (Manus, New Ireland, New Britain, and Bougainville), and around 600 smaller
islets and atolls. PNG is a highly climate vulnerable country241 and is also considered to be a Small Island
Developing State (SIDS). PNG has consistently ranked among the lowest 30 countries in the Human
Development Index, and has poverty rates between 30-40% and an adult literacy rate of around 50%. A
large proportion of its population is rural (87%). Agriculture, fishing, community forestry, and small-scale
mining are primary livelihood activities in rural areas. Estimate suggest that 70% of households in PNG
remain dependent on subsistence agriculture.242 The combined issues of widespread poverty, poor
infrastructure and dependence on climate sensitive livelihoods all heighten the vulnerability of the local
population. 83% of food consumed is produced in country, thus, any disruption to local food production (from
climate or other shocks) has an immediate and significant impact on food security.243 Climate change is likely
to increase hazards, and without adaptation measures, the exposure of the rural communities will further
increase. As an SIDS, PNG lacks the financial resources to address the very large climate threats, especially
for the most vulnerable, and the constraints on the public budget mean Government cannot fill the adaptation
funding gap. The COVID-19 crisis is having negative impacts on unemployment (31% of household heads lost
their jobs) and poverty (increase by 4.5 percentage points). The 2020 fiscal balance is estimated to worsen from
–5% of GDP pre-COVID-19 to –8.2% of GDP post-COVID-19. Public sector debt is expected to reach 49.8% of
GDP in 2020, compared with 39.8% in 2019.
Timor-Leste occupies the eastern half of the island of Timor, which it shares with the Indonesian province
of East Nussa Tengura. The island has an extensive coastline stretching 700km, while inland the topography
is mountainous. The country is one of the poorest countries in Asia and is a LDC. Data for 2016 estimate
that 30.7% of the population were living on less than the internationally recognised poverty line of
USD1.90/day, and 45.8% were classified as living in multi-dimensional poverty.244 Such conditions make the
population more vulnerable to shocks and stresses. Agriculture accounts for 9% of GDP, and 41% of
employment, however, excluding oil revenue plays a much more significant role in the economy.245 Most
agriculture is subsistence farming, with coffee the only major crop grown for export. Rural areas suffer from
food insecurity, due to a combination of low productivity, high population growth and unpredictable rainfall
coupled with extreme climate events.246 Gender analysis shows that for women, these circumstances are
felt even more acutely.247 Most farming households have minimal engagement with agricultural markets and
can be characterized as low-input, low-output producers. Although the Timor-Leste people have some
capacity to adapt to these complex changes, such coping strategies are still reliant on climate-sensitive
natural resources, aggravated by their limited access to alternative livelihoods. Traditional gender roles
exacerbate the risks for women in a changing climate, while minimal access to weather and climate
forecasting hinders adaptive actions. With agricultural systems, including the livelihood conditions and food
insecurity issues, expected to be severally affected by both by increases in extreme events, as well as
changes in temperature and rainfall36 solutions in adaptation are urgently needed. As an LDC, Timor-Leste
lacks the financial resources to address climate threats, especially for the most vulnerable, and the
constraints on the public budget mean Government cannot fill the adaptation funding gap. The COVID-19
crisis is expected to worsen the economic situation and result in large scale loss in livelihood and increase
in food insecurity.
Vanuatu is a small island developing state in the Pacific that is characterized by low-lying areas that have
high levels of climate risk, especially to tropical cyclones. Vanuatu was ranked as the country most at risk
from disasters in the annual World Risk Report (2019). As a series of islands and atolls lying in the tropics,
it faces both slow and rapid onset meteorological hazards. Disasters resulting from these climate hazards
are a very significant contributor to issues of social deprivation and impede economic development in
Vanuatu; these events cost on average an estimated 6% of GDP every year. As an island nation, the country
is particularly at risk from sea-level rise. Vanuatu lacks the financial resources to address climate threats,
especially for the most vulnerable, and the constraints on the public budget mean Government cannot fill the
adaptation funding gap. The country’s GDP is likely to contract by 9.8% in 2020 due to reduced tourism,

D.5. Country ownership
The CRPP IF will be implemented in seven countries. Consultations have been undertaken with stakeholders
from Cambodia, Lao PDR, Indonesia, Pakistan, PNG, Timor Leste, and Vanuatu. For these countries, ADB
has investments in the pipeline that have the potential to meet the objectives of the CRPP In-depth
consultations were also organized with selected development partners, civil society organizations and
grassroots women’s organizations, in order to understand local needs and most importantly the type of
transformational approaches needed at the local level.
In order to ensure scale, replicability and sustainability, implementation of the CRPP will be country-led and
tailored to fit country and local context, recognizing the broader political economy context. Thus the outputs
identified under CRPP IF are closely aligned with national climate priorities (as outlined in NDCs and/or
NAPs) and national poverty reduction priorities (as outlined in national development plans). For more
information, please refer to Annex 2.2.
Cambodia has prioritized climate adaptation as a priority and to reduce its vulnerability. It has identified
adaptation priorities in its National Adaptation Programme of Action (NAPA) and Climate Change Strategic Plan
(CCSP), 2014-2023, and has embedding adaptation in the National Sustainable Development Plan (NSDP)
and the sectoral development plans. The CCSP has 8 strategic objectives and several strategies that provide
entry points for a coherent approach to integrate with the national development processes. Within the
framework, sectoral plans have identified 171 actions of which 93% are adaptation actions. To support the
implementation of the adaptation actions the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) has been formulated and to
overcome the financing barrier the Government endorsed the NAP Financing Framework and Implementation
Plan in 2017. The Financing plan has identified 40 priority actions with an estimated budget of USD 530 million
covering key sectors including infrastructure and agriculture.248 Priority actions in agriculture sector includes
promoting and scaling up climate smart farming systems and promotion of post-harvest technology. In 2020,
Cambodia has developed its Updated Nationally Determined Contribution with identified priority adaptation
actions in agriculture and water resources, forestry, coastal zones, human health, energy, industry,
infrastructure, livelihoods and tourism. The government has identified the need to improve the climate risk
management into the provincial level policy, planning and budgeting process and also the opportunity to
integrate as part of the National Programme for Sub National Democratic Development (NPSNDD) process.
Budget availability, knowledge on climate change impacts and implications, lack of technical capacity across
ministries have been identified as key barriers for effective adaptation.249
Indonesia has put in place ambitious climate adaptation actions outlined in National Action Plan on Climate
Change Adaptation (RAN-API) and its Climate Resilient Development Policy 2020-2045, which prioritizes four
sectors– water, marine and coastal, agriculture, and health, each of which is critical for strengthening resilience
of the urban and rural poor population. It further identifies infrastructure, governance, technology and capacity
building measures for adaptation. In infrastructure, green infrastructure is recognized as a key priority, especially
for the low-income people and vulnerable groups. In governance, the RAN-API prioritizes strengthening of
institutions and information systems in order to ensure benefits of adaptation are reaching the poor and
vulnerable population. Further, the recently approved Rencana Pembangunan Jangka Menengah Nasional
(RPJMN) (National Medium-Term Development Plan) 2020-2024 has identified one of its seven
development agenda as development of living environment to increase resilience to disasters and climate
change. The Government of Indonesia has also recognized the role of social protection in resilience building
and the government has developed the Adaptive Social Protection Roadmap.
Lao PDR has prioritized increasing climate resilience in agriculture, forest and land-use and strengthening
management of water resources as top priorities of its NDC. This includes promoting climate resilience of
farming systems, strengthening resilience of infrastructure, and enhancing water resources information
system. Additionally, the NDC recognizes building capacity will be crucial for effective implementation of

D.5. Country ownership |  |  |  | 
 | The CRPP IF will be implemented in seven countries. Consultations have been undertaken with stakeholders |  |  | 
 | from Cambodia, Lao PDR, Indonesia, Pakistan, PNG, Timor Leste, and Vanuatu. For these countries, ADB |  |  | 
 | has investments in the pipeline that have the potential to meet the objectives of the CRPP In-depth |  |  | 
 | consultations were also organized with selected development partners, civil society organizations and |  |  | 
 | grassroots women’s organizations, in order to understand local needs and most importantly the type of |  |  | 
 | transformational approaches needed at the local level. |  |  | 
 |  |  |  | 
 | In order to ensure scale, replicability and sustainability, implementation of the CRPP will be country-led and |  |  | 
 | tailored to fit country and local context, recognizing the broader political economy context. Thus the outputs |  |  | 
 | identified under CRPP IF are closely aligned with national climate priorities (as outlined in NDCs and/or |  |  | 
 | NAPs) and national poverty reduction priorities (as outlined in national development plans). For more |  |  | 
 | information, please refer to Annex 2.2. |  |  | 
 |  |  |  | 
 | Cambodia has prioritized climate adaptation as a priority and to reduce its vulnerability. It has identified |  |  | 
 | adaptation priorities in its National Adaptation Programme of Action (NAPA) and Climate Change Strategic Plan |  |  | 
 | (CCSP), 2014-2023, and has embedding adaptation in the National Sustainable Development Plan (NSDP) |  |  | 
 | and the sectoral development plans. The CCSP has 8 strategic objectives and several strategies that provide |  |  | 
 | entry points for a coherent approach to integrate with the national development processes. Within the |  |  | 
 | framework, sectoral plans have identified 171 actions of which 93% are adaptation actions. To support the |  |  | 
 | implementation of the adaptation actions the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) has been formulated and to |  |  | 
 | overcome the financing barrier the Government endorsed the NAP Financing Framework and Implementation |  |  | 
 | Plan in 2017. The Financing plan has identified 40 priority actions with an estimated budget of USD 530 million |  |  | 
 | covering key sectors including infrastructure and agriculture.248 Priority actions in agriculture sector includes |  |  | 
 | promoting and scaling up climate smart farming systems and promotion of post-harvest technology. In 2020, |  |  | 
 | Cambodia has developed its Updated Nationally Determined Contribution with identified priority adaptation |  |  | 
 | actions in agriculture and water resources, forestry, coastal zones, human health, energy, industry, |  |  | 
 | infrastructure, livelihoods and tourism. The government has identified the need to improve the climate risk |  |  | 
 | management into the provincial level policy, planning and budgeting process and also the opportunity to |  |  | 
 | integrate as part of the National Programme for Sub National Democratic Development (NPSNDD) process. |  |  | 
 | Budget availability, knowledge on climate change impacts and implications, lack of technical capacity across |  |  | 
 | ministries have been identified as key barriers for effective adaptation.249 |  |  | 
 |  |  |  | 
 | Indonesia has put in place ambitious climate adaptation actions outlined in National Action Plan on Climate |  |  | 
 | Change Adaptation (RAN-API) and its Climate Resilient Development Policy 2020-2045, which prioritizes four |  |  | 
 | sectors– water, marine and coastal, agriculture, and health, each of which is critical for strengthening resilience |  |  | 
 | of the urban and rural poor population. It further identifies infrastructure, governance, technology and capacity |  |  | 
 | building measures for adaptation. In infrastructure, green infrastructure is recognized as a key priority, especially |  |  | 
 | for the low-income people and vulnerable groups. In governance, the RAN-API prioritizes strengthening of |  |  | 
 | institutions and information systems in order to ensure benefits of adaptation are reaching the poor and |  |  | 
 | vulnerable population. Further, the recently approved Rencana Pembangunan Jangka Menengah Nasional |  |  | 
 | (RPJMN) (National Medium-Term Development Plan) 2020-2024 has identified one of its seven |  |  | 
 | development agenda as development of living environment to increase resilience to disasters and climate |  |  | 
 | change. | The Government of Indonesia has also recognized | the role of social protection in resilience building | 
 | and the government has developed the Adaptive Social Protection Roadmap. |  |  |

adaptation measures, including capacity for risk-informed decision-making at all levels from national to local.
Further, the Agricultural Development Strategy to 2025 and Vision to 2030, have prioritized water resources
management to support the production of both wet and dry season crops.250 The government prioritizes
interventions in agriculture and rural development by: (i) improving agro-met information, and coverage to
reach target users; (ii) increasing forest and vegetative land cover; (iii) developing water management
infrastructure for flood control and irrigation; and (iv) modernizing irrigation technologies and practices.251
Timor Leste in the Dilli Declaration on Climate Change Adaptation recognizes that strong interdependence
of climate adaptation and development target, and that the national development priorities can only be
sustainably achieved by considering climate adaptation. The NDC identifies food security as a key adaptation
priority in order to reduce vulnerability of farmers to drought and flood by improving their capacity to plan for
and respond to future climate conditions. In particular, the NDC identifies agroforestry and water shed
management as key measures for strengthening food security. Priorities related to water resources
management includes enhancing government and community strategies to respond to drought exacerbated
by climate change; and enhancing water harvesting model, water distribution system and management
system at all levels to avoid water shortages due to climate change. Promoting subnational capacity
development for improved adaptation planning and implementation. In 2021, Timor Leste has developed its
National Adaptation Plan which has identified seven priority areas: agriculture, biodiversity and ecosystem,
disaster risk reduction, health, infrastructure, tourism, and water.
Pakistan in its updated NDC (2021) adopts a long-term vision of mainstreaming climate resilience
considerations in the economically and socially vulnerable sectors of the economy. In particular, it identifies
agriculture, water resources management, and infrastructure as key adaptation-related priorities. The
National Climate Change Policy (2012) spells out the policy measures for adaption in vulnerable ecosystems
including coastal and marine ecosystems. The framework for implementation of climate change policy (2014-
2030) provides a detailed list of actions with timeframe for implementation, including priorities related to
water sector, agriculture and livestock, marine and coastal ecosystems, and disaster preparedness. The
framework emphasizes the importance of implementation adaptation measures that focuses on women’s
needs.
PNG in its NDC has identified food security caused by crop failures a priority for adaptation purposes. In its
Second National Communication, PNG emphasizes the importance of agriculture, capacity building,
technology transfer, education and training to adaptation. The National Climate Compatible Development
Management Policy prioritizes provision of education and training on resilient agriculture and resilient
construction to poor and marginalized people. Further, the long-term development strategy: PNG Vision
2050 identifies environmental sustainability and climate change as one its seven strategic focus areas and
stresses the importance of engaging with communities in achieving inclusive sustainable development. PNG
has developed its National Adaptation Plan in 2023 which has prioritized four key sectors that include
agriculture, infrastructure, transport and health.
Vanuatu: The objectives of the CRPP are aligned with NAPA (2007), the Vanuatu Climate Change and
Disaster Risk Reduction Policy (2016-2030) and the Vanuatu Recovery Strategy, 2020 – 2023 (VRS,
developed in early 2020 in response to Typhoon Harold and to the Covid Pandemic). The Climate Change
and Disaster Risk Reduction Policy (2016-2030) has identified community focus is one of its principles of
implementing climate adaptation interventions, with an objective to empower communities at the local level
through bottom up approaches, drawing on local skills, values and traditional knowledge, and enhancing
decentralization in planning, programs and projects.
Consultation with NDAs. In the course of development of this proposal ADB has officially coordinated with
the NDAs, including having consultations with NDAs and relevant sector ministry to explain the program
proposal, understand their priorities and reflect such needs in the proposal. The NDAs were provided with
copy of the draft program proposal and no-objection letter has been obtained from 6 of the 7 countries.

D.6. Efficiency and effectiveness
The projects funded under the CRPP will be subject to ADB’s economic appraisal criteria and will have to
meet an economic internal rate of return (EIRR) threshold. This means that in present value terms, the total
economic benefits will exceed the total economic costs (when analysed in accordance with ADB’s 2017
Guidelines for the Economic Analysis of Projects).
The projects will also be subject to ADB’s requirements for financial management and analysis. For each
project, financial analysis will be prepared in accordance with ADB’s Financial Management and Analysis of
Projects guidelines. In particular (i) the estimated investment and operations costs, as well as cash inflows,
will be clearly presented and will be reasonable; (ii) the financial internal rate of return (FIRR) calculated on
a real basis consistent with the ADB Financial Management and Analysis of Projects guidelines will be
greater than the weighted average cost of capital; and (iii) the FIRR will be robust under various sensitivity
scenarios.
The CRPP programmatic approach proposed will deliver very high efficiency and effectiveness, because the
GCF funds will be leveraged against large volumes of ADB finance. At the CRPP IF level, the program will
use USD120 million from GCF and leverage USD 630 million from ADB and other TF donors. This will result
in a ratio of co-financing of more than 5:1, which is high for adaptation, especially when targeting the most
vulnerable. This will mean the GCF investments will benefit from existing ADB funded management and
implementation activities. The marginal transaction costs for implementing GCF funds will therefore be
extremely low (and highly efficient).
The use of GCF finance to fund the climate additionality on top of existing ADB funds will also be extremely
effective, because it will work with existing financial, governance and implementation activities, ensuring high
conversion of inputs to outputs and outcomes. This means the GCF funds will deliver a very large number
of beneficiaries/ USD invested.
The projects that are put forward for financing under CRPP IF will be scrutinized against strict economic and
financial viability prior to funding, and only those that pass these criteria will be taken forward. The exact
EIRR and FIRR will vary with the projects funded, and it is not possible at this stage to provide values for
individual pipeline projects. However, a review of the economic benefits of community level adaptation, as
well as the three main proposed outcome areas where GCF funds will be used, was undertaken. The
economic justification and rates of return are summarized below.
Community level adaptation: There are a wide set of interventions that can hence community-based
resilience, including local and community-based adaptation planning and financing. Evaluations of these
projects has found good benefit to cost ratios (BCR) in Asia252, 253 and there is good evidence from an ex-
post analysis of 23 field tested pilots.254 It is also highlighted that interventions that target the most vulnerable
are likely to have very positive distributional benefits. In theory these distributional issues can be taken into
account in economic appraisal (in cost-benefit analysis) by using equity (or distributional) weights to adjust
present values. Very few studies apply equity weights, thought such an approach would further increase the
benefits of the proposed interventions below.
Output 4: Improved information and systems for delivering applied climate-risk informed
investments at scale. These activities are primarily focused on integrating climate risk information into
decision-making processes. Social protection programs have positive benefit to cost ratios in themselves
and have been recommended255 as a form of climate sensitive development for small and frequent shocks
in their own right. Economic analysis of social protection programs256 show high benefit to cost ratios, e.g.,
one review study looking in detail at 8 studies (4 ex ante, 4 ex post) found BCRs that were as high as 6:1.
The GCF funds for this output will be focused on enhancing the climate targeting of funded social protection
activities. Numerous studies have identified the advantages and benefits of making social protection
programs climate smart,257 to explicitly target climate extremes and to ensure climate shocks do not
undermine social protection program effectiveness. The intervention will include the use of climate
information, including weather and climate services (including early warning), for social protection. Analysis
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

of such applications find high benefit to cost ratios (BCRs)258,259,260,261 and recent reviews identify on average
a benefit to cost ratio of 9:1.262 Benefits increase with increasing climate change (and shocks) and thus these
interventions are highly efficient as well as effective.
Output 5: Climate resilient pro-poor livelihoods investment. These activities are focused on additional
activities that climate smart livelihoods program investments. These include a wide range of types of
interventions but are often focused on agriculture. They can include activities that build the resilience of
current livelihoods, with weather and climate services, climate smart extension services, capacity building,
and climate smart agriculture, and these interventions have been found to have high benefit to cost
ratios.263,264 Economic review of Adaptation for Smallholder Agriculture Programme reported positive benefit
cost ratios across 32 country-level projects, up to 6:1 (and EIRRs of between 15% and 35%).265 The
interventions will also include some activities to help communities’ transition to new livelihoods due to climate
change threats. This may include moving to new resilient varieties, or developing new climate resilient
livelihoods, which are also found to generate positive benefits to cost ratios.266,267,268
Output 6. Climate adaptation pro-poor infrastructure investment. This activity is focused on climate
adaption infrastructure. Such interventions have been demonstrated to have very positive economic returns.
A systematic review269 of flood risk management appraisal (27 studies, mix ex ante and ex post) found a
BCR of 5 to 1 for flood related risks. Further review work, looking at 110 observations on investments/projects
from 32 studies and databases in 16 countries270 found a mean BCR of 6. These economic benefits have
been found for multiple hazards, which include sea level rise271 and floods.272 One particular focus of the
GCF funds will be the targeting of green infrastructure for resilience (ecosystem-based adaptation). These
provide alternatives to hard engineered protection, such as mangroves and wetlands, river catchment
management, and even small-scale local schemes. The review of the literature finds these have high benefit
to cost ratios, for example, coastal EBA was found to have among the highest BCR for coastal resilience
273,274. Importantly, these schemes have high co-benefits, which include environmental benefits (including
carbon sequestration), and these can be particularly high for local ecosystem-based community-based
adaptation.275

E.7. Monitoring, reporting and evaluation arrangements
Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MEL) are considered cornerstones of the CRPP, and the final detailed MEL framework and implementation
plan will reflect this commitment, not only to closely monitoring the progress of the individual sub-projects and the program as a whole according to
the results framework, but to using the CRPP as an opportunity to advance the collective understanding of how to design and implement effective
pro-poor and gender sensitive adaptation solutions. The principals that have informed the general approach to MEL under the CRPP and will guide
the development of the detailed MEL framework and implementation plan are based on a detailed study undertaken as part of the CRPP scoping
activities. A detailed review of large-scale climate adaptation financing mechanisms was carried out, and best practice and lessons learned were
consolidated into a set of general recommendations to guide MEL activities under the CRPP. The arrangement for monitoring, reporting and
evaluation are presented in more detail in Annex 11.

Participation: The procedures for monitoring will involve communities and local stakeholders, including civil society organizations, at all stages
of the project/program cycle from the beginning. This will not only build the capacity of local actors in monitoring and reporting techniques, but
create by-in to project outputs (thus supporting sustainability) and foster learning and awareness raising in terms of climate change adaptation.
Evaluations will be planned and conducted in ways that enhance the likely utilization of both the findings and of the process itself to inform
decisions and improve performance. Key to promoting the maximum utility of the evaluation outputs, will be the engagement of the primary user
groups. Under the CRPP IF, the primary user groups are the Executing Entity (EE), the National Designated Authority (NDA), ADB and GCF.
Accountability vs Learning: MEL activities under the CRPP must strike an appropriate balance between reporting against quantitative indicators
that tell us what milestones are being achieved, and a more qualitative and reflective approach that seeks to answer questions about how and
why these milestones are / are not being achieved.
Practicality: The CRPP MEL activities will have to balance and overcome multiple and competing demands, risks and constraints of monitoring
and evaluation of such a large program. The usual trade-offs between cost, reporting burden, and a desire for methodological rigor and
comprehensive learning are acknowledged, as is the need to accept reality on the ground in the project countries. These factors are to be
considered in the development of the detailed MEL plan and managed accordingly.
MEL Approach: The following points identify two of the key pillars of the CRPP MEL approach (further discussion on the CRPP MEL approach is
included in annex 11).
A multi-level approach: Monitoring and evaluation under the CRPP will be carried out at two levels; project level, and program level. Despite
the differences in scope of M&E at different levels, in order to achieve a sufficient level of evidence generation for reflection and learning for the
benefit of both projects and the program, the overarching fund level M&E framework and plan will be designed in conjunction with the project-
level frameworks and be guided by a common vision of the program across all levels of implementation. This will greatly facilitate the ability to
carry out coherent, coordinated MEL activities throughout the program. A multi-level approach which seeks the alignment of results frameworks
between the project, CRPP program, and GCF fund level is considered to be especially critical to generating comprehensive and consistent data
that can be used to measure the contribution of the program to transformative change and the assessment of key assumptions that provide the
logic for activities.
A flexible and adaptive approach: Responding and adapting to changing contexts and the evolution of knowledge and understanding is a key
enabling process for building resilience, and thus a learning approach may also involve adjusting the processes, results framework and indicators,
of the M&E framework. Experience over time will inform what works and does not work well, and periodic updates to all major components of the
M&E system should be expected. Thus, the MEL frameworks need to allow for continual adjustments based on the emerging body of knowledge
and experience regarding the monitoring and measuring of resilience. This means that the MEL framework should not be static, rather it should
be tailored to the implementation stage by, for example, evolving towards asking broader evaluation questions as the program moves through its
lifecycle.

Implementation Arrangements: A CRPP MEL Expert will be part of the CRPP secretariat and will be responsible for the coordination and
management of all MEL activities under the CRPP and ensuring independent and impartial review of the IF project activities and the CRPP program.
Full roles and responsibilities of the MEL expert will be established as part of the initial role out of the CRPP.
MEL Implementation Guidelines: At the CRPP inception, using the CRPP Trust Fund incubation resources, a MEL inception workshop, involving
the CRPP partnership group members, NDAs and EE’s, will be held to raise awareness on MEL and promote ownership of the CRPP MEL activities,
processes and future outcomes. The discussions from the workshop will feed into the development of the CRPP MEL plan and guidelines which will
provide specific and practical steps on how to align CRPP MEL requirements with existing ADB and other CRPP partner’s processes and a monitoring
system will be established to collect and collate information from projects. This integrated approach will minimize reporting burdens, while ensuring
that the CRPP results framework and GCF reporting requirements are adequately covered.
Establishing the baseline: Baselines and targets for the sub-project M&E frameworks will be established. In addition to the related CRPP program
indicators, the baseline assessments will include the articulation of qualitative and quantitative baselines and targets for paradigm shift and enabling
environment indicators as required for the GCF IRMF. Qualitative baselines will establish a narrative which articulates the current context in which
the project will be working and target scenarios hypothesising the paradigm shift potential and change to the enabling environment that the project
will support, including how the project will specifically contribute to that change. This will be aligned with the overall program narrative, but with
specific details related to the country and project context. The coverage, or unit of analysis, for this baseline exercise will depend on the country and
the type of sub-project proposed in the country as per the IRMF guidelines. Quantitative baselines will be developed for each paradigm shift
assessment dimension and enabling environment indicators using the three-point scaling rating in the corresponding scorecard.
Monitoring and Reporting Arrangements: Sub-project level monitoring and reporting under the CRPP will combine ADB policies and protocols
with GCF criteria to ensure that CRPP results framework is complementary to existing requirements, without adding unnecessary extra reporting
burden. ADB project monitoring systems will be followed to track implementation progress. Standard ADB policies, during the loan implementation
period, require the executing / implementing agency of individual projects prepare:
1. Semi-annual progress reports which provide:
a. progress achieved by output as measured through the indicator's performance targets in the design and monitoring framework
b. key implementation issues and solutions and
c. updated implementation plan;
2. Consolidated audited and entity financial statements;
3. Semi-annual environmental and social monitoring reports, including subprojects’ environmental management plans, gender action plans;
and
4. Project Completion Report within 3 months of physical completion of the project.
In line with GCF M&E policy, annual performance reports (APRs) for the CRPP will be undertaken by the project management units under the
guidance and supervision of the CRPP MEL Expert. The project level APRs will include a narrative report (with supporting data as needed) on
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

Evaluative Monitoring: Evaluative monitoring is an approach that will be used to bridge the gap between traditional monitoring and evaluation
timeframes, to understand how and why change is happening. An evaluative approach to monitoring goes beyond the typical focus on tracking
progress against milestones and is designed with the aim of understanding how resilience is being built. It is a complementary approach to traditional
monitoring, that will be included in order to support annual program-level analysis and synthesis of all projects progress against the ToC pathways.
In practice this will require integrating an evaluative lens into monitoring processes so that key evidence, findings and lessons can be generated as
projects are implemented.8
Evaluation Arrangements
The evaluation arrangements will consist of mid-term reviews and final evaluation reports for each sub-project with investment from GCF as well as
the CRPP program as a whole. As with monitoring and reporting, the CRPP evaluation plan will align GCF policies, especially the GCF Evaluation
Policy, with ADB policies and protocols to ensure that there is a coordinated and coherent approach to evaluation, that maximizes learning and
accountability, but is efficient in its allocation of resources, and does not overburden project management and other key stakeholders.
Mid-term review (projects): The CRPP MEL Expert will be responsible for overseeing the Mid-Term Review (MTR) and the Terminal Evaluation
(TE) of the GCF funded activities. The MEL Expert, in coordination with the project management units, will oversee the process of hiring external,
independent entities or consultants to carry out the MTR, which will provide an assessment of project performance at the project’s mid-point. This
will be a formative exercise and will include analyzing whether the project is on track, what problems and challenges the project is encountering, and
what corrective actions are required so that the project can achieve its intended outcomes by project completion in the most efficient and sustainable
way.
Mid-term review (Program): ADB will conduct a mid-term review of the program in the 5th year of the program implementation to take stock of
results and implementation of the first phase of investments under the program. This program-level evaluation will be undertaken by an independent
entity and coordinated by the MEL Expert, which will assess the performance of the program against the GCF evaluation criteria, including
financial/economic performances as part of the program efficiency and effectiveness criterion. The evaluation will determine progress being made
toward the achievement of outcomes and outputs and will identify course correction if needed. It will include a range of appropriate quantitative and

qualitative research methods such as surveys, and key informant interviews, to evaluate the program’s impacts on resilience, human well-being, and
other key indicators relevant to the result framework at the program levels. Recommendations of the mid-term review will be incorporated into the
design of the program to secure maximum results and sustainability during subsequent program implementation.
Terminal Evaluations (projects): A Terminal Evaluation (TE) will take place at the end of each sub-project implementation period, according to
ADB and GCF established policies. ADB’s Independent Evaluation Office will be responsible for assuring the quality and independence of the TE at
the end of project implementation, which is a summative evaluation, and will liaise with the CRPP MEL Expert throughout the process. An independent
assessment of project performance against standard evaluation criteria (e.g. strategic relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, likelihood of impact and
sustainability) will be made based on documentary evidence, stakeholder interviews and, in most cases, a field mission. . The draft TE report will
be sent to project stakeholders during a commenting process managed by the Evaluation Office and the CRPP MEL Expert. Formal comments on
the report will be shared in an open and transparent manner. The evaluation reports will be publicly disclosed and will be followed by a
recommendation compliance process.
Terminal Evaluation (Program): An independent Terminal Evaluation (TE) will take place at the end of programme implementation according to
ADB and GCF established policies, especially the Evaluation Policy. The TE will be an assessment of programme performance against standard
evaluation criteria (e.g., strategic relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, likelihood of impact and sustainability). The TE will use the paradigm shift and
enabling environment scorecards to report against the targets identified in the baseline. The draft TE report will be shared with programme
stakeholders for comment and subsequently disclosed publicly.
Knowledge management
The implementation of systematic MEL activities in the CRPP will generate information that will advance understanding, not only of how countries
can respond to the challenge of climate change, but also organizational performance and the relevance, efficiency and effectiveness of the approach
taken for the management and implementation of a large-scale climate adaptation fund. The CRPP will systematically record and disseminate lessons
learned in terms of its programmatic approach towards MEL, with their reflection papers and critical analysis providing a wealth of information that
can be used to continuously improve MEL practice in the context of resilience. In order to ensure that lessons learned from the CRPP have maximum
utility and contribute to inward and outward learning on climate resilience programming, a knowledge management strategy will be developed as
part of the roll-out of the CRPP and will include a clearly defined work program and accompanying budget.

RISK ASSESSMENT AND MANAGEMENT
F.1. Risk factors and mitigations measures (max. 3 pages)
The level of key risks that will affect the CRPP performance are generally low to medium and expected to
be mitigated with the ADB’s established rules and procedures. Key risks identified are related to
implementation delays due to COVID-19, changing government priorities, compliance to GCF and ADB
procurement rules and policies and environmental and social risks.
The CRPP builds on over 11 years of adaptation programming at scale, including 8 years of implementing
a systematic climate risk management framework in ADB, and over 50 years of development finance
operations. ADB will use existing institutional arrangements, thus there a high confidence on the project
delivery and success. For these reasons, the risks to the project implementation and execution are
considered low. ADB has existing and highly rigorous protocols and guidance for financial and operational
risk and these will be applied in the project. ADB’s Safeguards Policy Statement of 2009 that sets out the
policy objectives for key safeguards areas (namely environmental safeguards, involuntary resettlement
safeguards, and Indigenous Peoples safeguards) is in place and its effectiveness continually being assessed
and enhanced to better manage the environmental and social risks arising from projects and in ensuring
their social and environmental sustainability.
Selected Risk Factor 1 Implementation delays due to COVID-19
Category Probability Impact
Technical and operational Medium Medium
Description
Projects face implementation delays due to COVID-19 related lockdowns and travel restrictions
Mitigation Measure(s)
COVID 19 has caused delays in the preparation and implementation of many ADB projects. It has affected
schedules for feasibility studies, implementation of detailed designs, and initiating construction. In order to
keep the operations moving, ADB has adjusted its approaches and strategies to respond to the situation
such as use of online consultation meetings, and maximize engagement of available local experts to do
sections of feasibility studies that require ground work.
Selected Risk Factor 2 Lack of prioritization by governments for projects
Category Probability Impact
Governance Low Medium
Description
Borrower governments fiscal burden may not allow for external borrowing, and / or governments may
choose to invest in non-resilience projects with external financing.
Mitigation Measure(s)
The program will work closely with the governments to promote country ownership and help them understand
and prioritize resilience projects. This can be done through supporting policy dialogues to influence for
transformational planning and programming and investing in local adaptation, and targeted technical
assistance which aims to strengthen institutions and capacity to access funding, prepare and implement
adaptation projects. The potential and opportunities for resilience financing for COVID-19 recovery will also
be raised with governments during ADB country programming discussions, as part of project origination and
project identification processes.

F.1. Risk factors and mitigations measures (max. 3 pages) |  | 
The level of key risks that will affect the CRPP performance are generally low to medium and expected to

implementation delays due to COVID-19, changing government priorities, compliance to GCF and ADB
procurement rules and policies and environmental and social risks.
The CRPP builds on over 11 years of adaptation programming at scale, including 8 years of implementing
a systematic climate risk management framework in ADB, and over 50 years of development finance
operations. ADB will use existing institutional arrangements, thus there a high confidence on the project
delivery and success. For these reasons, the risks to the project implementation and execution are
considered low. ADB has existing and highly rigorous protocols and guidance for financial and operational
risk and these will be applied in the project. ADB’s Safeguards Policy Statement of 2009 that sets out the
policy objectives for key safeguards areas (namely environmental safeguards, involuntary resettlement
safeguards, and Indigenous Peoples safeguards) is in place and its effectiveness continually being assessed
and enhanced to better manage the environmental and social risks arising from projects and in ensuring
their social and environmental sustainability. |  |

Description

Mitigation Measure(s)
All procurement to be financed under the program must be carried out in accordance with ADB’s
