documents such as procurement plans, bidding documents, requests for quotation, contract monitoring
forms, among others. Such measures will lower the probability of the occurrence of procurement related
risks.
Selected Risk Factor 4 Project level: ESS and GESI alignment
Category Probability Impact
Technical and operational Low Low
Description
Beneficiaries’ limited capacity to comply with national regulations and/or ADB and GCF environmental and
social policy requirements and gender and inclusion requirements
Mitigation Measure(s)
To ensure that environmental and social risks and impacts of CRPP IF supported applications are managed,
an Environmental and Social Management Framework (ESMF) is in place that will apply to any project that
utilizes GCF funds through the program. The ESMF will be implemented and maintained by CRPP IF as
part of its risk assessment process and environmental and social safeguards compliance undertaking in
order to meet ADB safeguards requirements as per ADB SPS, GCF’s Environmental and Social Policy,
Good International Industry Practices and national and local laws of recipient governments. The policies,
set of procedures and designated staff responsible for implementation detailed in the ESMF will guide CRPP-
IF in manging its overall exposure to environmental and social risks of its current and future portfolio of
adaptation investments. The set of procedures integrated in the ESMF include screening and categorization,
conduct of due diligence, monitoring and managing non-compliance.
Furthermore, both ADB SPS and GCF’s ESS standards recognize stakeholder engagement and disclosure,
among others, as compliance benchmarks on ensuring broad multi-stakeholder support and participation
throughout project lifecycle and strengthening beneficiaries’ capacity for compliance with national and local
regulations and ADB and GCF environmental and social policy requirements and gender and inclusion
requirements which will be integrated in the CRPP IF ESMF.
Selected Risk Factor 5 Financial
Category Probability Impact
Credit Low Low
Description
Lack of ability of borrowers to meet repayment of debts from the program
Mitigation Measure(s)
ADB’s comprehensive due diligence and technical support will mitigate the risk that the borrower may have
related to inability to service the loan due to insufficient net operating cash flow to meet the debt service. In
addition, all loans from the program will be aligned with ADB sovereign loans and thus be covered by the
similar sovereign guarantees. As such the credit or loan default risk on repayment of program loans is low
and related only to risks of the sovereign itself.

Selected Risk Factor 6 Money laundering, terrorist financing and prohibited practices
Category Probability Impact
Prohibited practices Low Low
Description
GCF financing through CRPP IF results in money laundering, terrorist financing or other prohibited
practices.
Mitigation Measure(s)
GCF financing will be provided as loans and/or grants to sovereign entities. As GCF funds will be provided
alongside co-financing from ADB, ADB anticorruption and integrity policies and required due diligence will
apply at project level, which will mitigate this risk.
ADB conducts integrity due diligence (IDD) on nongovernment counterparts or recipients of ADB financing,
to assess any previous involvement in integrity-related or money-laundering issues. In addition, ADB
conducts proactive integrity reviews on ongoing sovereign projects to mitigate integrity risks. ADB’s Office
of Anticorruption and Integrity (OAI) through its Due Diligence Unit, is tasked to (i) advance awareness of
ADB’s anticorruption and AML/CFT policies in collaboration with other departments; (ii) act as focal point for
and provide independent advice to Management and concerned departments on significant integrity or
money laundering or financing of terrorism (ML/FT) concerns, including investigations as required to
facilitate ADB’s ability to assess significant integrity or ML/FT concerns; and (iii) provide oversight
and guidance to concerned departments on integrity and ML/FT risks, including AML/CFT internal
controls, and integrity due diligence, which encompasses ML/FT checks.
Furthermore, all projects must comply with ADB’s Anticorruption Policy (1998, as amended to date) and
acknowledge that ADB reserves the right to investigate directly, or through its agents, any alleged corrupt,
fraudulent, collusive or coercive practice relating to the projects; and recipients of the grant/loan shall
cooperate with any such investigation and extend all necessary assistance for satisfactory completion of
such investigation.
In terms of financial management assessment, in accordance with ADB’s Charter, all projects must take
necessary measures to ensure that the proceeds of any loan made, guaranteed or participated in by ADB
are used only for the purposes for which the loan was granted and with due attention to considerations of
economy and efficiency.276 Accordingly, ADB undertakes financial due diligence and financial management
assessment (FMA) of the executing agency and/or implementing agency of ADB-funded projects. The FMA
is a review of the entity’s systems, to assess gaps and mitigation measures for financial and management
accounting, reporting, auditing, and internal controls. It also involves an assessment of the entity’s
disbursement and cash flow management arrangements, and governance and anticorruption measures.277
ADB defines “executing agency” as the government agency with overall responsibility and oversight for the
carrying out of a loan, grant or a TA-grant funded project, and it will be specifically identified in the financing
agreement for the project. A project may also include one or more “implementing agencies”, which are
governmental or other bodies responsible for implementing specific activities under a project.
The proceeds for projects under the program will be disbursed in accordance with ADB’s Loan Disbursement
Handbook (2017, as amended from time to time), which sets out detailed parameters and procedures for the
release of funds to the borrower. Public disclosure of the audited project’s financial statements, including the
auditor’s opinion on the project financial statements, will be guided by ADB’s Access to Information Policy.
ADB’s OAI serves as the initial point of contact for all allegations of integrity violations in projects and other
activities of ADB. Allegations are independently and objectively assessed and, where necessary,
investigated pursuant to ADB’s Anticorruption Policy. OAI registers and reviews all complaints to determine
whether they require further investigation.278 Under ADB’s Administrative Order 2.10: Whistleblower and
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

GCF POLICIES AND STANDARDS
G.1. Environmental and social risk assessment
CRPP IF was screened in accordance with GCF’s Environmental and Social Policy (2018)279, Revised
Environmental and Social Policy (2021) 280 and ADB’s Safeguards Policy Statement (2009) 281 . While
both policies are generally substantively equivalent, the categorization is slightly different particularly
involving investments through financial intermediaries (this, including other emerging concerns that are
not common to both policies, will be addressed as compliance measures in the CRPP IF). The CRPP IF
proposes the establishment of an investment facility that will provide grant financing (proposed through
GCF) and ADB donor financing (and potentially other multi donor co-financing) to adaptation investments
that will implement climate risk information, climate resilient livelihoods and infrastructure and facilitate
transformation adaptation for the poor and vulnerable groups. ADB through SDCC, will host and manage
the CRPP IF operations, acting as financial intermediary for providing GCF funds alongside ADB funds
to support investments in selected countries. The CRPP IF is categorized as Category FI (financial
intermediary) in line with ADB SPS Safeguard requirements (SR 4: Special requirements for different
finance modalities) that include, among others, the need to establish an environmental and social
management framework (ESMF). The ESMF should have the following components: a) an indication of
relevant environmental and social policies, and applicable requirements; b) guidelines and procedures
for conducting due diligence of proposed investments, including screening of proposed projects to be
financed; c) identification of organization capacity and competency; d) guidelines for safeguards
monitoring; and e) guidelines for managing non-compliances. Screening and categorization of projects
will be undertaken in accordance with the ESMF to ensure compliance with ADB’s requirements
specified in Safeguard Requirements (SR) 1 on Environmental Safeguards; SR 2 on Involuntary
Resettlement Safeguards; and SR 3 on Indigenous Peoples Safeguards.
The GCF’s environmental and social risk category determines the extent of the due diligence required,
the scope of the mitigation measures and the resources necessary to implement environment and social
management plans, stakeholder engagement and information disclosure. Based on the screening and
categorization for investments through financial intermediation, the CRPP IF is rated as Category I-2 or
Medium level of intermediation. This is when an intermediary’s existing or proposed portfolio includes,
or is expected to include, financial exposure to category B activities. GCF defines category B activities
as moderate risk activities that include those with risks and impacts “that are less adverse than Category
A activities in terms of magnitude and likelihood of Occurrence” and where risks and impacts are
considered limited, and the magnitude is expected to be low to moderate. The safeguards’ risks and
impacts of Category B investments are few, contained within the footprint of the activities, largely
reversible, and readily mitigated through generally accepted mitigation measures and good international
industry practices.
Category I-2 is proposed for CRPP-IF on the basis of the investments that it will support, that falls under
the following: a) adaptation investments that support implementation of Information and systems for
delivering applied climate-risk informed investments at scale (directly linked to attainment of Output 4);
b) climate resilient pro-poor livelihoods investments (directly linked to attainment of Output 5; and c)
Investments on climate adaptation pro-poor infrastructure (directly linked to the attainment of Output 6).
Category I-2 is expected to include financial exposure to category B activities as defined above. An
ESMF is required for the CRPP IF where specific investments and their location have yet to be clearly
defined.
When project details are available, appropriate environmental and social due diligence should be
prepared. The CRPP IF ESMF will guide and provide the framework for managing environmental and
social risks associated with sub investments, and guide the risks evaluation at appraisal and monitoring
stages. This is to ensure that financial intermediation operations result in projects that are
environmentally and socially sound and in compliance with relevant national and local laws on
environmental and social regulations, ADB SPS and GCF’s ESP, and Good International Industry
Practices.
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

The establishment of the ESMF is in line with ADB SPS and GCF revised ESP and will be maintained
by the CRPP IF to guide the identification, assessment, management and monitoring of the
environmental and social risks, including risks of sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment (GCF’s
Revised Environmental and Social Policy (2021)) . This process is critical to support decision-making on
whether the level of risk associated with investment is acceptable to CRPP-IF, to minimize environmental
and social risks and impacts and to identify potential co-benefits associated with CRPP-IF investments.
The CRPP IF ESMF includes the following processes:
a) Screening and categorization. Screening is undertaken to determine if project falls on the list of
prohibited investment activities list (SPS, Appendix 5). The project will not be pursued if it is an
excluded activity. ADB adopts a classification system that assigns one of the following categories
to reflect the significance of a project’s potential environmental and social risks and impacts:
• Category A for projects likely to have significant adverse environmental impacts,
significant adverse involuntary resettlement impacts and significant impacts on
indigenous peoples that are irreversible, diverse and unprecedented. Safeguard
requirements include the preparation of environmental impact assessment and
development of resettlement plan and indigenous peoples plan;
• Category B for proposed projects with potential limited adverse environmental impacts,
involuntary resettlement impacts that are not deemed significant and limited impacts on
indigenous peoples. Safeguard requirements include the preparation of an initial
environmental examination, resettlement plan and indigenous peoples plan;
• Category C rating for activities with minimal or no adverse environmental risks or
impacts, no involuntary resettlement impacts and not expected to have impacts on
indigenous peoples require no further action; and
• Category FI when a proposed project involves the investment of ADB funds to or
through a financial intermediary with safeguard requirement include the need for the FI
to develop an environmental and social management system.
b) Due diligence and review including systematic identification, quantification and assessment of
environmental and social risks associated with sub projects will be undertaken, and the application
of the mitigation hierarchy (avoidance, minimization and mitigation, and eventually offset of
residual impacts) will be applied to the risks identified. The scope and extent of due diligence is
defined by the risk category identified in the screening and categorization procedures.
c) Information disclosure. In line with ADB’s Public Communications Policy (2018, as amended from
time to time), safeguards documents will be disclosed in the ADB website to make stakeholders be
aware of and understand the risks and impacts of the project. Full disclosure of the safeguard
reports to GCF Board and Active Observers will be coordinated with the GCF secretariat in line
with the GCF Information Disclosure Policy.
d) Consultation and participation. ADB requires borrowers and clients to undertake meaningful
consultations by engaging with communities, people affected by proposed projects (including
persons in vulnerable positions and situations), through consultation and informed participation.
e) Monitoring and reporting. Procedures to monitor ongoing compliance with and the progress of
implementation of safeguards plans will be integrated in the ESMF, including procedures for the
implementation of corrective actions to address non-compliance and unanticipated environmental
and social risks; and
f) Grievance redress mechanism (GRM). ADB requires the borrowers/clients to establish and
maintain a GRM to receive and facilitate resolution of affected people’s concerns and grievances.
In case of occurrence of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse and Sexual Harassment (SEAH), ensure
that there are established accessible and inclusive survivor-centred and gender-responsive
grievance redress mechanisms in place and procedures to address SEAH. The ADB
Accountability Mechanism is also in place to provide an independent forum and process whereby
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

people adversely affected by ADB-financed projects can voice, and seek a resolution of their
problems, as well as report alleged violations of ADB’s operational policies and procedures.
G.2. Gender assessment and action plan
Women have a critical role to play in advancing investment in building resilience to climate change,
especially at the local level, and must be recognized as vital drivers of resilient development. However,
social and political inequalities, as well as patriarchal power structures, remain deeply entrenched in
CRPP countries, often limiting women’s leadership and participation in decision-making, and contributing
to disproportionate levels of vulnerability and low adaptive capacity compared to men. This is particularly
the case in poor communities in low-income countries as multidimensional poverty significantly limits
women’s ability to confront climate change. The following are examples of factors identified in the CRPP
program level Gender Assessment that contribute to women’s increased vulnerability and lower adaptive
capacity compared to men in CRPP countries. They are closely related to socially created gender
functions, systemic discriminations, and the power imbalances between women and men, and include;
• Women typically have less access to all types of information including climate information and early
warning.282 This is related to gender-based differences in literacy rates and access to education that
are present in most CRPP countries, with differences often more pronounced in rural than urban
areas and in some countries more than others. In Pakistan for example, less than half of women are
literate (46%), compared with 71% of men, and in Cambodia, the gender gaps in education are most
prominently seen in rural areas.
• Significant gaps remain in social protection programs reaching women. In Indonesia, insufficient use
of up to date sex-disaggregated data for monitoring and targeting of beneficiaries, complicated
information about protective measures and limited assistance available from official sources, and
inadequate support to complete enrolment procedures have been identified as important issues283.
In Pakistan, large gender gaps in mobile phone ownership and national ID possession, has meant
that women are at risk of being disproportionately excluded from the Ehsaas Emergency Cash
Program, which was a key part of the government’s Covid-19 response284.
• Women in many CRPP countries are largely excluded from decision-making and are absent from
leadership positions. This is particularly true at the local level. This is often due to discriminatory
customary norms and cultural and structural barriers that prevent women from participating, such as
in Vanuatu were women are excluded from direct roles in the village decision-making body, and in
some cases women are invited to attend but decisions are already made by the men, or in Timor-
Leste where were 95% of the village chiefs are men, despite having a constitution that affirms the
right of equal participation of women and men in political life.
• Gender gaps in access to agricultural extension and rural advisory services are prevalent in many
CRPP countries, such as in Cambodia, were women receive only 10% of agricultural extensions
services despite comprising 51% of the primary workforce in subsistence agriculture and 57% of the
workforce in market-oriented agriculture285. This is despite evidence that suggests women are more
likely than men to use the information they receive286.
• Social, cultural and legal barriers prevent women from accessing financial services in many CRPP
countries, such as Pakistan, PNG, Timor-Leste, and Vanuatu. Women have limited ownership of
productive assets, such as agricultural land and property and the consequent lack of collateral
represents a barrier for women’s access to formal financial services. Other barriers include; lack of
collateral and ID documents that hinder the access to formal financial services; low digital literacy
and mobile phone ownership, that deter women’s outreach through digital financial services.
• There is a significant disparity between men and women in earnings, the quality of jobs, and
voice and representation in leadership positions in many CRPP countries, and women’s economic

people adversely affected by ADB-financed projects can voice, and seek a resolution of their
problems, as well as report alleged violations of ADB’s operational policies and procedures.
G.2. Gender assessment and action plan
Women have a critical role to play in advancing investment in building resilience to climate change,
especially at the local level, and must be recognized as vital drivers of resilient development. However,
social and political inequalities, as well as patriarchal power structures, remain deeply entrenched in
CRPP countries, often limiting women’s leadership and participation in decision-making, and contributing
to disproportionate levels of vulnerability and low adaptive capacity compared to men. This is particularly
the case in poor communities in low-income countries as multidimensional poverty significantly limits
women’s ability to confront climate change. The following are examples of factors identified in the CRPP
program level Gender Assessment that contribute to women’s increased vulnerability and lower adaptive
capacity compared to men in CRPP countries. They are closely related to socially created gender
functions, systemic discriminations, and the power imbalances between women and men, and include;
• Women typically have less access to all types of information including climate information and early
warning.282 This is related to gender-based differences in literacy rates and access to education that
are present in most CRPP countries, with differences often more pronounced in rural than urban
areas and in some countries more than others. In Pakistan for example, less than half of women are
literate (46%), compared with 71% of men, and in Cambodia, the gender gaps in education are most
prominently seen in rural areas.
• Significant gaps remain in social protection programs reaching women. In Indonesia, insufficient use
of up to date sex-disaggregated data for monitoring and targeting of beneficiaries, complicated
information about protective measures and limited assistance available from official sources, and
inadequate support to complete enrolment procedures have been identified as important issues283.
In Pakistan, large gender gaps in mobile phone ownership and national ID possession, has meant
that women are at risk of being disproportionately excluded from the Ehsaas Emergency Cash
Program, which was a key part of the government’s Covid-19 response284.
• Women in many CRPP countries are largely excluded from decision-making and are absent from
leadership positions. This is particularly true at the local level. This is often due to discriminatory
customary norms and cultural and structural barriers that prevent women from participating, such as
in Vanuatu were women are excluded from direct roles in the village decision-making body, and in
some cases women are invited to attend but decisions are already made by the men, or in Timor-
Leste where were 95% of the village chiefs are men, despite having a constitution that affirms the
right of equal participation of women and men in political life.
• Gender gaps in access to agricultural extension and rural advisory services are prevalent in many
CRPP countries, such as in Cambodia, were women receive only 10% of agricultural extensions
services despite comprising 51% of the primary workforce in subsistence agriculture and 57% of the
workforce in market-oriented agriculture285. This is despite evidence that suggests women are more
likely than men to use the information they receive286.
• Social, cultural and legal barriers prevent women from accessing financial services in many CRPP
countries, such as Pakistan, PNG, Timor-Leste, and Vanuatu. Women have limited ownership of
productive assets, such as agricultural land and property and the consequent lack of collateral
represents a barrier for women’s access to formal financial services. Other barriers include; lack of
collateral and ID documents that hinder the access to formal financial services; low digital literacy
and mobile phone ownership, that deter women’s outreach through digital financial services.
• There is a significant disparity between men and women in earnings, the quality of jobs, and
voice and representation in leadership positions in many CRPP countries, and women’s economic

=== PAGE 136 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 132
F
activities often involve low value-added activities. In Papua New Guinea, for example, there is a
strong gender gap in employment with only 14% of women as waged workers compared to 33% of
men, and 85% of women are in vulnerable employment compared with 65% of men287. In Lao PDR,
95.5% of women are informally employed and dominate small-scale retail and vending enterprises288.
Under-employed workers are also more likely to be women as they juggle employment and family
responsibilities. In Lao PDR, women spend significantly more time on unpaid domestic labour (4
hours per day on average) compared to men (30 minutes per day)289.
• Women’s adaptive capacity is also limited by the fact that they often face barriers to accessing and
control over natural resources. Women are underrepresented in environmental decision-making and
natural resources management, such as forest user groups, water user associations, and
environmental policy-making. Due to these disadvantages, women can be less likely to benefit from
projects that promote nature-based solutions.
• Women are often reluctant to use emergency shelters, and there are frequent examples of women
refusing to use emergency shelters due to either design concerns or because of their bad
experiences from the past290. This is often because basic gender needs like separation toilet facilities,
dedicated space for women, and private space for pregnant woman and nursing mothers are rarely
factored into the design and management of emergency shelters. Evidence shows that women and
girls are at greater risk of gender-based violence (GBV), including sexual harassment and domestic
violence during emergency situations and in the aftermath of disasters in part because of poor
emergency-shelter design and inadequate coordination by disaster responders291.
Building women’s resilience to climate change and empowering women through transformational
investments in climate adaptation at the community level are core pillars of the CRPP, reflecting ADBs
commitment to gender equality. The approach toward implementing investment activities that build
women’s resilience to climate change will emphasize women’s role in resilience as “active stakeholders”
and “game changers” rather than “vulnerable” and “victims.” The CRPP also understands that structural
gender inequalities are driving women’s climate risk in CRPP countries, and so a gender transformative
approach that aims to change structural inequalities and address issues of climate justice292, will be a
central element of CRPP investments. CRPP investments in climate resilience therefore represent an
opportunity to promote a positive change towards gender equality and challenge socially created gender
functions, systemic discriminations and the power imbalances between women and men, which intensify
the social and economic barriers faced by women to adapt to climate change293. As such, the CRPP will
go beyond mainstreaming gender considerations into programming, delivering specific outputs for
strengthening women’s adaptive capacity, and challenging the structural sociocultural norms that drive
their vulnerability through transformational investments.
Examples of gender interventions that are identified in the CRPP Program Level Action Plan, and
address some of the specific issues identified above include;
• Undertaking action research studies that address gaps in understanding around women and
resilience in CRPP countries and make the case for women-focused adaptation investments.
• Support innovative adaptation initiatives and pilot activities at the community level to identify and
test women-focused adaptation measures that could be scaled up through larger investments in
the future.
• Carry out policy dialogues and forums for exchange at the regional, national, and local levels that
bring together grassroots women’s organizations, government ministries from various sectors, the
private sector, academic institutions, and other civil society organizations, providing a platform for
exchange and collaboration between actors that may not traditionally work closely together.
INTERNAL. This information is accessible to ADB Management and staff. It may be shared outside ADB with appropriate permission.

=== PAGE 137 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 133
F
• Creating policy incentives and procedures for the inclusion of women in adaptation decision-making
at the local level and building their capacity to use participatory tools and procedures for climate
risk informed development planning and implementation to empower local women to act on
adaptation.
• The CRPP will seek to tackle the limitations of existing social protection schemes in terms of
reaching women, ensuring that social protection programs include specific identification of, and
outreach to, women, using sex-disaggregated data for targeting beneficiaries.
• Recognizing that financial inclusion is key to strengthening women’s resilience to climate related
shocks and stresses, the CRPP will seek to expand women’s access to instruments such as
indexed-based microinsurance, through targeted financial products and services as part of its
investment projects that can be paired with capacity building on savings and investments,
supporting preparedness to shocks while empowering women financially, socially and politically.
• CRPP investments will seek to address gender-related factors that influence women’s ability to
participate in value chains, increase access to and control over income, promote women’s
engagement in agricultural entrepreneurship orientated activities, deepen women’s chances to
increase value of their agricultural activities, as well as diversify their income-earning opportunities,
and provide women with leadership roles.
• Investments will also integrate initiatives that reduce women’s time poverty and burden of care in
ways that reduce and redistribute labor and time commitments to benefit them directly.
• The CRPP will integrate gender considerations in initiatives related natural resource management
that can make them more effective and sustainable294[xvi], as well as ensuring participation of women
in meetings where public works are designed and selected, including capacity-building activities
that specifically develop women’s technical and leadership skills.
• CRPP supported investments in safe shelter will ensure that shelter design includes features that
respond to specific needs of women, and increases their access, ensuring that women of all ages,
including those from marginalized groups, are properly engaged to understand their concerns and
needs and that designs respond accordingly. Women will also be equally represented in
governance structures such as shelter or community committees, to support empowerment through
participation and addressing gender norms in terms of decision-making.
The CRPP Gender Assessment and Action Plan are presented in detail in Annex 8. The Gender
Assessment provides a program level overview of some of the key gender issues that contribute to the
vulnerability of women to climate change in CRPP countries and that cause women’s lower capacity to
adapt than men. Detailed Gender Assessments will be undertaken as part of the detailed design and
preparation phase of each project and will be specific to the target area and context of the project.
Similarly, the CRPP Gender Action Plan presented in Annex 8 will provide an overarching framework for
CRPP implementation, and will be complemented by project specific Gender Action Plans to be
developed during detailed preparation phase.
G.3. Financial management and procurement
The CRPP supported projects will follow ADB systems for financial management, disbursement, audit
and procurement. Implementation of the program and projects must conform to all applicable ADB
policies including those concerning anticorruption measures, anti-money laundering, counter terrorist
financing, safeguards, gender, procurement, consulting services, and disbursement.
Financial Management. All projects’ financial accounting, disbursement procedures and auditing
requirements will be developed during project preparation and will be included their respective grant

together with an explanatory note regarding the said portions and the corresponding reason for
confidentiality under the accredited entity’s disclosure policy, and
• redacted copy for disclosure on the GCF website.

confidential information.

II. Summary of the Secretariat’s assessment
2.1 Project background
3. Countries in Asia and the Pacific region are highly exposed to the damaging impacts of
climate change. Between 2000 and 2019, the region experienced 3,068 disaster events
accounting for 42 per cent of global events. Adverse impacts of climate change will be largely
manifested at the local level. Poor and vulnerable populations face the brunt of climate impacts,
with women typically lacking equal preventive and coping capacity due to pre-existing gender
inequalities. This requires a large-scale intervention in order to address these issues at a
regional level.
4. In responding to the financial gap and needs, the proposed project (the Community
Resilience Partnership Program (CRPP)), a regional programme of the Asian Development Bank
(ADB), aims to scale up adaptation measures by mobilizing climate investment at large scale at
the community level. In particular, it will support measures that address the nexus between
climate change, poverty and gender inequality across seven countries (Cambodia, Indonesia, the
Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Pakistan, Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste and Vanuatu) in
Asia and the Pacific region.
5. This proposal is a unique and important programmatic concept for scaling up local
adaptation investments in the region, building on the lessons learned from similar programmes,
especially in Africa, funded by the Pilot Programme for Climate Resilience under the Climate
Investment Fund. The goal of this multi-country programme is to improve (i) the enabling
environment for knowledge, finance and implementation of local adaptation measures; (ii) the
mobilization of pro-poor adaptation finance at scale; (iii) food security of poor and vulnerable
communities; and (iv) mitigation of the exposure of poor and vulnerable people to climate
shocks and stresses.
6. The CRPP comprises two separate but interlinked components; the CRPP Trust Fund
(TF) focuses on upstream support to strengthen the enabling environment required for
implementing local adaptation measures at scale, funded by bilateral donors;1 and the CRPP
Investment Fund (IF) focuses on the actions for rolling out local adaptation measures through
downstream investment (subprojects), which will be co-financed by ADB and GCF. The CRPP
will be operationalized through a special vehicle established by the ADB (Community Resilience
Financing Partnership Facility).
7. The CRPP IF will provide grant and loan resources to implement outputs 4, 5 and 6 of
the wider CRPP programme (described below).
(a) Output 4: Information and systems for delivering applied climate risk informed
investments at scale improved;
(b) Output 5: Climate-resilient pro-poor livelihoods investments implemented; and
(c) Output 6: Climate adaptation pro-poor infrastructure implemented.
8. The CRPP IF will have a total of USD 120 million (USD 100 million grant and USD 20
million loan) from GCF for seven countries (with each country receiving between USD 10
million and USD 40 million) and will leverage at least USD 555 million from ADB’s resources and
USD 75 million from bilateral donors to support at least 10–15 subprojects (at least one project
in each country) from 2023 to 2030. Subprojects seeking financing from the IF will need to be
approved by the ADB Board between 2024 and 2027 and complete implementation by 2030.
1 The Trust Fund will be fully capitalized by bilateral donors and financial institutions, including UK Aid, Nordic
Development Fund and Agence française de développement. This total cost excludes the potential contribution from
respective governments that will be determined at the individual project level.

=== PAGE 164 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.06
Page 164
9. The combined effect of project interventions will result in strengthened locally led pro-
poor adaptation measures and knowledge transfer, enhanced finance mobilization and food
security, and reduced climate shocks and stress of poor and vulnerable people in seven
countries. The project will support 3,219,400 direct beneficiaries and will also indirectly benefit
4,465,000 people. Its coordinated and programmatic approach is expected to allow for
scalability, replication and sustainability of the programme between countries and within
countries across Asia and the Pacific region.
10. The CRPP will have environmental, economic, social and gender co-benefits, with strong
emphasis especially on women’s participation in decision-making and leadership and reduced
inequalities. It is expected to deliver against many Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs),
including SDG 1: no poverty; SDG 3: good health and well-being; SDG 5: Gender Equality; SDG
10: Reduced Inequalities; SDG 11: sustainable cities and communities; and SDG 13: climate
action. There are also potential mitigation co-benefits anticipated through some of the
interventions.
2.2 Component-by-component analysis
11. The goal of the proposal will be to deliver transformational adaptation solutions
through large-scale investments explicitly targeted at the poor and vulnerable population.
There are two main and complementary components to deliver its objective.
Component 1: CRPP TF – supporting countries to develop knowledge, build capacity, and structure
adaptation projects through an upstream programme (total cost: USD 72,500,000 grant from UK
Aid, Nordic Development Fund, Agence française de développement; GCF cost: 0 or 0 per cent of
GCF budget)
12. The first component will be financed through the CRPP TF and focus on the three
outputs: (i) strengthening knowledge and action research on climate risk informed pro-poor
community-level solutions (USD 15,500,000); (ii) strengthening institutional and community
capacity to develop and deliver climate adaptation investments at community level (USD
12,000,000); and (iii) Identifying and preparing inclusive and pro-poor adaptation investment
projects (USD 45,000,000).
13. Activities will focus on undertaking the analytical work that complements the design
and implementation of projects to be supported by the IF. It will develop climate risk
assessment and decision support tools, conduct training and capacity-building on designing and
implementing adaptation investments at the community level, prepare large-scale adaptation
investment projects, and pilot innovative transformational solutions. These activities will
generate knowledge and evidence to be shared.
14. The activities under component 1 are also complementary to the activities planned
under component 2. CRPP TF supports the development of the climate rationale and project
preparation, the implementation of which will be financed and scaled up by component 2.
Component 2: CRPP Investment Fund (IF) – supporting implementation of local adaptation
measures (information systems, resilient pro-poor livelihoods, adaptation infrastructure) through
a downstream investment programme (Total cost: USD 668,500,000; GCF cost: 120,000,000 or 100
per cent of GCF budget for the programme)
15. Component 2 will be financed through the CRPP IF, supporting activities under outputs
4, 5 and 6. The three outputs will deliver adaptation activities through the provision of
combined grant finance with major investment funding to deliver adaptation at scale at the local
level.
16. These outputs will be co-financed by the ADB and GCF. The focus will be to deliver: (iv)
improvement of information and systems for delivering applied climate risk informed

=== PAGE 165 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.06
Page 165
investments at scale (total cost: USD 118,000,000; GCF grants USD 20,000,000); (v)
implementation of climate-resilient pro-poor livelihoods investments (total cost: USD
238,000,000; GCF grants USD 40,000,000); and (vi) implementation of climate-resilient pro-
poor infrastructure investment (total cost: USD 312,500,000; GCF grants USD 40,000,000 and
loans USD 20,000,000).
(a) Output 4. Information and systems for delivering applied climate risk informed
investments at scale improved. The GCF grant finance for climate information for
delivering climate risk informed decisions is targeted to address information failures
that prevent climate-resilient development and will be largely focused on technical
assistance provision (which is eligible for grant finance under B.05/07) to cover the
additional activities to strengthen climate services at local level, to integrate climate risk
information into social protection programmes and decentralization policies. It is also
highlighted that these activities will cover activities that explicitly target the most
vulnerable groups.
(i) Activity area 4.1. Climate information services for key sectors to meet local
adaptation needs;
(ii) Activity area 4.2. Climate risk informed social protection systems; and
(iii) Activity area 4.3. Climate risk information systems for decentralisation policies.
(b) Output 5. Climate-resilient pro-poor livelihoods investments implemented. The
GCF grant and loan finance for climate-resilient pro-poor livelihood investment will
focus on addressing risk perceptions for new climate-resilient livelihoods or markets,
and covering the incremental cost or the risk premium required to make these new
livelihoods or investments viable. Again, the activities will also be targeted at the most
vulnerable groups.
(i) Activity area 5.1. Climate-resilient agroecological systems;
(ii) Activity area 5.2. Information technology and risk management services for
climate-resilient livelihoods; and
(iii) Activity area 5.3. Climate-resilient agriculture supply chains.
(c) Output 6. Climate adaptation pro-poor infrastructure implemented. The GCF grant
and loan finance for climate-resilient pro-poor infrastructure investment is targeted at
the additional costs of green, resilient infrastructure, necessary to deal with climate
risks but requiring finance that would otherwise not be available, for poor and
vulnerable groups. The primary focus is to invest in ecosystem-based adaptation, as this
provides a range of public good characteristics, and has potential benefits in reducing
non-market costs (providing environmental and social benefits).
(i) Activity area 6.1. Ecosystem-based infrastructure;
(ii) Activity area 6.2. Flood and landslide protection infrastructure; and
(iii) Activity area 6.3. Multipurpose emergency shelters.
17. The estimated impacts are considered significant and entail substantial adaptation
benefits as well as support the resilience of poor and vulnerable populations to climate change.
The proposed activities are assessed as being adequate and reasonable to support local
communities while contributing potential emissions reduction from activities related to climate-
resilient agriculture supply chains and ecosystem-based infrastructure.
18. The activities are also closely aligned with the four pillars of the United Nations’ newly
launched Early Warnings for All (EW4A) Initiative, which stipulates that every person in the
world should be protected by an early warning system by 2027 and aims to deliver multi-
hazard early warning systems (MHEWS) in over 100 countries. The proposed programme will

=== PAGE 166 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.06
Page 166
contribute to outcomes such as improved access and quality of risk data, and strengthened
capacity for developing procedures for holistic anticipatory action based on early warnings,
which has high potential for replication in Asia and the Pacific region.
19. The individual projects will align with the objectives of the CRPP and contribute to
specific outputs related to climate resilience, poverty reduction and adaptation measures. They
will be financed by the ADB and GCF, with GCF resources specifically supporting local-level
adaptation interventions. A list of potential idea notes of individual projects in each country is
summarized below with details annexed to the funding proposal.
(a) Cambodia: The Climate Resilient Smallholder Development Project aims to strengthen
community-led adaptation actions by taking a community-driven development
approach to promote climate-smart agricultural practices, rehabilitate and climate-
proof rural infrastructure, strengthen the capacity of local institutions to respond to
climate change, and develop financial risk management mechanisms such as crop
insurance.
(b) The Lao People’s Democratic Republic: The Building Resilience and Reducing Rural
Poverty Project aims to enhance the resilience of rural poor communities by expanding
non-contributory social assistance programmes to cover vulnerable people living in
areas of high climate risk, integrating early warning systems with the social registry to
expand coverage in response to climate shocks and stresses, and implementing an
economic inclusion programme tailored to address climate vulnerabilities through skills
training and financial services provision linked to conditional cash transfers.
(c) Pakistan: The Sindh Coastal Resilience Project aims to enhance the resilience of coastal
area livelihoods and infrastructure through integrated water resources and flood-risk
management schemes, as well as restored coastal defences using community-led natural
solutions. The project also emphasizes the role of women in building coastal resilience.
The project directly contributes to the activities under output 6 of the CRPP.
(d) Papua New Guinea: The proposed Improved Technical and Vocational Education and
Training for Climate Resilient Employment Project aims to strengthen climate resilience
through technical and vocational education. It includes specific measures to support
women and informal workers. Through the technical and vocational education system,
the project will develop climate-resilient agriculture, climate-resilient construction
processes and will help some vulnerable people to transition out of agriculture into
climate-resilient livelihoods. The project directly contributes to the activities under
output 5 of the CRPP.
(e) Timor-Leste: The Agriculture Value Chains and Water Harvesting Project aims to
enhance the sustainability of rural livelihoods by increasing the resilience of small-scale
agriculture. It focuses on community-led climate-smart production practices, water,
forest management, and enabling smallholder producers to participate in agricultural
value chains.
(f) Vanuatu: The Climate Change and COVID-19 Project aims to build comprehensive
resilience in poor and vulnerable groups. It focuses on creating climate-responsive
social protection systems and enhancing climate-resilient livelihood support
mechanisms, particularly for women. The project notably contributes to the activities
under output 4 of the CRPP.
III. Assessment of performance against investment criteria
3.1 Impact potential Scale: High

20. The project has medium-high impact potential as an adaptation project, with
approximately 3.2 million poor and vulnerable direct beneficiaries and 4.7 million indirect
beneficiaries over the 20 years of the programme’s lifespan. The CRPP will contribute to locally
led sustainable development in the region by strengthening the resilience of nearly five million
people and communities in seven countries across Asia and the Pacific region.
21. In all cases, women will make up at least 50 per cent of the beneficiaries. However, this
will be a minimum requirement for all individual projects, and it is anticipated that women will
make up more than 50 per cent of the total direct beneficiaries.
22. In addition, potential mitigation co-benefits are anticipated through planned activities,
such as promoting the uptake of climate-smart agricultural practices and forestation activities.
For example, rehabilitation of mangrove forests could lead to potential mitigation of upwards of
−27.6 ± 1.7 megagramme of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO -eq) per hectare per year.2.

3.2 Paradigm shift potential Scale: Medium to high
23. The core paradigm shift potential of this project centres on the enhanced mobilization of
climate investment at scale in the region. It will allow scaling up and replication, creation of an
enabling environment, contribution to the regulatory framework and policies, innovative
solutions and approaches, and, lastly, sharing knowledge and lessons.
24. Scaling up and replication: The CRPP IF will only support individual projects that
demonstrate the potential of being replicated elsewhere in the same country or other countries
in the region. By empowering government and communities with the knowledge and skills to
take appropriate action to adapt, improving systems for delivering climate-resilient
investments, and proving their effectiveness through pilots, the individual project will build the
foundations for replication, support transitions in key systems and thereby drive a paradigm
shift towards climate-resilient sustainable development. GCF funding will be used together with
the ADB investment to enable the individual project to deliver at scale.

Creation of an enabling environment (and sustainability of outcomes): The CRPP will
support outputs and outcomes that are closely aligned with national climate priorities. The
25.
CRPP TF will therefore catalyse impacts beyond a one-off project investment and deliver a
paradigm shift by ensuring that climate risk informed development becomes the new norm al.
The GCF financing will be used through the CRPP IF to support rolling out of such climate-
sensitive development, especially in the context of localization and decentralization. By
strengthening national and local institutions, the CRPP IF will ensure that its interventions will
contribute to building policy coherence around climate resilience and is taken up nation wide by
relevant agencies.
Contribution to the regulatory framework and policies: With a key focus on
mainstreaming, the CRPP will promote the integration of climate change considerations into
26.
policies and decision-making processes. The CRPP IF programming will capitalize o n ongoing
decentralization processes to support governments build robust, science-based local climate
assessment frameworks that can inform planning processes, equipping decision-makers with
the data, tools, guidance and information needed to inform local planning and investment.
Innovative solutions and approaches: The CRPP builds on the lessons learned from the
implementation of large-scale resilience programmes, which identify the need for innovative
27.
measures and approaches. The CRPP IF will support financing of adaptation projects. In
particular, GCF financing will be used to finance activities that can help overcome information ,
finance, institutional and gender-related barriers in an innovative way.
Sharing of knowledge and learning: Learning is critical to operationalize adaptive
management principles at a programme level. The CRPP TF will ensure that knowledge
28.
emerging from GCF-financed individual projects under the CRPP IF are shared with wider
stakeholders. The multi-country nature of the programme means there will be very larg e
potential for learning and replication, with the transfer of experience between programme s.
In addition, the proposed GCF CRPP-financed outputs will complement similar past and
ongoing initiatives in the countries that are financed by United Nations Framework Convention
29.
on Climate Change -related funds and contribute to the paradigm shift in the region.
30.
Global Framework for Climate Services (GFCS) has defined five priority sectors for
effective national development planning, comprising agriculture and food security, water,
health, disaster risk reduction, and energy. Depending on response capability of communities to
hazard types, the potential for benefit-cost of return on investment could be up to 500:1 for
densely-populate flood-prone areas, and 2500:1 for heat waves in populated urban centres. By
targeting different sectors, the programme will make a significant contribution to the GCF’s
support for building resilience of multi-sectoral livelihoods of most vulnerable communities.
31.
Although the specificities of the social, economic and environmental co-benefits of early
warning systems are context-specific, the proposal would benefit from exploring these in a
multi-hazard context for a range of priority hazards. ADB should explore the use of the regional,
national and subnational Climate Outlook Forum user-interfaces to co-design and co-produce
impact forecasts for priority sectors of the communities. This can be done during the
implementation of the project.
3.3 Sustainable development potential Scale: High
32. Through investments in local level adaptation, the proposal directly targets the pillars of
sustainable development – environmental, social, economic and gender. Thus, the CRPP will
deliver against several of the SDGs, including SDG 1: no poverty; SDG 3: good health and well-
being; SDG 5: gender equality; SDG 10: reduced inequalities; SDG 11: sustainable cities and
communities; and SDG 13: climate action.

=== PAGE 169 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.06
Page 169
(a) Environmental co-benefits: It is expected that CRPP TF and IF will promote nature-
based solutions through a wide range of investments, such as (i) community
infrastructure – adopting natural assets in place of/in mix with grey infrastructure to
build resilience of local communities; (ii) livelihoods – promoting nature-based
solutions as part of climate-smart agricultural practices; (iii) well-being – promoting
protection of natural assets as part of social protection programmes, such as public
works programmes; (iv) governance and decentralization – increasing the role of
women’s groups in protecting natural resources etc.
(b) Social co-benefits: All interventions supported by CRPP TF and IF will have strong social
benefits, because of the explicit focus on low-income and disadvantaged groups, and the
focus on poverty reduction and addressing existing inequalities associated with climate
change.
(c) Economic co-benefits: There is a strong economic element to the investments to be
promoted by CRPP TF and supported by CRPP IF, which is captured through the triple
dividend of investing in resilience. This includes (i) the economic activity stimulated by
reduced impacts, forward-looking planning, long-term capital investments and
entrepreneurship as well as macroeconomic benefits, and (ii) development co-benefits
from resilience investments, including positive spillovers as well as non-market
benefits.
(d) Gender-responsive development impact: Promoting gender equality is a core thrust of
the CRPP which will be promoted through the gender window of the CRPP TF. The focus
on gender equality extends from existing evidence that, when grassroot women’s groups
are involved in leading the identification and implementation of adaptation measures,
the benefits are manifold.
3.4 Needs of the recipient Scale: High
33. The poverty and vulnerability of the countries and target beneficiaries and their
adaptation needs are well elaborated throughout the proposal with descriptions of the scale and
intensity of each country’s exposure to climate risks. It highlights the increased socioeconomic
vulnerability resulting from the crisis of the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic, coupled with
the recurrence of climate hazards in these countries. Furthermore, the vulnerability of women,
especially woman in rural area, is well acknowledged in the funding proposal.
34. The recurrence of climate hazards continues to pose challenges to these countries.
Cambodia is a least developed country (LDC) in Southeast Asia with about 90 per cent of the
poor living in the countryside. Indonesia has the largest economy in Southeast Asia,
nonetheless, poverty remains high in absolute numbers with high inequality. The Lao People’s
Democratic Republic as a landlocked country is one of the LDCs with high vulnerability and low
readiness for climate change. A large percentage of the population remains close to the poverty
line. Pakistan is one of the countries most vulnerable to climate shocks in the world today with
high water stress. Papua New Guinea has consistently ranked among the lowest 30 countries in
the human development index with 30–40 per cent of poverty rates. While Timor-Leste ranked
as one of the poorest LDCs in Asia, Vanuatu, a small island developing state in the Pacific, is
exposed to high levels of climate risks, especially to tropical cyclones.
35. Most of the target countries are LDCs with high levels of vulnerability to climate change
and financial gaps to cover and sustain climate change adaptation. The proposal highlights the
lack of a pro-poor climate information system, public infrastructure, and social services as the
major vulnerability factors in the countries. The proposal also notes the lack of access to finance
as a constraint to building capacity of government, local governments, communities and
vulnerable groups, especially women.

=== PAGE 170 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.06
Page 170
3.5 Country ownership Scale: High
36. The proposal demonstrates alignment with national adaptation priorities of
participating governments, international commitments, and recommendations, such as the Paris
Agreement, the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, and the SDGs.
37. Furthermore, the CRPP will contribute to the AE’s climate targets and its ambition of
providing significant climate finance for adaptation in the region. It also responds directly to the
nationally determined contributions of beneficiary countries and builds on the
Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s call for increased feasibility and effectiveness of
adaptation through integrated, multisectoral solutions that address social inequities,
differentiated responses based on climate risk and vulnerabilities across a range of biophysical
and socioeconomic systems.
38. By strengthening national and local institutions, the proposal seeks to ensure that
investments will contribute to building policy coherence around climate resilience and is taken
up nationwide by relevant agencies. Countries’ ownership will be achieved through stakeholder
engagement and capacity-building at various decision-making levels – government, civil society
organizations, communities, financial intermediaries, and the private sector.
39. The ADB has demonstrated its strong track record as a credible AE and EE by working
with the target countries in the region to address related challenges. It has been developing and
implementing climate adaptation projects for the past decade and has the necessary expertise
and experience in implementing such projects in the region, including GCF projects in the past
years. The ADB builds local capacity on climate change to ensure national specialists as part of
the project team for each subproject.
40. The project was designed on the basis of rigorous consultations with relevant
stakeholders in the target countries. A stakeholder engagement plan was submitted as an annex
to the funding proposal.
3.6 Efficiency and effectiveness Scale: Medium to high
41. Of the project’s total proposed budget of USD 750 million, GCF funding represents 16
per cent of the estimated project cost, with co-financing at 84 per cent. The GCF financing
comprises a USD 100 million grant and USD 20 million senior loan. The ADB will provide USD
535 million in senior loans with variable, per-country loan values based on proposed
interventions and country-specific needs and USD 20 million in grants. Additionally, bilateral
donors including UK Aid, Nordic Development Fund, Agence française de développement will
deliver grants of USD 75 million (for more details, please refer to annex 4).
42. The proposed project will provide numerous interventions in multiple countries;
therefore, the full spectrum of economic and financial appraisals of proposed individual projects
was not feasible at the ex ante analysis. However, a thorough economic and financial analysis
(EFA) of selected pilot projects (annex 3) was pursued. At default, as a part of the internal ADB
policy guidelines, all other interventions destined for funding under the CRPP IF will be
scrutinized a priori against their financial and economic viability. Only subprojects that obtain
proper economic net present value (ENPV) and expected internal rate of return (EIRR)
thresholds will be funded by the CRPP IF.
43. The results of EFAs of individual pilot projects (tables 2, 3 and 4 below) were pursued
over 30 years (table 2) and 25 years (tables 3 and 4), starting from 2024, with a 6-year
implementation period and using the economic discount rate of 9 per cent. Please refer to tables
2, 3 and 4 below for detailed EFA estimates.

44. The CRPP IF project’s EFAs were carried out in accordance with the GCF EFA guidelines
and were conducted in financial and economic terms on a per-project basis. The results of
outlined EFAs suggest that the proposed investments are likely to be justified from the
economic point of view as ENPV and EIRR measures suggest the economic viability of proposed
indicative investments (e.g. ENPVs are positive and EIRRs are higher than a chosen economic
discount rate of 9 per cent). Furthermore, the results of the EFA suggest that the proposed
indicative investment will benefit the entire economy as the benefits of proposed interventions
will outweigh the investment costs. The positive direction of the pilot modelling presented is
additionally supported by convincing evidence from the ex-post analysis of 23 field pilot tests
that tested a set of interventions related to community-based resilience, including local and
community-based adaptation planning.3
45. The proposed structure and programmatic approach are assessed to be adequate and
reasonable, considering the level of vulnerability and poverty of the target beneficiaries in the
region. It is expected to deliver high efficiency and effectiveness as the GCF funds will be
leveraged against large volumes of ADB finance. At the CRPP IF level (where GCF funds will be
invested) USD 640 million will be leveraged from ADB and other bilateral donors. This results in
a ratio of co-financing of more than 5:1, which is assessed to be highly efficient compared to
benchmarks in similar/average investments in similar regional contexts, targeting the most
vulnerable.
46. The use of GCF finance to fund the climate additionality on top of existing ADB funds is
also assessed as effective. The GFC investment will benefit from the existing financial,
governance and implementation of activities, which ensure low risk and high conversion of
inputs to outputs and outcomes. Hence, the marginal transaction costs for implementing GCF
funds will be extremely low.
