4.1 Environmental and social safeguards
47. Project background. The CRPP is part of a regional partnership facility established by
the AE to scale up investments in climate adaptation at the community level explicitly targeting
the nexus between climate change, poverty and gender. The programme proposed for the GCF
financing aims to provides grants and loans funded through the CRPP Investment Fund (IF) to
support the efficient roll-out of local adaptation measures in seven host countries, namely
Cambodia, Indonesia, Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Pakistan, Papua New Guinea, Timor-
Leste, and Vanuatu. Complementary to the technical assistance and grant resources financed by
other development partners under the CRPP TF (not funded by GCF), the environmental and
social (E&S) risks and impacts of the programme concerned below arise from three outputs that
are proposed for the GCF financing as downstream investments on improving and
implementing (a) information and systems for delivering applied climate risk informed local
investments at scale; (b) climate-resilient pro-poor livelihoods; and (c) pro-poor climate
adaptation infrastructures. Among the E&S co-benefits are the empowerment of women’s
participation in adaptation decision-making and leadership, the reduction of inequalities and
poverty associated with climate change, and increases in resilience among low-income and
disadvantaged groups.
48. E&S risk category. The AE assigned the programme medium level of intermediation,
equivalent to the GCF E&S risk category I2. The Secretariat confirms the proposed E&S risk
category considering the proposed portfolio is expected to include financial exposure to
moderate-risk activities and that Category A activities of potentially significant adverse E&S
risks and impacts will not be considered eligible. The Secretariat also confirms that the assigned
risk category is within the accreditation level of the AE.
49. Safeguards instrument. The AE provided, under the CRPP IF, an Environment and
Social Management Framework (ESMF) to articulate the applicable environmental and social
policy and reference framework to be followed by the programme; detail the procedures for
addressing environmental, social and sustainability issues; prescribe standards and guidelines;
and set monitoring compliance procedures to manage E&S risks and impacts associated with
the portfolio of investments pursuant to AE’s safeguards policies and the requirements of AE’s
Safeguard Policy Statement (SPS).
50. Compliance with the GCF environmental and social safeguards (ESS) standards.
The paragraphs below provide a brief description of the programme’s compliance with the ESS
standards.
51. ESS 1: Assessment and management of E&S risks and impacts. As the specific details
of the component subprojects are yet to be determined during implementation, the ESMF
outlines the reference framework to be complied by the programme, the E&S management
procedures for subproject screening and categorization, and the requirements for E&S impact
assessments (ESIA) and E&S management plans (ESMP) to address the potential risks and
impacts identified. Further to the assessments per the AE’s SPS and safeguards policies, the
ESMF presents an assessment on the GCF E&S safeguards standards that are likely to be
triggered by the proposed CRPP IF investments and suggests the indicative mitigation measures
to be detailed at subproject level during implementation. The ESMF also entails three linked
documents that further elaborates the safeguards policy structure and requirements related to
the subproject E&S due diligence, including (a) the AE’s SPS; (b) rapid environmental
assessment checklist, various outlines, and monitoring template; and (c) SPS review and update:
policy architecture study. While the ESMF has made it clear that the CRPP IF will not finance
high-risk activities, the AE is recommended to substantiate the indications on the degree and
significance of the E&S risks based on the screening of the existing indicative pipeline and
foreseen portfolio of the CRPP IF, especially in relation to the envisioned climate adaptation
infrastructure investments.

=== PAGE 174 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.06
Page 174
52. The AE conducted a preliminary conflict sensitivity assessment as part of the
programme's design study to understand the conflict situation in the countries included in the
CRPP IF. Recognizing the close linkage between climate risk and conflict, where existing conflict
situation can exacerbate climate risks and climate change can drive conflict, the AE requires the
climate risk assessments to be undertaken as part of subproject identification and preparation
process adequately captures the linkage with conflict. Further conflict assessment will be
conducted during the programme implementation with focus on the potential of inducing
conflicts in relation to community health and safety, land acquisition, and indigenous peoples. In
case of expected adverse impacts, an action plan on human rights due diligence will be required.
Such action plan will identify national laws and obligations of the country directly applicable to
the activities under relevant international treaties and agreements and describe the mitigation
measures that will be taken to comply with those obligations and national laws. The AE will
ensure that the risks of conflict will be categorized and managed during implementation.
53. ESS 2: Labour and working conditions. Financing subprojects on climate-resilient
agroecological systems, climate-resilient agriculture supply chains, and the pro-poor climate
adaptation infrastructures under the programme may involve hiring of workers by contractors
during construction and the employment of workers to operate and maintain the
infrastructures following the construction phase. The ESMF triggered the AE’s own safeguards
policy principles (SPS Safeguard Requirements 1), which require the borrower/client to provide
workers with a safe and healthy working environment, taking into account risks inherent to the
particular sector and specific classes of hazards in the borrower’s/client’s work areas, including
physical, chemical, biological and radiological hazards, as well as to take steps to prevent
accidents, injury and disease arising from, being associated with or occurring during the course
of work. The borrower/client is also required to apply preventive and protective measures
consistent with international good practice, as reflected in internationally recognized standards
such as the World Bank Group’s Environment, Health and Safety Guidelines.4 Furthermore,
based on the Prohibited Investment Activities Lists (Appendix 5 of the AE’s SPS linked to the
programme’s ESMF), the programme will not finance projects or activities involving harmful or
exploitative forms of forced labour or child labour. The ESMF suggests mitigation measures to
ensure safe and healthy working conditions, compliance with national employment and labour
laws, non-discrimination and equal opportunity, access to a workers’ grievance redress
mechanism (GRM), and occupational health and safety. The AE is recommended to detail the
risk screening and mitigation measures on ESS 2 during the programme implementation at the
subproject level to make sure the above-mentioned safeguards requirements can be effectively
applied to the CRPP IF investments.
54. ESS 3: Resource efficiency and pollution control. The ESMF triggered this safeguard
standard following the AE’s SPS, which requires the borrower/client to apply pollution
prevention and control technologies and practices consistent with international good practice
during the design, construction, and operation of the programme. SPS Safeguard Requirements
1 covers requirements for pollution prevention, resource conservation, energy efficiency,
wastes, hazardous materials, and pesticide use and management. The AE’s Prohibited
Investment Activities Lists also include the production of or trade in any product or activity
deemed illegal under host country laws or regulations or international conventions and
agreements or subject to international phaseouts or bans, such as (a) pharmaceuticals,
pesticides, and herbicides; (b) ozone-depleting substances; (c) polychlorinated biphenyls and
other hazardous chemicals; (d) wildlife or wildlife products regulated under the Convention on
International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora; (e) transboundary trade in
waste or waste products; and (f), production of, trade in, or use of unbonded asbestos fibres. In
addition to the general requirements in the ESMF, the programme will require incorporation of
4 Available at https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-
reports/documentdetail/157871484635724258/environmental-health-and-safety-general-guidelines.

=== PAGE 175 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.06
Page 175
relevant mitigation measures, such as conserving raw materials and energy, reducing project-
related greenhouse gas emissions, reducing water usage, and putting in place solid and
hazardous waste management and integrated pest/vector management, within the ESIA and
ESMP. The AE is recommended to detail the risk screening and mitigation measures on ESS 3
during the programme implementation at the subproject level to make sure the above-
mentioned safeguards requirements can be effectively applied to the CRPP IF investments.
55. ESS 4: Community health, safety and security. The ESMF triggered this safeguard
standard and identified the main mitigation measures following the AE’s own safeguards policy
requirements. As per the AE’s SPS, the borrower/client needs to identify and assess the risks to,
and potential impacts on, the safety of affected communities during the design, construction,
operation and decommissioning of subprojects, and will establish preventive measures and
plans to address them in a manner commensurate with the identified risks and impacts.
Moreover, all the programme activities will require the establishment of preventive and
emergency preparedness and response measures to avoid and, where avoidance is impossible,
to minimize adverse impacts and risks to the health and safety of local communities. The
infrastructure projects to be funded under the programme may pose risks to health and safety
of local communities (during the construction and due to exposure to construction traffic and
other hazards at construction sites) as well as risks of diseases, gender-based violence, and
increase in criminality associated with the labour influx.
56. ESS 5: Land acquisition and involuntary resettlement. The ESMF triggered this
standard in recognition of the fact that the programme may involve land acquisition and
physical and economic displacement in the case of installation of MHEWS and equipment and
information and communications technology infrastructure; financing activities for climate-
resilient agriculture supply chains; investment in ecosystem-based infrastructure, flood and
landslide protection infrastructure; and build-up of multipurpose emergency shelters. As per
the programme’s ESMF, the AE will screen all subprojects to determine whether they involve
involuntary resettlement. For a project involving involuntary resettlement, a resettlement plan
will need to be prepared that is commensurate with the extent and degree of the impacts. The
degree of the impacts shall be determined by the scope of the physical and economic
displacement, and the vulnerability of the affected persons. The AE’s Safeguard Requirements 2
(Involuntary Resettlement) in the SPS provides for the scope, objectives and requirements of
involuntary resettlement safeguards. SR2 also provides an outline of the Resettlement Action
Plan to be detailed where necessary at the subproject level.
57. ESS 6: Biodiversity conservation and sustainable management of living natural
resources. The ESMF triggered this safeguard standard as, for example, the proposed climate
adaptation infrastructures may be located in sites near or within areas of natural habitat that
may or may not be officially declared protected. The AE’s SPS requires the borrower/client to
assess the significance of project impacts and risks for biodiversity and natural resources as an
integral part of the environmental assessment process. The assessment will focus on the major
threats to biodiversity, which include destruction of habitat and introduction of invasive alien
species, and on the use of natural resources in an unsustainable manner. The borrower/client
will need to identify measures to avoid, minimize or mitigate potentially adverse impacts and
risks and, as a last resort, propose compensatory measures, such as biodiversity offsets, to
achieve no net loss or a net gain for the affected biodiversity. SPS Safeguard Requirements 1
includes detailed provisions for assessing and mitigating impacts on the natural habitat
(including on the modified natural habitat, the critical natural habitat and legally protected
areas) and required screening and assessment of potential impacts on biodiversity. The ESMF
also required that activities shall avoid impacts on biodiversity and ecosystem services, and, if
avoidance of impacts is not possible, measures to minimize impacts and compensate and
restore biodiversity and ecosystem services will need to be implemented. For activities that
have potential adverse impacts on natural habitats, the preparation of a biodiversity action plan
(BAP) will be mandatory. The ESMF provides an outline of the BAP as referenced in Linked

=== PAGE 176 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.06
Page 176
Document 2 of the ESMF. The ESMF also requires the implementation of measures to minimize
habitat fragmentation (such as through biological corridors), restore habitats during and/or
after operations, and implement biodiversity offsets.
58. GCF Indigenous Peoples Policy and ESS 7: Indigenous Peoples. Indigenous Peoples
are present in all of the seven selected countries for the project, namely Cambodia, Indonesia,
Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Pakistan, Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste and Vanuatu. The
ESMF accordingly provides an Indigenous Peoples Impact Categorization (IPIC) assessment
process and the outline of an Indigenous Peoples Plan (IPP Outline), which is required for all
projects with impacts on Indigenous Peoples. The IPIC provides a detailed Indigenous Peoples
Impact Screening Checklist, which covers the triggers required by the GCF Indigenous Peoples
Policy (IPP), such as identification of Indigenous Peoples, identification of Indigenous Peoples
without requiring status of vulnerability, identification of potential impacts and identification
of special requirements. The IPP Outline provides guidance regarding social impact assessment,
information disclosure, consultation and participation, beneficial measures, mitigative
measures, GRM, monitoring, reporting and evaluation, institutional arrangements, and budget
and financing. While the ESMF meets the basic requirements of the GCF IPP, the following
recommendations are provided to cover remaining gaps: the AE will ensure that the broad
community support obtained for any subprojects will meet the free prior informed consent
requirements of the GCF IPP and that subprojects that only develop natural resources will also
require special procedures for consent. In line with its roles and functions, the GCF Indigenous
Peoples Advisory Group is available to provide advice to the AE, which is also encouraged to
share emerging good practices and success stories with the Group.
59. ESS 8: Cultural heritage. The ESMF triggered this safeguard standard. Climate
adaptation infrastructure projects to be funded by the programme might be located near and/or
affect cultural heritage structures or sites. The AE’s SPS defines physical cultural resources as
movable or immovable objects, sites, structures, groups of structures, and natural features and
landscapes that have archaeological, paleontological, historical, architectural, religious,
aesthetic, or other cultural significance. It requires chance finds procedures be included in the
ESMP when the proposed location of a subproject is in an area where physical cultural
resources are expected to be found as determined during the risk assessment process. The AE’s
SPS also requires that chance finds shall not be disturbed until an assessment by a competent
specialist has been made and actions consistent with these requirements have been identified.
The ESMF specifies that the programme will not remove any physical cultural resources unless
(a) no alternatives to removal are available; (b) the overall benefits of the subproject
substantially outweigh the anticipated cultural heritage loss from removal; and (c) any removal
is conducted in accordance with relevant provisions of national and/or local laws, regulations,
and protected area management plans and national obligations under international laws, and
employs the best available techniques. The detailed provisions for physical cultural resources
are discussed in SPS Safeguard Requirements 1, including the requirement to consult with
affected communities and the relevant national or local regulatory agencies, and measures to
avoid or mitigate impacts as part of the environmental planning process. The ESMF suggests the
main mitigation measures including compliance with local cultural heritage regulations or
protected area management plans, consultation with relevant stakeholders, and measures to
implement additional programmes to promote and enhance protected area conservation.
60. Sexual exploitation, sexual abuse and sexual harassment (SEAH)
safeguarding. The ESMF triggered SEAH safeguards specifying that the programme will not
finance investments that are anticipated to have significant SEAH risks and impacts. The AE will
take an approach of zero-tolerance towards SEAH and ensure that the risk category of CRPP IF
financing is proportional to the nature, scale and location of activity including in relation to
SEAH. In addition, the ESMF specifies that the AE is responsible for incorporating and
monitoring SEAH prevention, mitigation and response measures guided by the AE’s newly

=== PAGE 177 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.06
Page 177
published Good Practice Note 5to address SEAH risks in its operations focusing on sovereign
projects involving civil works. The AE will also ensure that adequate information related to
CRPP IF SEAH safeguarding is provided to GCF to enable review. The programme will address
SEAH risks and impacts as part of the subproject’s due diligence ESIA and ESMP. In the event of
SEAH incidents, the programme will establish a survivor-centred and gender-responsive GRM
for SEAH-related grievances including confidential reporting, safe and ethical documentation of
SEAH cases, and mechanisms for timely services and redress for survivors.
61. Implementation arrangements. The programme will be managed by the AE, which
also serves as the executing entity (EE). It has in-house safeguards staff in its Climate Change
and Sustainable Development Department (CCSD) to manage and operate the programme. At
the programme level, the AE will monitor portfolio-level safeguards implementation and
performance to ensure the transactions meet the AE’s safeguards requirements. The Facility
Manager of the CRPP IF’s umbrella programme will verify that the AE has conducted the
necessary safeguards review, ensuring ongoing compliance monitoring and reporting, and
confirming that the project aligns with the relevant safeguard policies of both the AE and the
GCF, as outlined in the CRPP IF ESMF. Training will be provided to borrowers/clients and
project developers as needed, as part of the AE’s broader SPS initiative aimed at strengthening
country systems. The AE will engage experts on human rights and SEAH from the roster of
consultants to contribute to the attainment of the CRPP IF ESMF objectives.
62. Stakeholder engagement and information disclosure. The AE provided a
stakeholder engagement plan with the proposal, which summarizes the stakeholders’
consultations conducted during the preparation and development of the CRPP concept and the
present proposal for the GCF. It also presents an analysis of stakeholders’ engagement, a brief
explanation of the AE’s policies and procedures relevant to stakeholders’ participation, and the
required processes to be implemented during key phases of the project lifecycle. The AE has
conducted stakeholder engagements in the preparation of the project, including consultations
with relevant national and local implementation partners in developing the project concepts
and with the national designated authorities to seek their guidance on project design and to
secure the no-objection letters for the programme. For the subprojects that will be supported
under the CRPP IF, the AE’s SPS requires the borrower/client to carry out meaningful
consultation with affected people and other concerned stakeholders, including civil society, and
facilitate their informed participation. Consultation will be carried out in a manner
commensurate with the impacts on affected communities. However, since the details of
subproject disclosure are yet to be agreed upon with the AE, it is recommended to include in the
funded activity agreement (FAA) the disclosure and communications process of ESS
documentation for Category B subprojects.
63. Grievance redress mechanism. The AE will establish a project-level GRM that will
address the affected people’s concerns and complaints including on SEAH. The ESMF requires
that the GRM address affected people’s concerns and complaints promptly, using an
understandable and transparent process that is gender responsive, culturally appropriate and
readily accessible to all segments of the affected people. The GRM will be accessible by the
affected stakeholders throughout the programme cycle. In addition to the project-specific GRM
and the GCF’s independent redress mechanism, the AE also maintains its own accountability
mechanism. The accountability mechanism provides an independent forum and process for
people adversely affected by projects financed by the AE, including in cases of allegations of
violation of the AE’s own operational policies and procedures. In line with the GCF Indigenous
Peoples Policy, the GCF indigenous peoples focal point will be available for assistance at any
stage, including before a claim has been made.

4.2 Gender policy
64. The AE has provided a gender assessment and gender action plan therefore complies
with the GCF gender policy. It has also provided a programme-level gender assessment and
gender action plan.
65. The gender assessment is undertaken through desk review and stakeholder
consultations, the latter being with government experts, community and several women’s
groups. Further assessments are planned at subproject level with a gender equity theme and
taking effective gender mainstreaming into consideration. This will be done to ensure key
gender-related issues in the project’s sectors of focus are understood and issues are addressed
based on country circumstances.
66. The current programme-level gender assessment describes the gender issues at the
country level and indicates that all seven countries are committed to gender equality and
women’s empowerment. The constitutions of all the countries guarantee equality for women
and men in the economic, political and social spheres.
67. Many of the countries have ratified international agreements such as the Convention on
the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) while having
introduced various policies and national frameworks to promote equality. Many of the countries
have national policy environment and supportive legislations such as national climate change
policies and financial inclusion strategies (Pakistan); national framework action (Papua New
Guinea); and Strategic Development Plan and National Adaptation Programme of Action
(Timor-Leste).
68. The assessment also shows that though the seven countries are committed to gender
equality and women’s empowerment, the ranking on the gender index varies and levels of
equality are different. Generally, however, all countries need to invest more to meet their own
commitments to gender equality and ensure that, as a population more vulnerable to climate
change, women are supported to help mitigate and adapt to climate change.
69. The assessment has also demonstrated that violence against women, inequality in
access to education, stark gaps in economic and labour force participation and limited
participation of women in the political space, are all factors that hinder progress for women.
Countries demonstrate gender-based barriers to women in areas of literacy and education,
skills to progress in the professional fields, violence during disasters, and the double burden of
domestic and reproductive roles. Yet women play a critical role and contribute in all facets of
each country’s economy and social well-being. The general gender issues as related to
programme sectors have been provided for each country.
70. The programme gender action plan (GAP) provided by the AE includes indicative actions
with corresponding indicators, targets, budget and timelines of the activities that will be
delivered. Gender expertise will be available to support the implementation of all activities
included in the plan and provide support in the supervision, monitoring and evaluation of the
GAP.
71. The activities of the GAP will address the challenges for women in accessing resources
(e.g. finance) and skills. Specific actions in this regard are: investments in technical assistance
and grant resources that will develop the capacities and knowledge of various actors to be
targeted by the projects; a trust fund with a gender window specifically targeting and investing
in women; building women’s knowledge and capacity to identify investment opportunities; and
preparation of women-focused investment projects.
72. Further actions include a focus on addressing women’s needs in accessing climate
information. This will be done by ensuring gender issues are mainstreamed in climate
information and in systems to deliver local investments that apply climate-risk information at

=== PAGE 179 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.06
Page 179
scale. Climate-resilient pro-poor livelihoods and adaptation investments will also focus on
women’s needs.
73. It was noted through the assessment that gender inequality emanates from, and
continues to be a barrier through, unequal norms and practices existing in countries. The GAP
includes activities that are targeted at addressing structural barriers to gender equality and
gender issues through policy reform and revision of regulations.
74. The programme will also ensure that employment and income-generation opportunities
are presented to women. The various actions and investments presented in the GAP are
expected to empower women, facilitating an increased role in decision-making, increasing
access to and control of resources in the agriculture sector, and to technologies. In addition, the
GAP is expected to build countries’ overall capacity to mainstream gender across sectors. The
programme will focus on and highlight women-led measures that could be scaled up through
larger investments in the future.
4.3 Risks
4.3.1. Overall programme assessment (medium risk)
75. GCF is requested to provide a grant of USD 100 million and a senior debt of USD 20
million for the CRPP covering seven countries. The AE is co-financing a senior debt of USD 535
million and a grant of USD 20 million. Bilateral donors are providing a total of USD 75 million in
the form of a grant.
76. The CRPP consists of two separate but interlinked funds; namely CRPP TF providing
technical assistance for upstream support, and CRPP Investment Fund (IF) focusing on the local
adaptation measures through downstream investment in projects. The GCF funds will be used to
finance CRPP IF only. Although projects supported under the TF may be financed by the IF and
countries may benefit from the TF to develop IF projects, TF support is not a pre-condition to be
eligible for IF investment and there is no direct sequencing between CRPP TF and IF.
4.3.2. Accredited entity/executing entity capability to execute the current programme
(low risk)
77. The ADB will be both AE and EE for the programme. The CRPP is operationalized
through the Community Resilience Financing Partnership Facility (CRFPF) which has been
administered by the ADB since 2021. GCF funds for the CRPP will be ring-fenced within an ADB
GCF TF. The AE has an extensive track record of managing more than 40 trust funds to support
programmes and technical assistance in the region.
4.3.3. Programme-specific execution risks (medium risk)
78. Demand risk: At least one project per country will be financed under CRPP, however the
allocation and use of resources under CRPP IF will be determined at a later stage. It will depend
on the AE to source projects that meet the eligibility criteria. In case there is a lack of pipelines,
the targeted impact will be reduced and GCF funds might not be fully utilized. Currently there is
no limit in terms of the extension of the CRPP.
79. Funding risk: The CRPP targets reaching a size of USD 750 million including USD 675
million for CRPP IF. The AE envisages that the time period of the IF will be from 2023 to 2030,
meaning individual projects will be likely to be approved between 2024 and 2027, and
completed by 2030. The GCF resource is expected to leverage at least USD 555 million from the
AE and USD 75 million from other co-financiers. However, the term sheet does not include any
timeline for the target fund size to be reached. Comfort can be derived from the covenants for

=== PAGE 180 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.06
Page 180
proportionate disbursement of GCF and co-financing amounts and the eligibility criteria, which
includes the ratio of GCF grant to AE loan/grant, should be at least 1:4. If the AE cannot reach its
target size, the unused funds need to be reflowed to GCF to avoid the fund being idle.
80. Credit risk: The borrower of the GCF loan will be sovereign or sovereign entity in
Pakistan (Caa3 by Moody’s), therefore GCF is exposed to the sovereign credit risk. The country
experiences several credit challenges with a weak fiscal position. However, the concessional
term from GCF will be conducive for the country’s debt affordability. The GCF loan will be
aligned with ADB sovereign loans, thus be covered by similar sovereign guarantees based on the
AE’s due diligence.
81. Project viability and concessionality: Since the CRPP will support a wide range of
interventions, the overall CRPP level ex ante economic and financial analyses are not feasible.
Instead, the AE carried out analyses in each component (Components 4, 5 and 6) with indicative
pilot projects. Components 4 and 6 show a relatively high benefit to cost ratio with a range of 6
to 9. Component 5 results in the EIRR between 15 per cent and 35 per cent. However, the exact
EIRR and financial internal rate of return will vary depending on the projects to be funded. All
the projects under CRPP IF will have to pass the economic and financial viability criteria to be
taken forward.
82. Apart from the loan provided to Pakistan, the remaining 83 per cent of GCF financing is a
full grant. The GCF grant will be blended with ADB grants and/or loan to pass down the
concessionality. One of the mandatory eligibility criteria is that the concessionality of GCF will
not substitute investments that might have taken place anyway using regular AE borrowing.
4.3.4. Compliance risk (medium risk)
83. ADB, as accredited entity (AE), has confirmed that the CRPP IF reveals a low-level risk
regarding prohibited practices, money laundering and terrorist financing, with a low probability
and impact. The ADB mitigation strategy includes enforcing ADB’s rigorous due diligence
policies at the subproject level. ADB conducts integrity due diligence, proactive integrity
reviews, and offers oversight through its Office of Anticorruption and Integrity (OAI).
84. ADB also confirmed that it enforces compliance with its Anticorruption Policy and
financial management assessments. Disbursements follow ADB’s Loan Disbursement Handbook,
reinforcing financial prudence and ensuring financial transparency. OAI handles integrity
violations, offering protection to whistleblowers. ADB confirmed that it strictly prohibits
individuals/entities on the United Nations Security Council sanctions list from participating in
CRPP contracts and avoids operations in sanctioned jurisdictions.
85. The Secretariat has conducted a review of the project in accordance with relevant GCF
Board-approved policies and does not find any material issue or deviation with respect to
compliance-related issues. The risk-mitigation measures informed by ADB appear to effectively
manage the low-level risk of prohibited practices, money laundering and terrorist financing,
ensuring transparency and accountability in CRPP IF activities. Based on available information
for this funding proposal, the Secretariat has determined a risk rating of “medium” and has no
objection to this proposal proceeding.
4.3.5. GCF portfolio concentration risk (low risk)
86. In case of approval, the impact of this proposal on the GCF portfolio concentration in
terms of result area and single proposal is not material.
4.3.6. Recommendation
87. It is recommended that the Board consider the above factors in its decision.

4.4 Fiduciary
88. The ADB will play the dual role of AE and EE in the programme.
89. As AE, the ADB will manage and operationalize the CRPP through the CRFPF. The ADB
will host and manage the CRPP IF operations through the Climate Change and Sustainable
Development Department (CCSD), acting as financial intermediary to ADB developing members
for providing funds from GCF alongside ADB funds to support investments in selected countries.
90. On the other hand, as the EE for the CRPP, ADB will be responsible for the overall
programme, particularly the provision of technical assistance support under the CRPP TF
(Component 1), and the provision of grants and loans for subprojects under the CRPP IF
(Component 2).
91. GCF funds for the CRPP will be ring-fenced within an ADB GCF TF which was created
pursuant to the accreditation master agreement, and as such benefit from the same privileges
and immunities as ADB resources. Usage of GCF funds will be based on criteria outlined in the
funding proposal which will be included in dedicated programme implementation guidelines to
be developed. These guidelines will complement the programme Term Sheet and FAA, and
include further guidance on implementation arrangements, project selection and prioritization,
monitoring and evaluation, and reporting.
92. The ADB will offer concessional loans and grants to sovereign borrowers to be funded
by GCF. For each CRPP IF project, the ADB will sign separate loan and/or grant agreements with
the sovereign borrowers/beneficiaries for each source of financing. Each project will be
implemented in compliance with ADB policies and CRPP requirements.
93. Disbursement requests from the ADB to GCF are expected to be made on an annual basis
in accordance with the expected ADB approval dates, and projected disbursement plans and
timelines of the projects in the CRPP pipeline. Payments of interest and principal for GCF-
funded subproject loans will be repaid to the ADB GCF TF. Principal, interest payments, and any
unused funds or income will be subsequently returned to GCF.
94. The CRPP-supported projects will follow ADB systems for financial management,
disbursement, audit and procurement. Implementation of the programme and projects will also
conform to all applicable ADB policies. In particular, all subprojects financial accounting,
disbursement procedures and auditing requirements will be developed during project
preparation and will be included in their respective grant implementation manuals. The ADB
shall ensure that these are in accordance with ADB policies, procedures and approach on
financial management and analysis of projects. Project disbursements will follow ADB’s Loan
Disbursement Handbook (2017, as amended from time to time) and detailed arrangements
agreed upon between the government and the ADB. Public disclosure of the audited project’s
financial statements, including the auditor’s opinion on the project financial statements, will be
guided by the ADB Public Communications Policy of 2011.

4.5 Results monitoring and reporting
96. As an adaptation initiative, the programme aims at generating diverse adaptation results
across all four GCF adaptation result areas. A minimum of 3,219,400 direct beneficiaries and
4,465,000 indirect beneficiaries are estimated to receive adaptation benefits, which account for
0.63 per cent and 0.87 per cent of the total population of seven target countries respectively.
Definitions and broad methodologies have been provided by the AE to estimate the adaptation
beneficiaries. Acknowledging the difficulties of beneficiary estimation at this stage without
detailed information about individual projects, it was recommended for the AE to develop and
submit a Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning Plan within 12 months of the programme
commencement.
97. The theory of change (TOC) diagram adequately captures different levels of expected
changes as well as logical linkages between them from the goal statement to the proposed
activities. It is helpful that the TOC diagram identifies co-benefits which can be achieved along
the way towards climate results and captures the causal relationships between outcomes and
co-benefits. The barriers and risks that may hinder the achievement of these changes are
identified and linked to pertinent activities which will tackle them accordingly. Project
components are well embedded into the project TOC.
98. The logical framework has been developed in accordance with the GCF integrated
results management framework. The programme is expected to have huge paradigm shift
potential across all seven target countries in all three dimensions: scale, replicability and
sustainability.
99. It will contribute to all four GCF adaptation result areas with the CRPP TF and IF which
will be established with the programme, and which will finance various individual projects.
Four outcomes are identified with six outputs with clear logical linkages. Adequate GCF core and
supplementary indicators are chosen to monitor the results of the programme, however it is
highly recommended for the AE to provide the Secretariat with concrete methodologies and
targets for each indicator once the detailed Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning Plan will be
developed. At the GCF outcome level of “Enabling environment”, two GCF core indicators have
been identified: institutional and knowledge generation, capture and learning. Given the
relatively low or medium baseline of each indicator, the programme is expected to build a
comprehensive enabling environment at multi-country level.
100. The programme has identified relevant project-specific indicators for project outcomes
and outputs. It is useful that the programme will measure co-benefits with specific indicators:
this will increase the level of understanding of the project and will give an opportunity for the
Secretariat to capture non-climate results that are worth monitoring and reporting.

Proposal name: Community Resilience Partnership Program

I. Assessment of the independent Technical Advisory Panel
1. This is the first submission of the “Community Resilience Partnership Program (CRPP)”
to the independent Technical Advisory Panel (iTAP) under the standard Proposal Approval
Process (PAP). The accredited entity (AE) is the Asian Development Bank (ADB). The funding
proposal covers seven countries: Cambodia, Indonesia, the Lao People’s Democratic Republic,
Pakistan, Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste, and Vanuatu.
2. The CRPP is aimed at helping countries and communities in Asia and the Pacific region
scale up investments in adaptation to climate change, especially investments at the community
level, and targeting the climate change-poverty-gender nexus.
3. The funding proposal has been prepared as a response to three challenges: (i) the
increasing climate shocks and stresses in Asia and the Pacific region; (ii) poor and already
vulnerable populations in the participating countries that are already suffering climate impacts
and require targeted adaptation solutions; and (iii) the need for climate finance, which is critical
for facilitating adaptation action by these highly vulnerable social groups.
4. ADB expects to reach a minimum of 3,219,400 direct and 4,465,00 indirect beneficiaries,
and to contribute to all four adaptation result areas as follows: most vulnerable people and
communities (30 per cent); health and well-being, and food and water security (30 per cent);
infrastructure and built environment (20 per cent); and ecosystems and ecosystem services (20
per cent).
5. The CRPP will be operationalized through the Community Resilience Financing
Partnership Facility (CRFPF)1 which was established by ADB in August 2021 and comprises two
separate but interlinked components: the CRPP Trust Fund (TF) and the CRPP Investment Fund
(IF). CRFPF is not a separate legal entity, but a facility administered within and by ADB.
6. Component 1, the CRPP Trust Fund (TF), focuses on upstream support to strengthen the
enabling environment required for implementing local adaptation measures at scale.
Component 2, the CRPP Investment Fund (IF) focuses on the efficient roll-out of local adaptation
measures through a downstream investment programme. According to its budget, the funding
proposal includes a third, smaller component dedicated to programme implementation,
monitoring and evaluation and learning (MEL) support.
7. The expected outputs from the CRPP are: (1) knowledge and action research on climate
risk-informed pro-poor community-level solutions strengthened; (2) institutional and
community capacity to develop and deliver climate adaptation investments at community-level
strengthened; (3) investments supporting inclusive pro-poor, community-level adaptation
1 Community Resilience Financing Partnership Facility (CRFPF).

=== PAGE 186 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.06
Page 186
measures prepared; (4) information and systems for delivering applied climate risk-informed
investments at scale improved; (5) climate resilient pro-poor livelihoods investments
implemented; and (6) pro-poor climate adaptation infrastructure investments implemented.
8. The first three outputs will be funded through the CRPP TF (USD 75 million), supported
by bilateral donors including the Government of the United Kingdom, the Nordic Development
Fund, and the French Development Agency. Outputs four to six are proposed to be funded
through the IF (USD 675 million), which will be financed by GCF (USD 120 million) and the
Asian Development Bank (USD 555 million). Thus, funding from GCF, consisting of USD 100
million in grants and USD 20 million in loans, will be channeled solely through the IF.
9. For the projects2 financed by the IF and implemented in host countries, the government
of the host country, acting through its relevant ministry or department, may be the executing
entity and/or implementing agency and will follow ADB procedures.
10. In its assessment the iTAP considered all documents as submitted on 8 August 2023, the
follow-up answers both in written form and during the meeting between the iTAP review team,
representatives from ADB and members from the Secretariat task team, and additional
documents sent to the iTAP as agreed during the question and answer session.

deploy under each project, both direct and indirect beneficiaries will vary widely and be
confirmed as part of annual reporting.
14. The proposal includes two levels, a programmatic and a project-specific level. The
current assessment was done differentiating the two levels.
15. Programmatic level: the funding proposal includes a climate profile for each of the
participating countries (annex 2.1). The profiles are based on the information from the World
Bank’s Climate Change Knowledge Portal3 for presenting the evolution of climate hazards,
exposure and vulnerability at the country level. Each profile includes climatological information
(e.g. average monthly temperature and rainfall), documented observations about past evolution
of climate variables (temperature and rain patterns), as well as future climate projections using
four representative concentration pathways.
16. The funding proposal further presents specific socioeconomic conditions of the
participating countries including a preliminary analysis of the link between social conflicts and
climate change. Based on the climate change-related information and considering the
socioeconomic context, the profiles introduce the climate risk in each country. In addition, the
profiles present the evolution of climate policy in each of the participating countries.
17. As a response, the proposal introduces indicative examples of activities aimed at
reducing climate risks per country as well as potential complementarity and synergies with
other ongoing projects that have been financed by the Adaptation Fund, GCF or the Global
Environment Facility.
18. The funding proposal explains existing barriers to scaling up adaptation at the livelihood
level and how the proposed CRPP will contribute to overcoming these (for more detail see
sections 1.2 “Paradigm shift potential” and 1.4 “Needs of the recipient”).
19. In terms of monitoring and evaluation, the funding proposal includes a preliminary
version of the CRPP monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL) system, based on the principles
of participation, focus on learning and practicality (annex 11). The MEL will combine a
multilevel monitoring and evaluation approach (project and programme level) with a theory-
based approach and a dynamic approach to monitoring and evaluation. The funding proposal
states that a baseline for MEL will be prepared at the beginning of the implementation phase.
However, the proposal is not yet clear about how to assess the outcomes of adaptation activities
or to quantify the adaptation beneficiaries.
20. Project level: The funding proposal includes a well-structured framework for selecting
projects and allocating resources, which comprises five overarching principles, eligibility
criteria, project selection process and assessment tools, as well as the governance structure that
clarifies the roles and responsibilities in selecting projects in host countries (annex 2.4).
21. The five principles are:
(a) Respond to current and future climate risks in the context of changing socio-economic
development;
(b) Promote adaptation measures that address underlying drivers of poverty and gender
inequality;
(c) Promote selection of adaptation measures based on the principle of subsidiarity;
(d) Promote adaptation measures in the context of physical, ecosystem-based, financial,
and/or social and institutional resilience; and
(e) Promote cross-sector linkages and mainstreaming into development.

extent by underlying socioeconomic inequality and vulnerability. Hence, the CRPP’s explicit
target on the nexus between climate change, poverty and gender.

24. The funding proposal economic and financial analysis (annex 3) develops three ideas on
project concepts based on projects from the ADB: (i) the Lao People’s Democratic Republic:

are examples of large-scale interventions that could serve as vehicles for the delivery of specific
local adaptation solutions promoted by the CRPP, using IF resources provided by GCF.
25. The iTAP acknowledges the completeness of the information regarding the climate
adaptation potential in this funding proposal as well as the alignment with three of the four
principles for demonstrating adaptation potential, as specified in GCF decision B.33/12:
identification, response and alignment. However, the iTAP assesses that the principle of
monitoring and evaluating adaptation outcomes is not yet fulfilled in the extent required by the
GCF Board Decision B.33/12. That said, the iTAP recognizes that this gap can be resolved during
the first year of implementation of the project.
26. Further, the iTAP acknowledges that due to the programmatic approach in this proposal
it is difficult to calculate the exact number of beneficiaries, and noted the clarification provided
by the AE for arriving at the figures in Table 1. However, the iTAP sees a possibility for over or
underestimating the number of beneficiaries at the present stage.
27. The iTAP assesses the adaptation impact potential as high and includes the
improvement of the MEL system during the first year of project implementation as a condition
for endorsement. Beyond the aspects already outlined in annex 11, the MEL system will include:
(a) A complete monitoring and evaluation system that allows assessment of adaptation
outcomes, including:
(i) The corresponding methods for the steps of data gathering, analysis and
interpretation, and the frequency of each step;
(ii) The roles and responsibilities for the steps above;
(iii) A method to assess progress in addressing the climate-gender-poverty nexus
that has been included as a key element of this funding proposal; and
(iv) A clear method for quantifying the number of direct and indirect beneficiaries;
and
(b) A strategy for linking the MEL of the CRPP’s national projects to the national systems for
monitoring and reporting progress under the United Nations Framework Convention on
Climate Change (UNFCCC).

1.2 Paradigm shift potential Scale: Medium
28. The funding proposal claims a “contribution to transformational change by: (i)
mobilizing large-scale public investments that support community-level adaptation of poor and
vulnerable people; (ii) developing national and local policies, plans, and programs that promote
financing for community-led adaptation; and (iii) increasing the meaningful participation of
poor women and men in resilience-related decision-making” (annex 11).
29. The funding proposal identifies four barriers to strengthening the climate resilience of
poor and vulnerable people in Asia and the Pacific Region:
(a) Lack of suitable, locally relevant and accessible climate information to inform resilience
investments targeted at the poor;
(b) Limited access to adaptation finance for implementing local solutions at scale;
(c) Weak institutional and technical capacity to mainstream climate adaptation in policy,
planning and implementing adaptation solutions; and
(d) Negative perceptions and risk aversion around community-level actions.
30. As a response to these barriers, the funding proposal proposes three pathways of
change. The first is strengthening the enabling environment for financing and implementing
pro-poor local adaptation measures at scale in the participating countries (Outputs 1 and 2).
The second pathway is mobilizing pro-poor adaptation finance at scale (Outputs 3 and 4) and
the third pathway for change is implementing large-scale pro-poor adaptation solutions to build
long-term capacity to deal with climate change shocks and stresses (Outputs 5 and 6).
31. According to the funding proposal, the components of the project are aimed at
operationalizing these pathways of change. The first component, the funding proposal CRPP
Trust Fund (no GCF contribution) will finance the three outputs looking at improving the
enabling conditions in the participating countries and securing a regulatory framework and
policies that facilitate adaptation to climate change. These three outputs are:
(a) Knowledge and action research on climate risk-informed pro-poor community-level
solutions strengthened;
(b) Institutional and community capacity to develop and deliver climate adaptation
investments at community level strengthened; and
(c) Inclusive and pro-poor adaptation investment projects identified and prepared.
32. The budget allocates USD 72.5 million for activities related to these outputs. Even if the
amount per country will not cover all costs for preparing and enforcing an institutional
framework that fully enables adaptation to climate change at the national, subnational and local
levels, the iTAP considers that the CRPP will contribute to building up and/or improving the
institutional framework at the national level. However, the iTAP is less confident that this will
lead in all countries to the establishment or improvement of institutional frameworks at the
subnational and local levels, where the second component of the CRPP will invest.
33. The second component of the funding proposal is the CRPP Investment Fund, where the
GCF funding will be placed. This component will finance the implementation projects
promoting:
(a) Information and systems for delivering applied climate-risk informed investments at
scale improved;
(b) Climate resilient pro-poor livelihoods investments implemented; and
(c) Climate adaptation pro-poor infrastructure implemented.

=== PAGE 191 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.06
Page 191
34. Almost 90 per cent of the total budget is allocated to the IF (USD 668.5 million out of a
total of USD 750 million).
35. It is promising that one of the eligibility criteria for proposals in the CRPP IF is a
paradigm shift potential defined as “the potential of the project to catalyse impact beyond a one-
off project investment” (annex 2.4 – eligibility criteria), and that, in line with this definition, the
project proposals will have to demonstrate sustainability in the long run, replicability and
innovation potential.
36. Further, because these projects will be implemented by the corresponding ministries in
the host countries, the iTAP sees a potential for replication and upscaling. However, this
potential is reduced by the low allocation of resources to training and learning (2.5 per cent of
the total amount for training, workshops and conferences, and 1.2 per cent for monitoring,
evaluation and learning) and the low number of beneficiaries in percentage of the total
population in most participating countries (see table 1).
37. The iTAP assesses that other factors will further reduce the paradigm shift potential.
First, the lack of a strategy for generating long-term adaptation finance at a programmatic level,
which is one of the key barriers identified in the theory of change. The iTAP recognizes that the
funding proposal mentions potential participation of the private sector and the need for
securing long-term financing sources (private or public), but there is no dedicated activity on
preparing and/or testing financing mechanisms for adaptation in the participating countries
that could contribute to long-term funding for those practices identified as resilient to climate
change.
38. Second, the iTAP noticed that the project concepts presented in the funding proposal
and in annex 2.3 are based on existing ADB projects, which implies a certain level of
continuation of business-as-usual for activities in a development bank. Although this is deemed
as a synergy between multilateral organizations and does not challenge the quality of the
projects, at the same time it reduces their innovative character.
39. Due to the above-mentioned reasons, the iTAP assesses the paradigm shift potential of
the CRPP funding proposal as medium.
1.3 Sustainable development potential Scale: High
40. Funded in 1966, the ADB has a long tradition of promoting sustainable development in
its member countries. The current funding proposal is based on and uses both lessons learned
and competences resulting from this experience. This is clearly reflected in the design of the
funding proposal as addressing the interface between the Paris Agreement , the Agenda 2030
and the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction.
Programme level
41. Based on the suggested project concepts included in the funding proposal, the iTAP
assesses that implementation of the proposed programme can contribute to achieving several
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) including, SDG 1: no poverty; SDG 5: gender equality;
SDG 10: reduced inequalities; and SDG 13: climate action. Contribution to further SDGs can be
achieved in the specific projects, for instance the concept for Papua New Guinea will address
SGD 4: quality education.
42. Economic co-benefits: The funding proposal aims at facilitating access to finance for
poor people in order to be trained for and/or to participate in climate resilient economic
activities including construction or agriculture. Therefore, the CRPP will secure income to
vulnerable households during implementation of the projects. According to the exit strategy of
the specific projects it is possible that such income may continue in the long term.

=== PAGE 192 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.06
Page 192
43. Social co-benefits: The CRPP focuses on reducing the vulnerability of people affected by
poverty, with special attention to vulnerable women. Depending on the characteristics of the
specific projects, the CRPP can promote additional social co-benefits including access to
decision-making, improvements in social protection systems, access to education and training,
or reduction of disaster risks and, last but not least, securing life through access to multipurpose
emergency shelters.
44. Environmental co-benefits: Several activities included in this proposal can have positive
environmental co-benefits including biodiversity conservation, soil protection or promoting and
securing other environmental services. Activities like the promotion of climate resilient
agroecological systems (Output 5) or the use of ecosystem-based infrastructure and nature-
based adaptation measures (Output 6) are examples of such. In addition, and depending on the
specific design of the projects, flood and landslide protection infrastructure can contribute to
protect important ecosystems.
45. Gender-related co-benefits: The promotion of gender equality is reflected in the funding
proposal through its focus on the climate-poverty-gender nexus. Consequently, a stand-alone
eligibility criterion on gender has been included for assessing the projects to be funded through
the CRPP IF, which will benefit from the GCF contribution. Furthermore, projects within the
CRPP have to be categorized as Gender Equity Theme or Effective Gender Mainstreaming. At the
programmatic level a Gender Assessment (annex 8.1) and Gender Plan (annex 8.2) are included.
The Gender Assessment includes a detailed analysis of gender issues per country, providing a
good information basis that justifies considering gender issues as a central element in the
proposal. It is highly recommended to strengthen the assessment, the gender criterion for
project selection, and to secure the inclusion of gender-related indicators in the MEL system, so
that progress in addressing gender-related inequalities can be perceived throughout
programme implementation.
46. The iTAP deems the climate-poverty-gender nexus as a promising approach for
addressing climate change adaptation and vulnerability.
Portfolio level
47. According to the funding proposal, the CRPP IF “will establish and maintain an effective
environmental and social management system to identify, assess, manage, and monitor the
potential environmental and social impacts and risks associated with its portfolio of
investments on climate adaptation” (annex 6, Environmental and Social Management
Framework). This framework is built on the ADB Safeguard Policy Statement and follows the
GCF revised Environmental and Social Policy. The annex further states a list of environmental
and social safeguard requirements and clarifies that during implementation of the CRPP IF
environmental and social due diligence (including sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment
[SEAH] due diligence) will be undertaken by the specific project’s entities.
48. As part of the Environmental and Social Management Framework, the CRPP IF will
respect the ADB Prohibited Investment List, a generic list applied by the bank. The
Environmental and Social Management Framework includes a list of templates and checklists
that should facilitate due diligence and monitoring of environmental and social impacts in a
consistent manner across the projects in the CRPP portfolio.
49. Considering the above, the iTAP assesses the potential contribution of the CRPP to
sustainable development as high, as long as the r4ecommendation from the iTAP with regard to
monitoring, reporting and evaluation of gender issues at the programmatic level is followed.

51. With its focus on the climate-poverty-gender nexus, the CRPP IF is well designed for
contributing to key climate and development concerns in the participating countries.
Furthermore, in the examples of possible projects at the country level included in the funding
proposal, the ADB shows how these projects can address the specific characteristics of the
nexus at the national level.
52. The proposal identifies limited access to adaptation finance for implementing local
solutions at scale as one of the three key barriers to climate change adaptation. With an
investment of over 50 per cent of the total budget in implementing adaptation measures (27.5
per cent civil works and 23.5 per cent equipment), the CRPP will certainly facilitate financial
means for adaptation measures during its implementation period.
53. The inclusion of “needs of the recipient” as an eligibility criterion formalizes the
assessment of the potential to overcome barriers and to strengthen the capacity of local
institutions at the project/portfolio level.
54. Further, several activities in the CRPP are aimed at strengthening institutions and
implementation capacity, especially those under Outputs 1 and 2 (CRPP Trust Fund). These
activities contribute to satisfying the needs of the recipient, even though these are not co-
funded by the GCF contribution.
55. Based on the analysis above, the iTAP assesses the response of the CRPP to the needs of
the recipients as high.

58. In the climate policies of all seven countries there is an explicit or implicit mention of the

and climate change and mentions rural infrastructure, institutional resilience or
insurance schemes for reducing climate and disaster risks; and

adaptation areas.

59. The ADB has currently 12 projects approved by GCF, with a volume of funded activity
financing of USD 947,481,020 and in different stages of implementation. These figures
demonstrate the implementation capacity of the AE.
60. However, the iTAP could not assess the capacity of executing entities because these have
been identified in the funding proposal only in a generic manner and no assessment of the
capacity of possible executive entities for the proposed ideas has been submitted. The funding
proposal states that “for Projects implemented in Host Countries, the government of the Host
Country, acting through its relevant ministry or department, may be the executing agency
and/or implementing agency”. It is noted that among the participating countries uneven
capacity at the ministerial level is to be expected. Where the capacity of the executing or
implementing entities is a matter of concern, the iTAP recommends that capacity development
or other support should be added to project implementation, as appropriate.
61. A further reason for concern is the level of engagement with the civil society
organizations (CSOs) and other relevant stakeholders in each country. Although the iTAP
recognizes the consultations related to the proposal preparation and the stakeholder mapping
and engagement plan (annex 7), three further reasons for concern were observed:
(a) According to information in the proposal, most of the consultation and dialogue
meetings focused on national government representatives, international donors and
international non-governmental organizations. National consultations were also
conducted in some countries with the participation of representatives of the national
level, but it remains unclear if and how the subnational and local levels participated and
if they had any influence on the project design or will have in future. The iTAP also notes
that engagement with representatives of CSOs for preparation of this funding proposal
has been limited;
(b) The language relating to the Stakeholder Engagement Plan (annex 7) is very vague and
would apply to any development initiative. For instance, it is not clear how a legitimate
representation of key stakeholders will be secured and their participation financed
during the design of the projects or how/which subnational authorities will be included,
or how competences and expertise from the subnational and local levels will be used in
the design and implementation phases; and
(c) The main clients of the CRPP Investment Fund will be the ADB User Departments. This
poses the risk that local community representatives and organizations will have less
access to prepare and/or contribute to project proposals to be submitted to the CRPP
Investment Fund.
62. Considering the above, the iTAP assesses the country ownership as medium, and
recommends that the envisaged future stakeholder consultations during the design of the
countries’ projects will be given high priority.
1.6 Efficiency and effectiveness Scale: Medium to High
63. Out of the USD 120 million GCF funds, USD 20 million will be lent in United States dollars
to the Government of Pakistan (loan component). The GCF loan will be disbursed in line with
the project implementation. For the Pakistan project, the project implementation is assumed to
develop over four years as follows: 20 per cent in year 1, 25 per cent each in years 2 and 3 and
30 per cent in year 4. The GCF loan would be for a period of 40 years, including a grace period of
10 years. The GCF loan will be priced at a fixed interest rate of zero per cent for Pakistan (high
concessionality).

=== PAGE 196 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.06
Page 196
64. USD 100 million from GCF funds will be provided as grants in United States dollars to
the Governments of Cambodia, Indonesia, the Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Pakistan,
Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste and Vanuatu.
65. ADB will manage GCF funds through a Trust Fund. All interest income against GCF
investments will flow through GCF and all surplus funds of GCF in the ADB Trust Fund (after the
first-phase repayments commence) will be invested in approved treasury investment vehicles at
an annual interest rate of 1 per cent.
66. The ratio of co-finance in the CRPP IF is USD 1:4.60 for GCF and USD 1:5.25 in the whole
CRPP (Trust Fund and Investment Fund). This high co-funding can also be seen in the expected
distribution of funds for the projects in the pipeline (see figure 1).

67. The CRPP IF will be implemented from 2023 to 2030. Projects seeking financing from IF
will probably need to be approved by the ADB Board between 2024 and 2027 and complete
implementation by 2030. Projects which will be supported by the programme will be identified
in accordance with ADB’s country programming process and selected using the eligibility
criteria presented in this proposal.
68. The funding proposal does not include a co-financing letter from ADB. For every project
with GCF co-financing, the CRPP secretariat/screening committee will ensure that the eligibility
criteria have been met to enable the project to access CRPP funding and ADB will secure the co-
investment ratio is maintained. Figure 2 shows the governance structure of the CRPP including
the roles and responsibilities in selecting projects in the CRPP IF.

69. The iTAP is aware of the financial record of the ADB as a major advantage for increasing
the viability of the CRPP. The iTAP already expressed its concern about the long-term
sustainability of the programme, due to the fact that no long-term financing mechanisms are
foreseen. The iTAP assesses the efficiency and effectiveness of this funding proposal as medium
to high.
II. Overall remarks from the independent Technical Advisory Panel
70. The iTAP notes that the CRPP mirrors the GCF investment criteria as their own
eligibility criteria for the projects to be funded through the Investment Fund. The iTAP
highlights that the level of stringency used when applying and assessing these criteria prior to
funding projects will determine the success of the CRPP, and therefore recommends to the AE to
include indicators related to the GCF sub-criteria, as well as on the additional criterion on
gender, when preparing the guidance for project preparation.
71. The iTAP recognizes that stakeholder consultation is an important part of the envisaged
programme activities, and that the lack of stakeholder engagement constitutes a barrier in the
implementation of climate change adaptation measures. Therefore, the iTAP recommends that
the forthcoming stakeholder consultations and engagement in the respective countries ensure
to include civil society and private sector actors, and to institutionalise stakeholder involvement
processes throughout programme implementation.
72. Further, the iTAP noticed the shared concern with the secretariat with regard to the
monitoring and evaluation plan, as expressed in the draft term sheet that was included in the FP
package submitted to iTAP.
73. The iTAP endorses this full proposal Community Resilience Partnership Program (CRPP)
for approval by the GCF Board, with one condition:
Condition precedent to second disbursement:

=== PAGE 198 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.06
Page 198
74. The Accredited Entity shall design an updated Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning
(MEL) System and provide to the Fund, in a form and substance satisfactory to the GCF
Secretariat, evidence of the adoption of this system. The system shall include the following
aspects, in addition to the requirements of the MEL system submitted with the Funding
Proposal:
(a) a methodology for checking compliance with progress against the eligibility criteria of
the CRPP.
(b) a complete monitoring and evaluation system that allows the Accredited Entity to assess
the adaptation outcomes, including:
(i) the corresponding methods for the steps of data gathering, analysis and
interpretation, and the frequency of the performance of each step;
(ii) the roles and responsibilities for performing the steps above;
(iii) a method to assess progress in addressing the climate-gender-poverty nexus as
described in the Funding Proposal; and
(iv) a clear method for quantifying the number of direct and indirect beneficiaries.
(c) a strategy for linking the MEL system of the CRPP’s national projects to the national
systems for monitoring, evaluation and reporting progress under the UNFCCC in the
relevant Host Countries.

Proposal name: Community Resilience Partnership Program
Accredited entity: Asian Development Bank
Country/(ies): Cambodia, Indonesia, the Lao People’s Democratic Republic,
Papua New Guinea, Pakistan, Timor Leste and Vanuatu
Project/programme size: Large
Impact potential
The AE appreciates that the iTAP recognizes the impact potential of the program to be high and
that the monitoring, evaluation and learning systems of the program can be finalized in the first
year of the program implementation.
Paradigm shift potential
The AE appreciates that the iTAP considers that the program will contribute to strengthening
institutional framework at the national level which is essential for paradigm shift and takes
note of ITAPs views on the need for similar frameworks at the subnational/local level and the
need for new generation of investment projects by development bank’s such as the AE in
concern.
Sustainable development potential
The AE appreciates that the iTAP recognizes that the sustainable development potential of the
program is high and the program’s approach of dealing with climate-poverty-gender nexus as
a promising approach for addressing climate risk and vulnerability.
Needs of the recipient
The AE appreciates that the iTAP recognizes that program’s high responses to the needs of the
recipient countries.
Country ownership
The AE appreciates the iTAP suggestions for the program to strengthen capacity development

1. ABOUT THE ANNEX
This annex presents the gender assessment for the Community Resilience Partnership Program
(CRPP). The Gender Assessment describes the CRPPs guiding principles and approach for
responding to the specific needs of women through its investments in climate change adaptation
before presenting an overview of the gender context in CRPP countries. This provides backdrop
for a description of critical gender issues related to the types of investments that are likely to be
supported by the CRPP, and how such investments can address specific issues that contribute
to women’s vulnerability and help to build their resilience to climate change. These sections
provide the basis for the Gender Action Plan, which identifies specific actions, design features,
and monitoring indicators and targets that will be implemented through the CRPP as part of its
supported investments.
The CRPP program level gender assessment presented in this annex has been informed by
extensive desk-based research carried out as part of the CRPP scoping studies, as well as
consultations with governments and communities and expert insights from ADB and CRPP
implementation partners such as the Huairou Commission, a women-led social movement of
grassroots groups from poor urban, rural and indigenous communities in 45+ countries. As the
CRPP is a large program that will consist of a number of sub-projects that are still at concept
stage, the aim of the assessment presented in this annex is to provide an overview of key issues
related to the sectors and areas of activity of the CRPP. This will serve as a foundation for
developing more detailed and project specific gender assessments as part of the sub-project
design and preparation.
2. INTRODUCTION
Women have a critical role to play in advancing investment in building resilience to climate
change, especially at the local level, and must be recognized as vital drivers of resilient
development. However, social and political inequalities, as well as patriarchal power structures,
remain deeply entrenched, often limiting women’s leadership and participation in decision-
making, and contributing to disproportionate levels of vulnerability and low adaptive capacity
compared to men.
This is particularly the case in poor communities in low income countries as multidimensional
poverty significantly limits women’s ability to confront climate change. In Asia, women account for
80% of all people living on less than $2 per day1, and their economic activities are often highly
concentrated in sectors that are dependent on natural resources such as agriculture. For
example, women represent 73% of the agricultural labor force in Pakistan, and 70% in Papua
New Guinea and the Lao People’s Democratic Republic2. Women also tend to be overly burdened
with household work and caring for children, the sick, and the elderly; women do not always have
the same rights as men to land; women often have less access to financial services, technology,
information, and early warning systems;a and women, particularly rural women, are often held
back from fully participating in their community and in formal decision-making processes. All of
these factors contribute to increased vulnerability and lower adaptive capacity, and are closely
related to socially created gender functions, systemic discriminations, and the power imbalances
between women and men.
a For further details on the specific vulnerability context of women, see Habtezion (2016); Miles and Wiedmaier-Pfister
(2018); and Neumayer and Plümper (2007).

=== PAGE 204 ===
While it is crucial to recognize and address women’s vulnerabilities to climate change and
understand the structural causes for them, it is fundamental to refrain from categorizing women
as innately weak, passive receivers of protection and support. In the past, this approach has
prevented women from being recognized as active agents in resilience-building programs. The
adoption of programs designed on the assumption that women are powerless further exposes
them to climate change shocks and disasters, as well as hinders the realization of women’s rights
to full and equal participation and decision-making3. Women’s unique knowledge, skills, and
perspectives, mean that they can contribute positively to the identification of appropriate
adaptation measures and ensure that they are implemented effectively and efficiently. Women
can also play a leadership role in accessing public and private resources for adaptation, which in
turn can give them recognition within the community and promote their position in the family and
wider society, creating a positive feedback loop for women’s empowerment. There are increasing
examples of grassroots women organizations closely collaborating with local governments to
make use of their knowledge and capacity to assess, prioritize, negotiate, and influence resource
allocation for resilience investments targeted at vulnerable communities4.
3. ADB’s GENDER POLICY FRAMEWORK
Accelerating progress in gender equality in Asia and the Pacific is one of the seven operational
priorities in ADB’s Strategy 2030. ADB recognizes that gender equality is critical in its own right
as well as for helping realize socio-economic development. Strategy 2030 holds that, to achieve
a prosperous, inclusive, resilient, and sustainable region, it is imperative that ADB contributes to
the efforts of accelerating gender equality outcomes in the region in five areas: economic
empowerment, human development, decision-making and leadership, time poverty reduction,
and resilience to external shocks. As such, the CRPP contributes towards the gender operational
priorities of ADB’s Strategy 2030, and achieving the following target - “by 2030, at least 75% of
the number of ADB’s committed operations (on a 3-year rolling average, including both sovereign
and non-sovereign operations) will promote gender equality.”.
ADB has established an institutional framework on gender and development—consisting of its
Gender and Development Policy and Gender Operational Plan (OP2). The Gender Operational
Plan, 2013–2020 is the latest action plan to operationalize the GAD policy. The plan adopts a twin
approach of gender mainstreaming and targeted investments in women and girls.
4. CRPP AND GENDER EQUALITY
4.1 The CRPP’s Approach to Gender Equality
Building women’s resilience to climate change and empowering women through transformational
investments in climate adaptation at the community level are core pillars of the CRPP, reflecting
ADBs commitment to gender equality. This is demonstrated in the CRPP program architecture.
The CRPP is operationalized through the Community Resilience Financing Partnership Facility
(CRFPF) which comprises two core components; (i) a multidonor Trust Fund, which provides
technical assistance and grant resources for improving knowledge and understanding, and
strengthening institutions, processes, financial architecture, and capacity needed for building local
resilience; and (ii) the proposed Investment Fund, which will be co-financed by GCF and
administered by ADB that will provide critical grant and loan resources to implement local
adaptation measures as part of ADB financed investments (sub-projects) in seven countries. The
CRPP Trust Fund includes a dedicated Gender Window that will support the identification,
development, and implementation of investments that have the explicit objective of strengthening
the resilience of women to climate change. As such, support will be provided through (i)
